parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when 3x³ + 5x² − 2x + 7 is divided by (x + 2).
parts.working: Long division: 3x² first (M1), then −x, giving remainder 7 (M1 A1 for quotient, A1 for remainder)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the remainder when 2x⁴ + x³ − 7x + 1 is divided by (2x − 1).
parts.working: The remainder is the value of the polynomial at x = 1/2 (M1): 2/16 + 1/8 − 7/2 + 1 = −9/4 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when 4x³ + 2x² − 3x + 5 is divided by (x + 1).
parts.working: Divide step by step: 4x², then −2x, then −1 (M1 A1); remainder 6 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when 6x³ − 7x² − 4x + 9 is divided by (3x − 2).
parts.working: First term 2x² (M1), then −x and −2 (M1 A1); remainder 5 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The polynomial x⁴ + 2x³ + ax + b, where a and b are constants, is divided by x² + x − 2. The remainder is 3x + 1. Find the quotient and the values of a and b.
parts.working: Divide: quotient x² + x + 1 M1 A1; remainder (a + 1)x + (b + 2) A1; a + 1 = 3, a = 2 A1; b + 2 = 1, b = −1 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using these values of a and b, find the remainder when the polynomial is divided by (x − 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when x⁴ − 2x³ + 5x − 1 is divided by x² − 3.
parts.working: Divide: x² then −2x then +3 (M1 M1 A1); remainder −x + 8 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: When 2x³ + ax² + bx − 4 is divided by x² − 1, the remainder is 3x − 2. Find the values of a and b, and the quotient.
parts.working: Write 2x³ + ax² + bx − 4 = (x² − 1)(2x + c) + 3x − 2 (M1); compare coefficients: x² gives a = c; x gives b = −2 + 3 = 1; constant gives −c − 2 = −4, so c = 2 (M1 A1); hence a = 2, b = 1 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The polynomial x⁴ + px³ + qx² + 1, where p and q are constants, is exactly divisible by x² + x + 1. (a) Find the values of p and q. (b) Hence write the quotient.
parts.working: Remainder must be zero: using x³ ≡ 1 and x² ≡ −x − 1 (mod x² + x + 1) gives (1 − q)x + (p + 1 − q) = 0 (M1 A1 A1); quotient found by division (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The polynomial f(x) = 2x³ + px² − 5x + q, where p and q are constants, has (x − 2) and (2x + 1) as factors. Find the values of p and q.
parts.working: f(2) = 0 gives 4p + q = −6 (M1 A1); f(−1/2) = 0 gives p + 4q = −9 (M1 A1); solving gives p = −1 and q = −2 (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Factorise f(x) completely.
parts.working: f(x) = 2x³ − x² − 5x − 2 and f(−1) = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor (M1); dividing by (x + 1) leaves (x − 2)(2x + 1) (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when x⁴ + 3x³ − x + 2 is divided by x² + x − 1.
parts.working: Divide: x² then 2x then −1 (M1 M1 A1); remainder 2x + 1 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and remainder when 2x³ + x² + 4x + 5 is divided by x² + 1.
parts.working: Long division M1; quotient 2x + 1 A1; remainder 2x + 4 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of the integral of (2x³ + x² + 4x + 5)/(x² + 1) with respect to x from 0 to 1.
parts.working: Integrand = 2x + 1 + 2x/(x² + 1) + 4/(x² + 1) B1; [x² + x] B1; ln(x² + 1) B1; 4 tan⁻¹x B1; = 2 + ln 2 + π A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: When x³ + kx + m is divided by x² + x + 2, the remainder is 2x + 1. Find the values of k and m, and the quotient.
parts.working: Write x³ + kx + m = (x² + x + 2)(x + c) + 2x + 1 (M1); comparing x² terms gives c + 1 = 0, so c = −1 (A1); comparing x terms gives k = c + 4 = 3 (M1 A1); constant terms give m = 2c + 1 = −1 (A1); the quotient is x + c = x − 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when x⁵ + 3x³ − 2 is divided by x² − 1.
parts.working: Using x² ≡ 1 (mod x² − 1) gives the remainder (1 + 3)x − 2 = 4x − 2 (M1 A1); then x⁵ + 3x³ − 2 − (4x − 2) = x(x² − 1)(x² + 4) gives the quotient x³ + 4x (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The polynomial f(x) = x⁴ + px³ + 7x² + qx + 6, where p and q are constants, is divided by x² + 1. The remainder is 2x. It is also given that (x + 1) is a factor of f(x). (a) Find the values of p and q. (b) Show that f(x) = (x + 1)(x³ + 5x² + 2x + 6).
parts.working: (a) With x² ≡ −1 (mod x² + 1), f(x) ≡ (q − p)x + 0, so q − p = 2 (M1 A1); f(−1) = 0 gives p + q = 14 (M1 A1); so p = 6, q = 8 (A1). (b) Expand and compare coefficients (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity t seconds after leaving a fixed point O is v m s⁻¹, where v = 6t − t² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Find the acceleration of the particle when t = 2.
parts.working: a = dv/dt = 6 − 2t M1; = 2 m s⁻² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the 6 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle starts from rest at a point O and moves in a straight line. Its acceleration t seconds later is (4 − 2t) m s⁻². Find an expression for the velocity of the particle in terms of t.
parts.working: v = ∫(4 − 2t) dt = 4t − t² + c M1; v = 0 at t = 0 so c = 0 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the displacement of the particle from O when it next comes to instantaneous rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P moves along a straight line so that its displacement from a fixed point O after t seconds is s m, where s = t³ − 9t² + 24t. Find the values of t when P is at instantaneous rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by P in the first 4 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car moves between two sets of traffic lights in Karachi. It starts from rest and its velocity t seconds later is v m s⁻¹, where v = 0.3t² − 0.02t³. Show that the car comes to rest again when t = 15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum speed of the car.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance between the two sets of traffic lights.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line from rest at O. Its velocity t seconds later is v m s⁻¹, where v = 3√t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. Find the acceleration of the particle when t = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the 4 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle starts from rest at O and moves in a straight line. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 its velocity is v = 1.5t² − 0.25t³ m s⁻¹. For t ≥ 4 it decelerates uniformly, its velocity being v = 24 − 4t, until it comes to rest. Find the maximum acceleration of the particle for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the velocity is continuous at t = 4 and find the time at which the particle comes to rest.
parts.answer: v(4) = 8 in both; rest at t = 6

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the particle.
parts.working: ∫₀⁴(1.5t² − 0.25t³) dt = [0.5t³ − t⁴/16] M1; = 32 − 16 = 16 A1; second stage ½ × 2 × 8 = 8 M1; total 24 m A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line, starting at O. Its velocity after t seconds is v m s⁻¹, where v = t² − 7t + 10. Find the times at which the particle changes its direction of motion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle leaves a point O with velocity 9 m s⁻¹ and moves in a straight line. Its acceleration t seconds later is (6t − 12) m s⁻². Find an expression for the velocity of the particle and its minimum velocity.
parts.working: v = 3t² − 12t + c M1; c = 9 A1; minimum when a = 0, t = 2 M1; v = 12 − 24 + 9 = −3 m s⁻¹ A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the particle returns to O when t = 3, and find the total distance it has travelled by then.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A train travels between two stations. Its velocity t seconds after leaving the first station is v m s⁻¹, where v = kt(100 − t) and k is a constant; it stops at the second station when t = 100. The distance between the stations is 2500 m. Find k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum speed of the train.
parts.working: Maximum at t = 50 M1; v = 0.015 × 50 × 50 = 37.5 m s⁻¹ A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle starts from rest at a point O and moves in a straight line. Its velocity t seconds later is v m s⁻¹, where v = 4 − 16/(t + 2)². Find the initial acceleration of the particle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the displacement of the particle from O when t = 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value that the velocity approaches as t becomes large.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lift in a tall building in Dubai starts from rest and moves upwards. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 its velocity is v = t − 0.25t² m s⁻¹. Find the velocity and the acceleration of the lift when t = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the lift in the first 2 seconds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The lift then moves at constant speed 1 m s⁻¹ and finally slows down to rest, the final stage taking 2 seconds and covering 4/3 m. The lift rises 30 m in total. Find the total time of the journey.
parts.working: Constant-speed distance = 30 − 8/3 = 82/3 m M1; time at constant speed = 82/3 s A1; total = 4 + 82/3 = 94/3 s A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist P passes a point O at time t = 0 and continues along a straight road at a constant speed of 9 m s⁻¹. Two seconds later a motorcyclist Q starts from rest at O and follows P along the same road. The velocity of Q is (t − 2)² m s⁻¹ for t ≥ 2, where t is the time in seconds after P passed O. Writing τ = t − 2, show that Q catches up with P when τ³ − 27τ − 54 = 0.
parts.working: Displacement of Q = ∫(t − 2)² dt = (t − 2)³/3 = τ³/3 M1 A1; P: 9t = 9(τ + 2); τ³/3 = 9τ + 18 ⇒ τ³ − 27τ − 54 = 0 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the time at which Q catches up with P, the distance from O at that moment, and the speed of Q at that moment.
parts.answer: t = 8 s; 72 m from O; Q's speed 36 m s⁻¹
parts.working: (τ − 6)(τ + 3)² = 0 M1; τ = 6, so t = 8 s A1; distance = 9 × 8 = 72 m A1; v_Q = 6² = 36 m s⁻¹ A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle starts from rest at O and moves in a straight line. Its velocity, in m s⁻¹, at time t s is v = 6t − 1.5t² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 and v = −0.5(t − 4)(10 − t) for 4 ≤ t ≤ 10. Find the greatest speed of the particle during the 10 seconds.
parts.working: First stage: 6 − 3t = 0, t = 2, v = 6 M1 A1; second stage: minimum at t = 7, v = −4.5, speed 4.5 M1; greatest speed 6 m s⁻¹ A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the particle and its final distance from O.
parts.answer: Total distance 34 m; finally 2 m from O (on the opposite side of O)
parts.working: ∫₀⁴ = [3t² − 0.5t³] = 16 M1 A1; ∫₄¹⁰ −0.5(t − 4)(10 − t) dt = −18 M1 A1; distance 16 + 18 = 34 m, displacement −2, so 2 m from O A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity at time t s is v = pt² + qt + r m s⁻¹, where p, q and r are constants. Initially its velocity is 5 m s⁻¹ and its acceleration is −6 m s⁻². It is at instantaneous rest when t = 1. Find p, q and r.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance between the two positions where the particle is at instantaneous rest.
parts.working: (t − 1)(t − 5) = 0, second rest at t = 5 B1; s = t³/3 − 3t² + 5t M1; s(1) = 7/3, s(5) = −25/3 A1; distance 32/3 m A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line from rest at O. Its velocity after t seconds is v = 4√t − t m s⁻¹ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 16. Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time at which the acceleration of the particle is 0.5 m s⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the particle is at rest when t = 16, and find its distance from O at that time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P moves in a straight line, starting from a point O. Its displacement from O after t seconds is s = t³ − 12t metres. Find the total distance travelled by P in the first 4 seconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact time at which P returns to O, and its acceleration at that moment, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A metro train starts from rest at a station and accelerates uniformly to a speed of 12 m s⁻¹ in 8 s. It travels at this speed for 20 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest at the next station in 6 s. Sketch the velocity-time graph for the journey.
parts.answer: Trapezium: (0, 0) to (8, 12), horizontal to (28, 12), down to (34, 0)
parts.working: Correct shape B1; values 8, 28, 34 and 12 marked B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance between the two stations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the average speed of the train for the journey, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A girl walks from her home to a shop and back. Her displacement–time graph consists of straight line segments joining the points (0, 0), (10, 50), (25, 50) and (40, 0), where time is in seconds and displacement from home is in metres. Find her velocity in each of the three stages.
parts.answer: 5 m s⁻¹, 0 m s⁻¹, −10/3 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find her average speed and her average velocity for the whole 40 seconds.
parts.answer: Average speed 2.5 m s⁻¹; average velocity 0
parts.working: 100/40 = 2.5 B1; displacement 0 so average velocity 0 B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ decelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. Find the speed of the car at the end of the 5 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The car then travels at a constant speed for 12 s. Find the total distance travelled by the car in the 17 s.
parts.working: Distance while decelerating: ½ × (20 + 10) × 5 = 75 (M1 A1); distance at constant speed: 10 × 12 = 120; total 195 m (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The displacement–time graph of a drone, relative to a fixed point O, consists of three straight line segments. From t = 0 to t = 5 s the displacement increases uniformly from 0 to 15 m. From t = 5 s to t = 9 s the displacement stays at 15 m. From t = 9 s to t = 12 s the displacement decreases uniformly from 15 m to 0. (a) Find the velocity during the first 5 s. (b) Find the total distance travelled in the 12 s. (c) Find the average velocity over the 12 s.
parts.working: (a) gradient = 15/5 = 3 (B1); (b) 15 m out and 15 m back (M1 A1); (c) displacement is zero, so the average velocity is 0 (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lorry leaves a depot and travels 300 m due north in 50 s at constant speed. Find the speed of the lorry during these first 50 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lorry then waits at a junction for 30 s before travelling a further 200 m due north in 40 s at constant speed. Find the total distance travelled in the 120 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the average velocity of the lorry over the whole 120 s, giving your answer in m s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures and stating its direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bus on a route in Islamabad starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 9 m s⁻¹ in 30 s. It then travels at 9 m s⁻¹ for 60 s and decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. (a) Find the total distance travelled. (b) Find the average speed for the whole journey.
parts.working: Area under the velocity–time graph: ½ × 30 × 9 + 9 × 60 + ½ × 10 × 9 = 135 + 540 + 45 = 720 (M1 A1); average speed = 720/100 = 7.2 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to a speed of V m s⁻¹ in 10 s. It then travels at V m s⁻¹ for 40 s before decelerating uniformly to rest in 6 s. The total distance travelled is 1260 m. Use a velocity-time graph to find V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the deceleration of the car.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Car A passes a point X at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹. At the same instant car B starts from rest at X and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² until it reaches 30 m s⁻¹, after which it travels at constant speed. Both cars travel along the same straight road. Sketch on the same axes the velocity-time graphs for the two cars.
parts.answer: A: horizontal line v = 20; B: line from (0, 0) to (12, 30) then horizontal at 30
parts.working: A correct B1; B correct with t = 12 shown B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time at which car B overtakes car A and the distance from X at that time.
parts.working: B reaches 30 m s⁻¹ at t = 12, having travelled 180 m (A has travelled 240 m) M1 A1; 180 + 30(t − 12) = 20t M1; t = 18 s, distance 360 m A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: The velocity–time graph of a particle moving in a straight line from a fixed point O consists of three straight line segments. The velocity increases uniformly from 0 to 8 m s⁻¹ in the first 2 s, stays at 8 m s⁻¹ until t = 6 s, and then decreases uniformly to −4 m s⁻¹ at t = 10 s. (a) Find the displacement of the particle from O at t = 10 s. (b) Find the total distance travelled in the 10 s.
parts.working: Areas: 0 to 2 s, ½ × 2 × 8 = 8; 2 to 6 s, 8 × 4 = 32 (M1 A1); velocity is zero at t = 26/3, so the segment from 6 to 26/3 has area ½ × (8/3) × 8 = 32/3 and the segment from 26/3 to 10 has signed area ½ × (4/3) × (−4) = −8/3 (M1 A1); displacement 48 m (A1); distance 8 + 32 + 32/3 + 8/3 = 160/3 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Car P starts from rest at a point O at t = 0 and its velocity increases uniformly to 15 m s⁻¹ at t = 10 s, after which it moves at a constant 15 m s⁻¹. Car Q starts from rest at O at t = 4 s and accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² in the same direction. (a) Find the time, measured from t = 0, at which Q catches P, giving your answer exactly and then to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the speed of Q at this instant, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: For t ≤ 10, P is at 0.75t² and at t = 10 it is at 75 m (M1); for t ≥ 10, P is at 75 + 15(t − 10) and Q is at 1.5(t − 4)² (M1); equating gives t² − 18t + 66 = 0 (A1); t = 9 + √15 is the root with t > 10 (A1); speed 3(t − 4) = 15 + 3√15 ≈ 26.6 (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A van starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. It travels at this constant speed for 20 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4 s. Find the acceleration during the first 6 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the deceleration during the last 4 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the van during the final 4 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line, starting at O. Its velocity-time graph consists of straight line segments joining (0, 10), (8, −6), (12, −6) and (15, 0), where t is in seconds and v in m s⁻¹. Find the time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest for the first time, and the total distance travelled in the 15 seconds.
parts.working: Gradient −2, so v = 0 at t = 5 B1; area above axis ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 B1; area below: ½ × 3 × 6 + 4 × 6 + ½ × 3 × 6 = 42 M1; total 67 m A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time at which the particle passes back through O, and its final displacement from O.
parts.answer: t = 32/3 s (10.7 s); 17 m on the negative side of O
parts.working: Need 25 m below the axis: 9 m by t = 8, then 16 m more at 6 m s⁻¹ M1; t = 8 + 16/6 = 32/3 s A1; final displacement 25 − 42 = −17 m A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bus starts from rest at one stop and accelerates uniformly at a m s⁻² until its speed is 15 m s⁻¹. It travels at 15 m s⁻¹ and then decelerates uniformly at 2a m s⁻² to rest at the next stop. The journey takes 120 s and the distance between the stops is 1575 m. Show that the total time spent accelerating and decelerating is 22.5/a seconds.
parts.working: Accelerating time 15/a B1; decelerating time 15/(2a) = 7.5/a B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a velocity-time graph to find a.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle starts at O with velocity 12 m s⁻¹. Its velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0, 12) to (6, 0), followed by a straight line from (6, 0) to (10, −8). (a) Find the displacement of the particle from O at t = 10 s. (b) Find the greatest distance of the particle from O during the first 10 s, and the time at which this occurs.
parts.working: Displacement at t = 6 is ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 (M1 A1); from 6 to 10 the area is ½ × 4 × (−8) = −16, so the displacement at t = 10 is 20 (M1 A1); the velocity changes from positive to negative at t = 6, so the greatest distance from O is 36 m at t = 6 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A train starts from rest and its velocity–time graph consists of three straight line segments. The velocity increases uniformly from 0 to V m s⁻¹ in 3 s, remains at V m s⁻¹ for 9 s, and then decreases uniformly to 0 in 6 s. The total distance travelled is 210 m. (a) Find V, giving your answer exactly. (b) Find the acceleration in the first 3 s and the deceleration in the last 6 s, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: (a) V = 140/9 m s⁻¹  (b) 5.19 m s⁻² and 2.59 m s⁻²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with speed 14 m s⁻¹. Find the greatest height reached by the ball.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time taken for the ball to return to the ground.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of time for which the ball is more than 5 m above the ground, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with speed 19.6 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². (a) Find the greatest height reached by the ball. (b) Find the total time for the ball to return to ground level. (c) Find the velocity of the ball at t = 3 s, giving its direction.
parts.working: (a) v² = u² − 2gh with v = 0: h = 19.6²/(2 × 9.8) = 19.6 (M1 A1); (b) time to top is 2 s, so total 4 s (B1); (c) v = 19.6 − 9.8 × 3 = −9.8, so 9.8 m s⁻¹ downwards (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge 20 m above the surface of a river. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². (a) Find the time taken for the stone to reach the water, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the speed of the stone as it hits the water, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: s = ½gt² gives t² = 40/9.8, so t = 2.02 (M1 A1); v² = 2gs = 392, so v = 19.8 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with speed 21 m s⁻¹. Take g = 10 m s⁻². (a) Find the time at which the ball has a velocity of 7 m s⁻¹ upwards. (b) Find the height of the ball at this instant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with speed 12 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.8 m above the ground. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find the speed with which the ball hits the ground, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Taking the downward displacement as 1.8 m after the ball returns through the launch point: v² = u² + 2gs = 144 + 2 × 9.8 × 1.8 (M1); v² = 179.28 (A1); v = 13.4 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A stone is thrown vertically upwards with speed 8 m s⁻¹ from a point at the top of a vertical sea cliff, 40 m above the sea. Find the time taken for the stone to reach the sea, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed with which the stone hits the sea, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle A is projected vertically upwards from a point O with speed 20 m s⁻¹. One second later a particle B is projected vertically upwards from O with speed 25 m s⁻¹. Find the time after A is projected at which the two particles are at the same height.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find this height and the velocity of each particle at that moment.
parts.answer: 20 m; A at rest (0 m s⁻¹), B moving upwards at 15 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is projected vertically upwards with speed 10 m s⁻¹ from a point 30 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m s⁻² and find the time taken for the ball to reach the ground, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Taking upwards as positive, −30 = 10t − 5t² (M1); t² − 2t − 6 = 0 (M1); t = 1 + √7 ≈ 3.65 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is projected vertically upwards from a point O with speed u m s⁻¹. Take g = 10 m s⁻². The ball is at a height of h m above O when t = 1 and again when t = 4 (with t in seconds). (a) Find the values of u and h. (b) Find the time at which the ball returns to O.
parts.working: Height at time t is ut − 5t²: u − 5 = 4u − 80 (M1 A1); u = 25 and h = 20 (A1); returns to O when 25t − 5t² = 0, so t = 5 (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An object is projected vertically upwards with speed 16 m s⁻¹ from the bottom of a well, 12 m below ground level. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find the time taken for the object to reach ground level for the first time.
parts.working: Taking ground level as the origin and upwards as positive, −12 + 16t − 5t² = 0, so 5t² − 16t + 12 = 0 and (5t − 6)(t − 2) = 0 (M1 A1); the first time is t = 1.2 (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the object at this instant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is thrown vertically downwards with speed 4 m s⁻¹ from a window 20 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m s⁻². (a) Find the speed of the ball when it reaches the ground, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the time taken to reach the ground, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A model rocket is launched vertically from rest on level ground. For the first 4 s its engine gives it a constant upward acceleration of 15 m s⁻². The engine then cuts off, and the rocket moves freely under gravity (take g = 10 m s⁻²). (a) Find the height and the speed of the rocket when the engine cuts off. (b) Find the greatest height reached by the rocket and the total time from launch to this greatest height.
parts.answer: (a) 120 m and 60 m s⁻¹  (b) 300 m, 10 s
parts.working: (a) s = ½ × 15 × 4² = 120 and v = 15 × 4 = 60 (M1 A1); after cut-off, 0 = 60² − 2 × 10 × s gives extra height 180 (M1 A1); total height 300 (A1); time 4 + 60/10 = 10 s (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A ball is projected vertically upwards from ground level with speed 25 m s⁻¹. Find the greatest height reached by the ball and the time taken to reach this height.
parts.working: v² = u² − 2gh with v = 0 gives h = 25²/(2 × 10) = 31.25 (M1 A1); time to the top is 25/10 = 2.5 s (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the ball when it is 20 m above the ground on its way down.
parts.working: 20 = 25t − 5t² gives t² − 5t + 4 = 0, so t = 1 or t = 4 (M1 A1); on the way down t = 4 and v = 25 − 40 = −15, so the speed is 15 m s⁻¹ downwards (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A ball P is released from rest at the top of a building 45 m high. At the same instant a ball Q is thrown vertically upwards with speed 18 m s⁻¹ from the ground directly below. Show that the balls meet 2.5 s later, and find their height above the ground when they meet.
parts.working: Distance fallen by P = 5t², height of Q = 18t − 5t² M1; 5t² + 18t − 5t² = 45 M1; t = 2.5 A1; height = 45 − 5(2.5)² = 13.75 m A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that Q is moving downwards when the balls meet, and find the speed of each ball at that moment.
parts.answer: v_Q = −7 m s⁻¹ (downwards, speed 7); P speed 25 m s⁻¹
parts.working: Q reaches its highest point at t = 1.8 s < 2.5 s, so it is moving down B1; v_Q = 18 − 25 = −7, speed 7 m s⁻¹ B1; v_P = 10 × 2.5 = 25 m s⁻¹ B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is projected vertically upwards with speed 14 m s⁻¹ from ground level. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². (a) Find the two times, measured from projection, at which the ball is 5 m above the ground, giving each to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the time between these two instants to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car slows down uniformly from 25 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ while travelling 105 m along a straight road. Find the deceleration of the car.
parts.working: 10² = 25² + 2a(105) M1; a = −2.5, deceleration 2.5 m s⁻² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time taken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist passes a point A at 4 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 0.8 m s⁻² for 10 s. Find her speed at the end of the 10 s and the distance travelled in that time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance she travels during the tenth second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cable car at Murree starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m s⁻² for 20 s. Find its speed at the end of the 20 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the cable car in these 20 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lorry travelling at 18 m s⁻¹ on a motorway in Pakistan brakes uniformly and comes to rest after 12 s. Find the deceleration of the lorry.
parts.working: a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 18)/12 = −1.5, so the deceleration is 1.5 m s⁻² (M1 A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the lorry while it is braking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A motorbike accelerates uniformly from 5 m s⁻¹ to 17 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. (a) Find its acceleration. (b) Find the distance it travels in this time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration 2.5 m s⁻². It passes a point A with speed u m s⁻¹. Six seconds later it has travelled 90 m from A. Find the value of u.
parts.working: s = ut + ½at² gives 90 = 6u + ½ × 2.5 × 36 (M1 A1); 6u = 45, so u = 7.5 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration. It passes point A, then point B 3 s later, then point C a further 2 s later. AB = 24 m and BC = 26 m. Find the acceleration of the particle and its speed at A.
parts.answer: a = 2 m s⁻²; u = 5 m s⁻¹
parts.working: A to B: 24 = 3u + 4.5a M1 A1; A to C: 50 = 5u + 12.5a M1; solving: a = 2 A1, u = 5 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the particle at C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist's speed increases uniformly from 3 m s⁻¹ to 9 m s⁻¹ while she travels 48 m in a straight line. (a) Find her acceleration. (b) Find the time taken for this 48 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. Its displacement s m from a fixed point O after t s is given by s = ut + ½at². It is known that s = 36 when t = 4 and s = 72 when t = 6. (a) Find the values of u and a. (b) Find the speed of the particle when t = 10.
parts.working: 4u + 8a = 36 and 6u + 18a = 72 (M1); solving gives a = 3 and u = 3 (M1 A1); v = u + at = 3 + 3 × 10 = 33 (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A van decelerates uniformly at 4 m s⁻² and comes to rest in a distance of 25 m. Find the speed of the van when it begins to decelerate. Give your answer exactly, then to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. Its speed is 4 m s⁻¹ at t = 2 s and 16 m s⁻¹ at t = 5 s. (a) Find the acceleration. (b) Find the distance travelled between t = 2 s and t = 5 s.
parts.working: (a) a = (16 − 4)/(5 − 2) = 4 (M1 A1); (b) average speed (4 + 16)/2 = 10 for 3 s gives 30 m (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Car P passes a point O travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ and immediately decelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² until it stops. Car Q passes O 4 s after P, travelling at a constant 18 m s⁻¹ in the same direction along the same straight road. Find the time taken for P to stop and the distance from O at which it stops.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student writes 30t − 0.75t² = 18(t − 4) to find when Q reaches P. Explain why this equation does not give the correct answer.
parts.answer: Its positive root is t ≈ 20.6 s > 20 s, but P has already stopped at t = 20, so the formula for P's displacement no longer applies
parts.working: Solves t² − 16t − 96 = 0, t = 8 + 4√10 ≈ 20.6 M1; this is after P stops at t = 20, so the equation is invalid A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the time, measured from when P passes O, at which Q reaches P.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist starts from rest at a point O at time t = 0 and accelerates uniformly at 0.6 m s⁻² along a straight road. At t = 0 a bus is 120 m ahead of O, travelling in the same direction at a constant speed of 12 m s⁻¹. (a) Find the time at which the cyclist catches the bus, giving your answer exactly and then to 3 significant figures. (b) Find the distance of this point from O.
parts.working: Bus position 120 + 12t, cyclist position 0.3t² (M1); 0.3t² − 12t − 120 = 0, so t² − 40t − 400 = 0 (M1); t = 20 ± 20√2, take the positive root (A1); distance 0.3t² = 360 + 240√2 (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. It travels 30 m during its third second of motion and 50 m during its fifth second. (a) Find the initial velocity u and the acceleration a. (b) Find the distance travelled in the first 4 s.
parts.answer: (a) u = 5 m s⁻², a = 10 m s⁻²  (b) 100 m
parts.working: Distance in the nth second is u + a(n − ½): 30 = u + 2.5a and 50 = u + 4.5a (M1 A1); solving gives a = 10 and u = 5 (M1 A1); s = 5 × 4 + ½ × 10 × 16 = 100 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car is travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ when the driver sees a hazard 60 m ahead. There is a reaction time of 0.6 s, during which the car moves at constant speed. After this the car decelerates uniformly at 4 m s⁻² until it stops. (a) Find the total stopping distance. (b) State whether the car stops before reaching the hazard, giving a reason.
parts.answer: (a) 62 m  (b) No: the stopping distance (62 m) is greater than 60 m, so the car reaches the hazard
parts.working: Distance during reaction 0.6 × 20 = 12 m (B1); braking distance v²/(2a) = 400/8 = 50 m (M1 A1); total 62 m (A1); 62 > 60 so the car does not stop in time (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rice mill in Sindh fills bags with a nominal mass of 5 kg. The masses are normally distributed with standard deviation 0.08 kg. An inspector suspects that the mean mass is less than 5 kg. A random sample of 20 bags has mean mass 4.962 kg. Test at the 5% significance level whether the inspector's suspicion is justified.
parts.answer: z = −2.12 < −1.645, so reject H₀: there is evidence that the mean mass is less than 5 kg.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 5, H₁: μ < 5; M1 standardise with 0.08/√20; A1 z = −2.12 (or p = 0.0168); M1 compare with −1.645 (or 0.0168 < 0.05); A1 reject H₀, conclusion in context, not over-assertive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The heights of seedlings of a certain plant after 4 weeks are normally distributed with mean 12.4 cm and standard deviation 1.8 cm. A gardener uses a new fertiliser on 40 randomly chosen seedlings and their mean height after 4 weeks is 12.95 cm. Assuming the standard deviation is unchanged, test at the 5% significance level whether the fertiliser increases the mean height.
parts.answer: z = 1.93 > 1.645, so reject H₀: evidence that the mean height has increased.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 12.4, H₁: μ > 12.4; M1 (12.95 − 12.4)/(1.8/√40); A1 1.93; M1 compare with 1.645; A1 conclusion in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A health magazine claims that university students sleep 8 hours per night on average. A researcher believes the true mean is lower. The number of hours of sleep is normally distributed with standard deviation 1.2 hours. A random sample of 50 students has mean 7.6 hours. Explain why a one-tailed test is appropriate.
parts.answer: The researcher is only looking for evidence that the mean is lower than 8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: z = −2.36 < −1.645, so reject H₀: evidence that the mean sleep time is less than 8 hours.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 8, H₁: μ < 8; M1 (7.6 − 8)/(1.2/√50); A1 −2.36; M1 compare with −1.645; A1 conclusion in context.

practice.stem: A machine fills bags of rice that are nominally 2 kg. The masses of the bags are normally distributed with standard deviation 0.05 kg. A random sample of 25 bags has mean mass 2.012 kg. Test, at the 5% significance level, H₀: μ = 2 against H₁: μ ≠ 2, where μ is the population mean mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a two-tailed test is appropriate here.
parts.answer: The question is whether the mean differs from 2 kg in either direction (it could be too high or too low), so H₁: μ ≠ 2.
parts.working: B1 a difference in either direction is being tested

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test, giving the test statistic and the critical values.
parts.working:
M1 z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) = (2.012 − 2) ÷ (0.05 ÷ 5)
A1 z = 1.20
B1 two-tailed 5% critical values ±1.96

parts.label: c
parts.text: State your conclusion in context.
parts.answer: Since 1.2 lies between −1.96 and 1.96, H₀ is not rejected: there is no evidence at the 5% level that the mean mass of the bags differs from 2 kg.
parts.working:
B1 not significant, H₀ not rejected
B1 conclusion in context (mean mass not shown to differ from 2 kg)

practice.stem: A machine cuts metal rods to a target length of 50 cm. The lengths are normally distributed with standard deviation 2.4 cm. A random sample of 36 rods has mean length 49.6 cm. Test, at the 5% significance level, H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ < 50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the test statistic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the critical value for a one-tailed test at the 5% significance level.
parts.working: B1 lower-tail critical value for 5% is −1.645

parts.label: c
parts.text: State your conclusion.
parts.answer: z = −1 is not less than −1.645, so H₀ is not rejected: there is insufficient evidence that the mean length is less than 50 cm.
parts.working:
B1 z lies outside the critical region, so H₀ is not rejected
B1 conclusion in context

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lifetimes, x hours, of a random sample of 50 batteries of a certain brand were recorded, giving Σx = 1218 and Σx² = 29 900. Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The manufacturer claims that the mean lifetime is 25 hours. Test at the 2% significance level whether the mean lifetime differs from 25 hours.
parts.answer: z = −2.09; |z| < 2.326, so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence that the mean lifetime differs from 25 hours.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 25, H₁: μ ≠ 25; M1 standardise using √(4.684/50); A1 z = −2.09; M1 compare with ±2.326 (two-tailed 2%); A1 do not reject H₀, conclusion in context.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it was not necessary to assume that the lifetimes are normally distributed.
parts.answer: The sample is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem the sample mean is approximately normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A food delivery company says its delivery times have mean 30 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. After a change of routes, a random sample of 36 deliveries has mean 32.1 minutes. Assuming the standard deviation is unchanged, test at the 1% significance level whether the mean delivery time has increased.
parts.answer: z = 2.1 < 2.326, so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence at 1% that the mean has increased.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 30, H₁: μ > 30; M1 (32.1 − 30)/(6/√36); A1 z = 2.1; M1 compare with 2.326; A1 conclusion in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the p-value of the test and state the smallest significance level, to the nearest 0.1%, at which H₀ would be rejected.
parts.working: M1 1 − Φ(2.1); A1 0.0179, so reject at levels above 1.79%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A machine fills bottles with mineral water. The volume is normally distributed with mean 500 ml and standard deviation 4 ml when the machine is working correctly. A random sample of 15 bottles has mean volume 498.1 ml. Test at the 10% significance level whether the mean volume has changed.
parts.answer: z = −1.84; |z| > 1.645, so reject H₀: evidence that the mean volume has changed.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 500, H₁: μ ≠ 500; M1 (498.1 − 500)/(4/√15); A1 −1.84; M1 compare with ±1.645 (5% in each tail); A1 reject H₀, in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption about the sample needed for the test to be valid.
parts.answer: The sample is random (the bottles are chosen independently).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The journey time, x minutes, of a bus route in Karachi was recorded for a random sample of 60 journeys, giving Σ(x − 40) = 90 and Σ(x − 40)² = 1505. Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of the journey time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The bus company states that the mean journey time is 40 minutes. Test at the 1% significance level whether the mean journey time is greater than 40 minutes.
parts.answer: z = 2.41 > 2.326, so reject H₀: evidence that the mean journey time is greater than 40 minutes.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 40, H₁: μ > 40; M1 1.5/√(23.22/60); A1 2.41; M1 compare with 2.326; A1 conclusion in context.

practice.stem: A manufacturer claims its batteries last 25 hours on average. The lifetimes are normally distributed with standard deviation 4 hours. A random sample of 49 batteries has mean lifetime 26.3 hours. Test whether there is evidence that the mean lifetime is greater than 25 hours, with H₀: μ = 25 and H₁: μ > 25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the test statistic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the p-value for this test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using a 10% significance level, state the critical value and your conclusion.
parts.answer: Critical value 1.2816; z = 2.275 > 1.282, so H₀ is rejected: there is evidence at the 10% level that the mean battery life exceeds 25 hours.
parts.working:
B1 critical value 1.2816 for a one-tailed test at 10%
B1 reject H₀, conclusion in context

practice.stem: A clinic claims that the mean waiting time for patients is 12 minutes. The waiting times are normally distributed with standard deviation 3 minutes. After a new booking system is introduced, a random sample of 9 patients has mean waiting time 10.2 minutes. Test, at the 1% significance level, whether the mean waiting time has decreased, using H₀: μ = 12 and H₁: μ < 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the test statistic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the critical value at the 1% significance level for a one-tailed test, and state the conclusion.
parts.answer: Critical value −2.326; z = −1.8 does not fall in the critical region, so H₀ is not rejected at the 1% level.
parts.working:
B1 critical value −2.326
B1 comparison: −1.8 > −2.326
B1 H₀ not rejected: no evidence at the 1% level that the mean waiting time has fallen

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the probability of a Type I error for this test.
parts.working: B1 a Type I error has probability equal to the significance level, 1%

parts.label: a
parts.text: The scores in an aptitude test are normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation 4.5. A coaching centre suspects that students from a certain region score lower on average. A random sample of 25 such students is taken. Find the critical region for the sample mean for a test at the 5% significance level.
parts.working: B1 H₀: μ = 60, H₁: μ < 60; M1 60 − 1.645 × 4.5/√25; A1 58.52; B1 critical region stated as x̄ < 58.52.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sample mean is found to be 58.7. State, with a reason, the conclusion of the test.
parts.answer: 58.7 is not in the critical region, so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence that students from the region score lower.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The masses of mangoes from an orchard are normally distributed with mean 80 g and standard deviation 10 g. After a new irrigation system is installed, a random sample of n mangoes has mean mass 82.5 g. A test at the 5% significance level of H₀: μ = 80 against H₁: μ > 80 leads to rejection of H₀. Find the least possible value of n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A test of H₀: μ = 15 against H₁: μ ≠ 15 is carried out on a normal population with standard deviation 2.4. A random sample of size 30 gives a sample mean of 15.82. Find the p-value of the test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence state the set of significance levels, α%, for which H₀ would be rejected.

practice.stem: The lengths of a particular type of component are normally distributed with standard deviation 4 mm. The manufacturer tests H₀: μ = 20 against H₁: μ ≠ 20 at the 5% significance level, using the sample mean x̄ of a random sample of 25 components.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the critical values for the sample mean x̄ and state the rejection region for x̄.
parts.answer: Reject H₀ if x̄ ≤ 18.43 or x̄ ≥ 21.57
parts.working:
M1 standard error = 4 ÷ √25 = 0.8
M1 critical values 20 ± 1.96 × 0.8 = 20 ± 1.568
A1 x̄ ≤ 18.43 or x̄ ≥ 21.57

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of 25 values gives x̄ = 21.2. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 21.2 is not in the rejection region, so H₀ is not rejected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sample size is increased to 100 and the test is repeated at the same level. Find the new critical values for x̄.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory tests whether the mean breaking strength of its cables has fallen below 400 N, using a 5% significance level. Explain what is meant by a Type I error in this context.
parts.answer: Concluding that the mean breaking strength has fallen below 400 N when in fact it has not.
parts.working: B1 rejecting H₀ when it is true, in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a Type II error in this context.
parts.answer: Concluding that the mean breaking strength has not fallen when in fact it has fallen below 400 N.
parts.working: B1 not rejecting H₀ when it is false, in context.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the probability of making a Type I error.
parts.working: B1 equal to the significance level (the test statistic has a continuous distribution).

parts.label: a

practice.stem: A helpline receives calls at random at a mean rate of 2.4 per 10 minutes. A new advert is used, and 9 calls arrive in a randomly chosen 25-minute period. The number of calls in a 25-minute period is X.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the mean for the 25-minute period under H₀, and find P(X ≥ 9) for this period.
parts.working:
M1 rate 2.4 per 10 min gives 6 per 25 min, so λ = 6
M1 X ~ Po(6)
M1 P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8)
A1 = 0.1528

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased, using H₁: λ > 6. State your conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.153 > 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected: there is insufficient evidence that the call rate has increased.
parts.working:
B1 compare with 0.05
B1 conclusion in context

practice.stem: A test of H₀: λ = 2 against H₁: λ > 2 is based on the number of events X in a fixed period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the critical region X ≥ 5 does not give a significance level of at most 5%.
parts.working:
M1 P(X ≥ 5) = 1 − P(X ≤ 4) for X ~ Po(2)
A1 = 0.0527, which is more than 0.05

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the smallest critical value k for which X ≥ k is a valid critical region at the 5% level, and its significance level.
parts.working:
M1 P(X ≥ 6) = 1 − P(X ≤ 5)
A1 k = 6, significance level 0.0166

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the power of this test when the true mean is 4, that is P(X ≥ 6) for X ~ Po(4).

practice.stem: The number of phone calls received by a small office in one hour is modelled by a Poisson distribution with mean 9. The manager wants to test whether the mean has changed, using the count X in one hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the critical region for a two-tailed test of H₀: λ = 9 against H₁: λ ≠ 9 at the 5% level, with each tail having probability at most 2.5%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A count of 17 is observed in one period. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: H₀ is rejected, since 17 ≥ 16 lies in the critical region.
parts.working: B1 17 is in the upper critical region

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the actual significance level of this two-tailed test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of x, of the expansion of (2 − x/4)⁶. Simplify each coefficient.
parts.working:
B1 64
M1 6 × 2⁵ × (−x/4) and 15 × 2⁴ × (x/4)²
A1 −48x, A1 15x² (A1 A1 for both correct, A1 for one)

parts.working:
M1 general term ⁶Cᵣ (x²)⁶⁻ʳ (−3/x)ʳ, power of x is 12 − 3r
M1 12 − 3r = 0 so r = 4
A1 15 × (−3)⁴ = 1215

parts.text: Expand (1 − 4x)^(−1/2) in ascending powers of x, up to and including the term in x³, simplifying the coefficients.

A1 1 + 2x
A1 6x²
A1 20x³

parts.label: b

parts.label: b

parts.text: In the expansion of (1 + ax)⁷, where a is a positive constant, the coefficient of x² is 189. Find the value of a.

M1 ⁷C₂ a² = 189
A1 21a² = 189, a² = 9

parts.label: b

parts.text: The term independent of x in the expansion of (2x + k/x)⁶, where k is a constant, is 4320. Find the value of k.
parts.working:
M1 middle term ⁶C₃ (2x)³ (k/x)³
A1 160k³ = 4320
A1 k³ = 27, k = 3

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coefficient of x² in the expansion.

parts.label: b

parts.working:
M1 multiply (3 − x) by the result of (a) and collect terms
A1 3/4 − x + 13x²/16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Expand ∛(8 + 3x) in ascending powers of x, up to and including the term in x², simplifying the coefficients.
parts.working:
M1 write as 2(1 + 3x/8)^(1/3)
M1 correct binomial terms with n = 1/3
A1 2 + x/4
A1 −x²/32

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your expansion, with a suitable value of x, to find an approximation to ∛8.3. Give your answer correct to 5 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Expand √(16 − 4x) in ascending powers of x, up to and including the term in x², simplifying each coefficient.
parts.working: Write √(16 − 4x) = 4(1 − x/4)^(1/2). Use (1 + y)^(1/2) = 1 + y/2 − y²/8 + … with y = −x/4: 1 − x/8 − x²/128. Multiply by 4: 4 − x/2 − x²/32. M1 for factor 4 and y = −x/4, A1 for x term, A1 for x² term, A1 for 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the set of values of x for which this expansion is valid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your expansion with x = 0.1 to estimate √15.6, giving your answer correct to 5 decimal places.
parts.working: 4 − 0.05 − 0.01/32 = 3.9496875, so 3.94969 to 5 decimal places (M1 substitution, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Expand (1 + 2x)⁻³ in ascending powers of x, up to and including the term in x³.
parts.working: (1 + y)⁻³ = 1 − 3y + 6y² − 10y³ + … with y = 2x: coefficients −3 × 2 = −6, 6 × 4 = 24, −10 × 8 = −80 (M1 for the binomial coefficients, A1 for −6x and 24x², A1 for −80x³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 + x)(1 + 2x)⁻³.
parts.working: Coefficient of x³ = (coefficient of x³ in (1+2x)⁻³) + (coefficient of x² in (1+2x)⁻³) = −80 + 24 = −56 (M1, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the expansion of (1 + px)ⁿ, where n is a positive integer and p is a constant, the coefficient of x is 20 and the coefficient of x² is 160. Find the values of n and p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coefficient of x³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the expansion of (1 + ax)(1 + bx)^(−2) in ascending powers of x, where a and b are constants with b > 0, the coefficient of x is 1 and the coefficient of x² is −8. Find the values of a and b.
parts.working:
B1 (1 + bx)^(−2) = 1 − 2bx + 3b²x² + …
M1 a − 2b = 1 and 3b² − 2ab = −8
M1 substitute a = 1 + 2b: b² + 2b − 8 = 0
A1 b = 2 (b = −4 rejected)
A1 a = 5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coefficient of x³ and state the set of values of x for which the expansion is valid.
parts.working:
M1 x³ coefficient of (1 + 2x)^(−2) is −4b³ = −32
A1 −32 + 5 × 12 = 28
B1 |x| < 1/2

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the expansion of (1 + px)⁹, where p is a non-zero constant, the coefficient of x² is equal to the coefficient of x³. Show that p = 3/7.
parts.working: Coefficient of x² = C(9,2)p² = 36p²; coefficient of x³ = C(9,3)p³ = 84p³ (M1 both). Equate: 36p² = 84p³, divide by 36p² (p ≠ 0): 1 = (84/36)p gives p = 3/7 (M1 division by p², A1 and A1 for working shown).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using p = 3/7, find the coefficient of x⁴ in the expansion. Give your answer as an exact fraction.

parts.text: The 3rd term of a geometric progression is 28 and the 6th term is −224. Find the common ratio and the first term.
parts.working: ar² = 28 and ar⁵ = −224, so r³ = −8 and r = −2 (M1 for ratio of terms, A1 r = −2). a = 28/4 = 7 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the first 5 terms.

parts.label: a

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the least number of terms of the geometric progression 5 + 10 + 20 + … that must be added for the sum to exceed 100 000.
parts.working:
M1 Sₙ = 5(2ⁿ − 1)
M1 5(2ⁿ − 1) > 100 000 so 2ⁿ > 20 001
M1 use logarithms or trial: n > 14.29
A1 n = 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is dropped from a height of 2.5 m onto a hard floor. After each bounce it rises to 70% of the height from which it last fell. Find the height it reaches after the 4th bounce.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance the ball travels before it comes to rest, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 2nd term of a geometric progression is 6 and the 4th term is 1.5. All the terms of the progression are positive. Find the common ratio and the first term.
parts.working: ar = 6 and ar³ = 1.5 so r² = 1/4. Terms positive gives r > 0, so r = 1/2 (M1 A1). a = 6/(1/2) = 12 (A1). Negative ratio excluded by 'all terms positive' (A1 for the reason).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity of the progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first 3 terms of a geometric progression is 49 and its sum to infinity is 56. Show that the common ratio is 1/2 and find the first term.
parts.working: S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 56 and S₃ = a(1 − r³)/(1 − r) = 49. Dividing: (1 − r³) = 49/56 = 7/8, so r³ = 1/8 and r = 1/2 (M1 A1 for the ratio of the two sums, A1). a = 56 × (1 − 1/2) = 28 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the 6th term of the progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first three terms of a geometric progression are k + 6, k and k − 4, where k is a constant. Find the value of k.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term a and common ratio r, where |r| < 1. Its sum to infinity is 36. A second progression is formed by squaring each term of the first; its sum to infinity is 432. Find a and r.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 1 and common ratio 0.7. Let Sₙ be the sum of the first n terms. Show that S∞ − Sₙ = (10/3) × 0.7ⁿ.
parts.working: S∞ = 1/0.3 = 10/3 and Sₙ = (1 − 0.7ⁿ)/0.3, so S∞ − Sₙ = 0.7ⁿ/0.3 = (10/3)(0.7)ⁿ (M1 for both sums, A1 for the shown result).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which S∞ − Sₙ < 0.01.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write 0.136136136… as the sum of an infinite geometric progression. Hence show that 0.136136136… = 136/999.
parts.working: First term 0.136 and common ratio 0.001 (since each block is 1/1000 of the previous): S∞ = 0.136/(1 − 0.001) = 136/999 (M1 for GP terms, M1 for formula, A1 for 136/999).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence express 2.136136136… as a fraction in its simplest form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first 5 terms of an arithmetic progression is 45 and the 5th term is 15. Find the first term and the common difference.
parts.working: S₅ = (5/2)(2a + 4d) = 45 gives a + 2d = 9. T₅ = a + 4d = 15. Solving: 2d = 6, so d = 3 and a = 3 (M1 for S₅ equation, M1 for solving, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the terms from the 6th term to the 30th term inclusive.
parts.working: S₃₀ − S₅ = 1395 − 45 = 1350, since S₅ = 45 (M1 for the difference of sums, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A common format for a timber stack: the bottom layer has 20 logs, each layer above has 2 fewer logs than the layer below, and the top layer has 2 logs. Find the number of layers.
parts.working: Terms 20, 18, …, 2 form an AP with a = 20, d = −2 and last term 2: n = (2 − 20)/(−2) + 1 = 10 (M1, A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total number of logs in the stack.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal saves Rs 500 in the first week of a year and increases the amount by Rs 150 each week. Find how much he saves in week 26 and his total savings after 26 weeks.

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first n terms of a sequence is given by Sₙ = 3n² + 5n. Find the first term and the second term, and show that the sequence is an arithmetic progression.
parts.working:
B1 u₁ = S₁ = 8
M1 u₂ = S₂ − S₁ = 22 − 8
A1 14
B1 uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = 6n + 2, constant difference 6

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the 15th term.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the sum of the multiples of 5 from 5 to 200 inclusive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is Sₙ = (7n − n²)/2. Find the first term and the common difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of n for which Sₙ is greatest, and state this greatest value.
parts.working: Tₙ = 4 − n, so terms are positive up to n = 3, T₄ = 0 and then negative. S₃ = 6 and S₄ = 6, both the greatest; S₅ = 5 (M1 for using Tₙ or S values, M1 for both values, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The numbers 2k + 1, k + 7 and 3k − 1 are three consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression. Show that k = 14/3.
parts.working: The middle term is the average of the others: 2(k + 7) = (2k + 1) + (3k − 1), so 2k + 14 = 5k, giving k = 14/3 (M1 for the average condition, M1 for simplifying, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the common difference of the progression.
parts.working: With k = 14/3 the terms are 31/3, 35/3, 39/3, so d = 4/3 (M1, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first 10 terms of an arithmetic progression is 175 and the sum of the next 10 terms is 575. Find the first term and the common difference.

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha trains for a marathon. On day 1 she runs 3 km and each day she runs 0.25 km more than the day before, until her daily distance reaches 10 km. After that she runs 10 km every day. Find on which day she first runs 10 km.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance she runs in the first 40 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has first term a and common difference d. The sum of its first 15 terms is 4 times the sum of its first 5 terms. Show that a = 13d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the 10th term is 44, find a and d.
parts.working: T₁₀ = a + 9d = 44. With a = 13d: 22d = 44, so d = 2 and a = 26 (M1 substitution, M1 solving, A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which the nth term is greater than 100.
parts.working: Tₙ = 26 + 2(n − 1) > 100 gives n − 1 > 37, so n ≥ 39 (M1, A1). Check: T₃₈ = 100 (not greater), T₃₉ = 102.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sum of the first 20 terms of an arithmetic progression is 750 and the sum of the first 30 terms is 1305. Find the first term and the common difference.
parts.working: S₂₀ = 10(2a + 19d) = 750 gives 2a + 19d = 75. S₃₀ = 15(2a + 29d) = 1305 gives 2a + 29d = 87. Subtracting: 10d = 12, so d = 1.2 (M1 A1 for the equations, M1 for solving). 2a = 75 − 22.8 gives a = 26.1 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which the nth term exceeds 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first three terms of an arithmetic progression are 5, 5 + d and 5 + 2d. A geometric progression also has first term 5 and second term 10. The third term of the arithmetic progression equals the third term of the geometric progression. Find d.
parts.working: GP ratio 2, so its 3rd term is 5 × 2² = 20. AP: 5 + 2d = 20 gives d = 7.5 (M1 for GP 3rd term, M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The numbers 4, x and 25 are three consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression. Find x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The numbers 4, y and 25 are three consecutive terms of a geometric progression with positive terms. Find y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the sum of the first 5 terms of this geometric progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 3 and common ratio 2. A second progression is arithmetic with first term 3. The 10th term of the arithmetic progression equals the 4th term of the geometric progression. Find the common difference of the arithmetic progression.
parts.working: GP 4th term = 3 × 2³ = 24. AP: 3 + 9d = 24 gives d = 7/3 (M1, M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic progression, giving your answer as an exact fraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first three terms of a geometric progression are 2, 6, 18. The first three terms of an arithmetic progression are 2, 6, 10. Show that every term of the geometric progression is also a term of the arithmetic progression.
parts.answer: Terms are 2·3^(k−1); AP terms are 2 + 4m; 2·3^(k−1) = 2 + 4m gives m = (3^(k−1) − 1)/2, a non-negative integer since 3^(k−1) is odd
parts.working: Write the kth GP term as 2 × 3ᵏ⁻¹. Each AP term is 2 + 4m for m ≥ 0. Solve 2 × 3ᵏ⁻¹ = 2 + 4m to get m = (3ᵏ⁻¹ − 1)/2. Since 3ᵏ⁻¹ is odd, m is a whole number, so each GP term is an AP term (M1 for AP form, M1 for solving, A1 for the integer argument).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the first term of the geometric progression that is greater than 1000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has first term 2 and non-zero common difference d. The 1st, 3rd and 13th terms of the arithmetic progression are the first three terms of a geometric progression. Find d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the first 6 terms of the geometric progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 16 and common ratio 1/2. The sum to infinity of this geometric progression equals the sum of the first 4 terms of an arithmetic progression with first term 2 and common difference d. Find d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the 10th term of the arithmetic progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three numbers form an arithmetic progression with positive common difference d. Their sum is 24 and their product is 480. Show that d² = 4.
parts.working: Terms 8 − d, 8, 8 + d have sum 24 (so middle term 8) and product 8(64 − d²) = 480. So 64 − d² = 60 and d² = 4 (M1 for product, M1 for simplifying, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the three numbers in increasing order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 1st, 4th and 10th terms of an arithmetic progression with first term 2 and common difference d are consecutive terms of a geometric progression. Show that 9d² − 6d = 0.
parts.working: The terms are 2, 2 + 3d and 2 + 9d. Consecutive GP terms: (2 + 3d)² = 2(2 + 9d), so 4 + 12d + 9d² = 4 + 18d and 9d² − 6d = 0 (M1, M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that d ≠ 0, find d and the common ratio of the geometric progression.
parts.working: d = 6/9 = 2/3. The terms are 2, 4, 8 with common ratio 2 (M1 for d, A1 for d, A1 for ratio 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 2 and common ratio 2. An arithmetic progression has first term 2 and common difference 2. Find the smallest n for which the nth term of the geometric progression is greater than the nth term of the arithmetic progression.
parts.working: GP term 2ⁿ, AP term 2n. For n = 2 both are 4; for n = 3, 8 > 6 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the smallest n for which the sum of the first n terms of the geometric progression is greater than the sum of the first n terms of the arithmetic progression.
parts.working: GP sum 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2, AP sum n(n + 1). n = 2: 6 and 6 (not greater). n = 3: 14 and 12, so n = 3 (M1 for both sums, M1 test, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An arithmetic progression and a geometric progression both have first term 12. The second terms of the two progressions are equal. The sum to infinity of the geometric progression is 48. Find the common ratio of the geometric progression and the common difference of the arithmetic progression.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of n for which the sum of the first n terms of the arithmetic progression is zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company offers two pay plans. Plan A pays Rs 20 000 in year 1, increasing by Rs 2500 each year. Plan B pays Rs 20 000 in year 1, increasing by 8% each year. Find the total paid under each plan over 15 years, giving Plan B correct to the nearest rupee.
parts.answer: Plan A: Rs 562 500; Plan B: Rs 543 042

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the first year in which the annual payment under Plan B is greater than under Plan A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 3 and common ratio 1/3. Its sum to infinity equals the sum of the first three terms of an arithmetic progression with first term 3 and common difference d. Find d.
parts.working: Sum to infinity of GP = 3/(1 − 1/3) = 4.5. AP sum of first three terms = (3/2)(2 × 3 + 2d) = 9 + 3d = 4.5, so d = −1.5 (M1 for the GP sum, M1 for the AP sum, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which the sum of the first n terms of this arithmetic progression is negative.
parts.working: Sₙ = (n/2)(6 − 1.5(n − 1)) = 0.75n(5 − n). S₅ = 0, S₆ = −4.5, so the least n is 6 (M1 for a formula for Sₙ, M1 for testing values, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three numbers are in arithmetic progression and their sum is 27. Show that the middle number is 9.
parts.working: Numbers 9 − d, 9, 9 + d have sum 27 = 3 × 9, so the middle number is 9 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The three numbers are in arithmetic progression with sum 27 and positive common difference. If 1 is subtracted from the first number, 1 is subtracted from the second number and 3 is added to the third number, the results form a geometric progression. Find the three original numbers.
parts.working: Numbers 9 − d, 9, 9 + d. GP condition: (8 − d)(12 + d) = 64, so d² + 4d − 32 = 0 and (d + 8)(d − 4) = 0. Positive d gives d = 4; numbers 5, 9, 13 (M1 for GP condition, M1 for quadratic, A1 d = 4, A1 numbers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the common ratio of the resulting geometric progression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term 6 and sum to infinity 8. Show that its common ratio is 1/4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has first term 6. Its 4th term equals the 3rd term of the geometric progression. Find the common difference of the arithmetic progression.

parts.label: c

parts.label: a
parts.text: The output X of a machine is N(50, 4²). Find the value of c such that P(|X − 50| < c) = 0.9. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: P(|X − 50| < c) = 0.9 means P(−c/4 < Z < c/4) = 0.9, so c/4 = 1.645 (two-tailed 0.9 is z = 1.645). c = 4 × 1.645 = 6.58. M1 two-tail idea, M1 z value, A1.

parts.label: b

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X is normally distributed with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Find the value of c such that P(X > c) = 0.2. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: P(Z > z) = 0.2 gives z = 0.8416. c = 100 + 0.8416 × 15 = 112.62. M1 z value, M1 unstandardise, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Five independent values of X are chosen at random. Find the probability that at least two of them are greater than c. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Let Y = number greater than c, Y ~ B(5, 0.2). P(Y ≥ 2) = 1 − 0.8⁵ − 5 × 0.2 × 0.8⁴ = 1 − 0.32768 − 0.4096 = 0.2627 ≈ 0.263. M1 binomial model, M1 complement, M1 terms, A1.

parts.text: It is known that 15% of the population of a town are left-handed. A random sample of 120 people is taken. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that more than 22 of them are left-handed.

parts.text: The probability that a seed of a certain variety of wheat germinates is 0.85. A packet contains 200 seeds. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that at least 165 of the seeds germinate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has distribution B(120, 0.45). Find the mean and variance of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a suitable normal approximation to find P(X ≥ 60). Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Normal approximation N(54, 29.7), with np and nq both greater than 5. Continuity correction: P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Y > 59.5), z = (59.5 − 54)/√29.7 = 1.009. P = 1 − 0.8436 = 0.1564 ≈ 0.156. M1 approximation justified, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair coin is tossed 200 times. Use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability that the number of heads is between 90 and 110 inclusive. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: X ~ B(200, 0.5), approximately N(100, 50). With continuity correction P(89.5 < Y < 110.5): z = ±10.5/√50 = ±1.485, so P = 2 × 0.9312 − 1 = 0.862. M1 mean and variance, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A telephone helpline has 500 calls on a day. Each call has probability 0.12 of not being answered within 30 seconds, independently of the other calls. Use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability that more than 70 calls are not answered within 30 seconds. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: X ~ B(500, 0.12), approximately N(60, 52.8). P(X > 70) = P(X ≥ 71) ≈ P(Y > 70.5), z = (70.5 − 60)/√52.8 = 1.445. P = 1 − 0.9258 = 0.0742. M1 mean and variance, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A survey suggests that 60% of commuters in Karachi travel to work by bus. A random sample of 50 commuters is taken. Show that a normal approximation is appropriate.
parts.working: B1 both np and nq calculated and compared with 5

parts.answer: np = 15 and nq = 45 are both greater than 5, so suitable

parts.text: In a class of 75 students, each student independently has probability 0.4 of obtaining a distinction in a test. Use a suitable normal approximation with continuity correction to find the probability that exactly 30 students obtain a distinction. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: X ~ B(75, 0.4), approximately N(30, 18). P(29.5 < Y < 30.5) with sd 4.243: z = ±0.1179, so P = 2 × 0.0469 = 0.0938. M1 approximation, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At a fruit grading centre in Multan, 70% of mangoes pass the grading. A batch of 180 mangoes is graded. Use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability that at least 130 mangoes pass. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: X ~ B(180, 0.7), approximately N(126, 37.8). P(X ≥ 130) ≈ P(Y > 129.5), z = (129.5 − 126)/√37.8 = 0.569. P = 1 − 0.7153 = 0.2847 ≈ 0.285. M1 mean and variance, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer service centre receives 400 calls in a day. Each call is a complaint with probability 0.3, independently. Use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability that complaints are more than one third of the calls. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Complaints X ~ B(400, 0.3), approximately N(120, 84). More than one third of calls means X > 133.33, so X ≥ 134 and P(Y > 133.5). z = (133.5 − 120)/9.165 = 1.473. P = 1 − 0.9296 = 0.0704. M1 mean, variance, M1 133.33 threshold, M1 continuity correction, M1 standardise, A1.

parts.text: A shop has a probability 0.6 that each customer who enters buys something. Find the smallest number of customers, n, such that the probability that at least 100 customers buy something is at least 0.9. Use a normal approximation with continuity correction, and state your answer as an integer.
parts.working: X ~ B(n, 0.6) ≈ N(0.6n, 0.24n). Need P(X ≥ 100) = P(Y > 99.5) ≥ 0.9, so (0.6n − 99.5)/√(0.24n) ≥ 1.2816. Trial: n = 179 gives 0.8860 (fails); n = 180 gives 0.9020 (works). M1 mean and variance, M1 continuity correction, M1 equation with z = 1.2816, M1 trial, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: X has distribution B(250, 0.3). Use a suitable normal approximation with continuity correction to find the smallest integer k such that P(X ≤ k) ≥ 0.95.
parts.working: X ≈ N(75, 52.5), standard deviation 7.246. P(X ≤ k) ≈ P(Y < k + 0.5) ≥ 0.95 requires (k + 0.5 − 75)/7.246 ≥ 1.6449, so k ≥ 86.42. k = 86 gives 0.9438 (fails); k = 87 gives 0.9578 (works). M1 mean and variance, M1 continuity correction, M1 z = 1.645, M1 trial, A1.

parts.working: Standardising: (50 − μ)/σ = −1.2816 and (70 − μ)/σ = 1.2816. Adding gives μ = 60; subtracting gives 20 = 2.5632σ, σ = 7.80. M1 two equations, M1 solve μ, M1 solve σ, A1.

parts.text: Show that α satisfies the equation x = √(3 + 1/x).

parts.text: The equation x³ + 3x − 7 = 0 has a root α between 1 and 2. Show that the equation can be written as x = ∛(7 − 3x).
parts.working: Rearranging x³ + 3x − 7 = 0 gives x³ = 7 − 3x, so x = ∛(7 − 3x). M1 rearrange, A1.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.working: Values continue 1.4126, 1.4031, 1.4079, 1.4055, 1.4067, … converging to 1.4063, so α = 1.406. M1 converging, A1.
