parts.text: Show that the equation has a root between 0.5 and 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula cₙ₊₁ = 0.4 + 0.6e^(−cₙ), with c₁ = 0.5, to find c correct to 3 significant figures. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation e^x + x = 4 has a root α between 1 and 1.1. Show that α satisfies x = ln(4 − x).
parts.answer: e^x = 4 − x, so x = ln(4 − x)
parts.working: Rearranging e^x = 4 − x gives x = ln(4 − x). M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = ln(4 − x_n), with x₁ = 2, to find x₂ and x₃. Give each value correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find α correct to 3 decimal places, giving each iteration to 4 decimal places until the answer is confirmed.
parts.working: Continuing: 1.0310, 1.0882, 1.0688, 1.0754, 1.0731, 1.0739 → α = 1.074. M1 iterating, M1 convergence check, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x³ + 2x² − 12 = 0 has one real root α. Show that the equation can be written as x = √(12/(x + 2)), and show that α lies between 1.7 and 1.8.
parts.working: x²(x + 2) = 12 so x² = 12/(x + 2) and x = √(12/(x+2)). f(1.7) < 0, f(1.8) > 0 and f is continuous, so root in (1.7, 1.8). M1 rearrange, M1 values, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = √(12/(x_n + 2)) with x₁ = 1.5 to find α correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.
parts.working: x₂ = 1.8516, x₃ = 1.7651, x₄ = 1.7853, x₅ = 1.7805, x₆ = 1.7816, x₇ = 1.7814 → α = 1.781. M1 first iterations, M1 convergence, A1, A1.

practice.stem: The positive constant a is such that ∫₁ᵃ ln x dx = 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a = e^(1 + 1/a).
parts.answer: a ln a − a + 1 = 2, so ln a = 1 + 1/a
parts.working: By parts: ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x (M1 A1). [x ln x − x] from 1 to a = a ln a − a + 1 = 2 (M1). ln a = (a + 1)/a = 1 + 1/a, so a = e^(1 + 1/a) (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that a lies between 3 and 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use an iterative formula based on the equation in part (a), with a₁ = 3.5, to find a correct to 3 decimal places. Give the result of each iteration to 4 decimal places.

practice.stem: The curve y = x² cos x has a stationary point at x = α, where 0 < α < ½π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that α satisfies the equation α = tan⁻¹(2/α).
parts.answer: dy/dx = 2x cos x − x² sin x = 0 gives tan x = 2/x
parts.working: Product rule: dy/dx = 2x cos x − x² sin x (M1 A1). Set to 0, divide by x² cos x: tan x = 2/x, so x = tan⁻¹(2/x) (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = tan⁻¹(2/xₙ), with x₁ = 1, to find α correct to 3 decimal places. Give the result of each iteration to 4 decimal places.

practice.stem:
The equation x³ − 6x + 2 = 0 has a root α between 2 and 2.5. Two rearrangements are suggested:
A: xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ³ + 2)/6
B: xₙ₊₁ = ∛(6xₙ − 2)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting with x₁ = 2.3, find x₂, x₃, x₄ and x₅ using formula A, giving answers to 4 decimal places, and describe what happens.
parts.answer: 2.3000, 2.3612, 2.5273, 3.0237, 4.9409; the values move away from α (diverge)
parts.working: Values 2.3000, 2.3612, 2.5273, 3.0237, 4.9409 (M1). They increase rapidly away from the root, so A does not converge to α (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use formula B with x₁ = 2.3 to find α correct to 2 decimal places, giving each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: By considering the gradient of each iteration function near x = 2.26, explain why B converges but A does not.

practice.stem: The equation eˣ = 2x + 3 has two roots, α > 0 and β < 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = ln(2xₙ + 3), with x₁ = 2, to find α correct to 2 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the formula in part (a) cannot be used to find β, which is close to −1.37.
parts.answer: g′(x) = 2/(2x + 3) ≈ 7.7 at x = −1.37, so |g′| > 1 and iterates move away
parts.working: g(x) = ln(2x + 3), g′(x) = 2/(2x + 3) (M1). At x ≈ −1.37 this is about 7.7 > 1, so the iteration diverges from β (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = ½(e^(xₙ) − 3), with x₁ = −1, to find β correct to 2 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

practice.stem: The sequence defined by xₙ₊₁ = (2xₙ³ + 5)/(3xₙ² + 1), with x₁ = 1.5, converges to α.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that α is a root of the equation x³ + x − 5 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that x³ + x − 5 = 0 has only one real root.
parts.answer: Derivative 3x² + 1 > 0, so the function is increasing
parts.working: d/dx(x³ + x − 5) = 3x² + 1 > 0 for all x (M1), so the curve crosses the x-axis once only (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the iteration to find α correct to 4 decimal places, giving each iteration to 5 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x³ + x − 4 = 0 has a root α between 1 and 2. Show that the Newton–Raphson iteration can be written as x_{n+1} = (2x_n³ + 4)/(3x_n² + 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iteration with x₁ = 1.5 to find α correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation f(x) = 0 has a root between 2 and 3.
parts.working: f(2) = 8 − 8 − 2 = −2, f(3) = 27 − 12 − 2 = 13 (M1). Sign change and f continuous (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation also has a root between −1 and 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show by calculation that the equation eˣ = 5 − x has a root between 1 and 2.
parts.working: Let f(x) = eˣ + x − 5 (M1). f(1) = −1.28, f(2) = 4.39; sign change (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By considering the graphs of y = eˣ and y = 5 − x, explain why this is the only root.
parts.answer: y = eˣ is increasing and y = 5 − x is decreasing, so they cross once
parts.working: eˣ increases for all x (B1); 5 − x decreases for all x, so they meet exactly once (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: By sketching the graphs of y = ln x and y = 3 − x on the same axes, state the number of roots of the equation ln x = 3 − x.
parts.working: ln x is increasing for x > 0, 3 − x is decreasing (B1); the graphs cross once (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that this root lies between 2 and 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By sketching the graphs of y = cos x and y = x², where x is in radians, state the number of real roots of the equation cos x = x².
parts.working: Both graphs are symmetrical about the y-axis (B1); they cross once for x > 0 and once for x < 0 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that the positive root lies between 0.8 and 0.9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x³ − 9x + 1 = 0 has three real roots. Show that one root lies between 2 and 3, and that another lies between 0 and 1.
parts.working: Sign changes at both intervals; f is continuous, so each interval contains a root. M1 both f-values, A1 both intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the third root lies between −4 and −3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that x = 2 is a root of the equation 2ˣ = x + 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation has another root between −2 and −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By sketching the graphs of y = eˣ and y = 2/x, show that the equation eˣ = 2/x has exactly one real root.
parts.answer: For x < 0, 2/x < 0 < eˣ, no root; for x > 0, eˣ increases and 2/x decreases, so exactly one crossing
parts.working: Sketch shape of both graphs (B1). No intersection for x < 0 since eˣ > 0 > 2/x (B1). One intersection for x > 0 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the root lies between 0.8 and 0.9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By sketching the graphs of y = ln(x + 1) and y = 4 − x² for x > −1, show that the equation ln(x + 1) = 4 − x² has exactly one root.
parts.answer: ln(x + 1) is increasing from −∞; 4 − x² is a ∩ parabola; they cross once, for some x > 0
parts.working: Correct shape of y = ln(x + 1) with asymptote x = −1 (B1). Correct parabola (B1). Near x = −1 the log graph is below the parabola, and they cross once for x > 0 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that the root lies between 1.7 and 1.8.

practice.stem: The curve y = x sin x, for 0 < x < π, has a maximum point at x = α.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that α satisfies the equation tan α = −α.
parts.answer: dy/dx = sin x + x cos x = 0 gives tan x = −x
parts.working: dy/dx = sin x + x cos x (M1 A1). = 0, divide by cos x: tan x = −x (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that α lies between 2 and 2.1.
parts.answer: sin x + x cos x: at 2 it is 0.077, at 2.1 it is −0.197
parts.working: g(x) = sin x + x cos x: g(2) = 0.077 > 0, g(2.1) = −0.197 < 0 (M1). Sign change, so dy/dx = 0 between 2 and 2.1 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation x³ + 2x − 7 = 0 has exactly one real root.
parts.working: f′(x) = 3x² + 2 (M1), always positive, so f is increasing and crosses the axis once (A1).

parts.label: b

parts.text: Show that the equation f(x) = 0 has a root α between 1.6 and 1.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By calculating f(1.65), state whether α is closer to 1.6 or to 1.7.
parts.answer: f(1.65) = −0.183 < 0, so α lies between 1.65 and 1.7: closer to 1.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x eˣ = 2 has a root α. Show that α lies between 0.8 and 0.9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that α lies between 0.85 and 0.86, and hence state α correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x tan x = 1, where x is in radians, has a root α between 0.8 and 0.9. Show that α lies between 0.86 and 0.87.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the root α correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x⁴ + x − 3 = 0 has a positive root α. Show that α lies between 1.1 and 1.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the root is 1.16 correct to 2 decimal places, by considering the sign of f(1.155) and f(1.165).
parts.answer: f(1.155) < 0 and f(1.165) > 0, so α lies between 1.155 and 1.165, and α = 1.16 to 2 d.p.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By considering the graphs of y = sec x and y = 3 − x² for 0 ≤ x < ½π, show that the equation sec x = 3 − x² has exactly one root in this interval.
parts.answer: At x = 0, sec x = 1 < 3; sec x increases (to ∞) while 3 − x² decreases, so one crossing
parts.working: sec 0 = 1 below 3 − 0 = 3 (B1). sec x is increasing and tends to infinity as x → ½π (B1); 3 − x² decreases, so they cross exactly once (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that this root lies between 1 and 1.1.

practice.stem: The curves y = 4 − x² and y = e^(−x) meet at two points, with x-coordinates α and β, where α < 0 < β.

practice.stem: f(x) = tan x − 2, where x is in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student finds that f(1.5) > 0 and f(1.6) < 0 and says that the equation f(x) = 0 has a root between 1.5 and 1.6. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: tan x has a vertical asymptote at x = ½π ≈ 1.571 in this interval, so f is not continuous there
parts.working: ½π ≈ 1.571 lies in (1.5, 1.6) (B1); f is discontinuous there, so the sign change comes from the asymptote, not a root (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that the equation has a root between 1 and 1.2, and state its exact value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By sketching the graphs of y = ln x and y = x − 2, show that the equation ln x = x − 2 has two roots.
parts.answer: The line y = x − 2 cuts the curve y = ln x twice: once for 0 < x < 1 and once for x > 1
parts.working: Correct sketches (B1). For small x, ln x is below x − 2; at x = 1, ln x = 0 > −1; for large x the line is above again, so two intersections (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that one root lies between 0.1 and 0.2 and the other between 3 and 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation 2 cos x = x, where x is in radians, has a root in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ π/2. Explain, by considering the graphs of y = 2 cos x and y = x on this interval, why there is exactly one root.
parts.answer: y = 2 cos x decreases from 2 to 0 and y = x increases from 0 to π/2 ≈ 1.57, so the graphs meet exactly once
parts.working: On [0, π/2], 2 cos x falls monotonically from 2 to 0 and x rises from 0 to π/2, so they intersect exactly once. M1 monotonic argument for 2 cos x, M1 for x, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by a sign change that the root lies between 1 and 1.1, and hence find the root correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: f(x) = 2 cos x − x. f(1) = 2cos 1 − 1 = 0.0806, f(1.1) = 2cos 1.1 − 1.1 = −0.1928. Root 1.0299, so 1.0 to 1 d.p. M1 both values, M1 interval, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x⁵ − 3x + 1 = 0 has real roots. Show that it has a root in each of the intervals (−2, −1), (0, 1) and (1, 2).
parts.working: Sign changes in each interval. M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The equation f′(x) = 0 has stationary points at x = ±0.880, correct to 3 decimal places. Use this, together with the value of f at these points, to show that the equation has exactly three real roots.
parts.answer: f(−0.880) = 3.112 > 0 and f(0.880) = −1.112 < 0, so exactly three real roots
parts.working: f′(x) = 5x⁴ − 3 = 0 gives x = ±(3/5)^(1/4) = ±0.880. The cubic-like shape: local max at x = −0.880 with f = 3.112 > 0, local min at x = 0.880 with f = −1.112 < 0. The graph crosses the x-axis once for each monotonic section, giving exactly three roots (f → −∞ as x → −∞ and f → ∞ as x → ∞). M1 stationary points, M1 values, M1 argument, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rectangular sheet of card measures 30 cm by 20 cm. A square of side x cm is cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to make an open box of volume 800 cm³. Show that x³ − 25x² + 150x − 200 = 0.
parts.answer: V = x(30 − 2x)(20 − 2x) = 4x³ − 100x² + 600x; setting V = 800 and dividing by 4 gives x³ − 25x² + 150x − 200 = 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation has a root between 1 and 2. Use the Newton–Raphson method with x₁ = 2 to find this root correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cylindrical tank has radius r cm and height h cm, where h = 2r + 1. The volume of the tank is 500 cm³. Show that r satisfies πr²(2r + 1) = 500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation has a root between 4 and 4.2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the iterative formula r_{n+1} = √(500/(π(2r_n + 1))) with r₁ = 4 to find r correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circle has centre O and radius 6 cm. A chord AB of the circle cuts off a minor segment of area 10 cm², where the angle AOB is θ radians. Show that θ − sin θ = 5/9.
parts.answer: Segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 18(θ − sin θ) = 10, so θ − sin θ = 5/9
parts.working: Segment area = ½ × 36(θ − sin θ) = 18(θ − sin θ). Setting equal to 10 gives θ − sin θ = 10/18 = 5/9. M1 segment formula, M1 r = 6, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula θ_{n+1} = sin θ_n + 5/9 with θ₁ = 1.5 to find θ correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x³ − 2 and the line y = 4 − 2x meet at one point with x > 0. Show that the x-coordinate of this point satisfies x³ + 2x − 6 = 0.
parts.working: Equating the two expressions for y: x³ − 2 = 4 − 2x → x³ + 2x − 6 = 0. M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the root lies between 1 and 2, and use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = ∛(6 − 2x_n) with x₁ = 1.5 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x³ − 2x and the line y = 2 meet at a point with x > 0. Show that the x-coordinate of this point is a root of x³ − 2x − 2 = 0, and show that this root lies between 1.7 and 1.8.
parts.answer: f(1.7) = −0.487 < 0 and f(1.8) = 0.232 > 0, so the root lies between 1.7 and 1.8

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = ∛(2x_n + 2) with x₁ = 1.5 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A loan of Rs 500 000 is repaid by five equal annual payments of Rs 120 000, the first made one year after the loan is taken out. The annual interest rate is r (as a decimal), compounded annually. Show that r = 0.24(1 − (1 + r)⁻⁵).
parts.working: Present value of annuity: 500 000 = 120 000 × (1 − (1 + r)⁻⁵)/r. Dividing by 500 000 and multiplying by r: r = 0.24(1 − (1 + r)⁻⁵). M1 annuity formula, M1 rearrange, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the root lies between 6% and 7%, and use the Newton–Raphson method with r₁ = 0.06 to find r correct to 4 significant figures, giving the rate as a percentage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x³ = 4 cos x has a root α, where x is in radians. Show that α lies between 1.15 and 1.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that α is 1.16 correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x⁵ − x − 2 = 0 has a real root α between 1 and 2. Show that α satisfies x = (x + 2)^(1/5).
parts.working: Rearranging x⁵ = x + 2 and taking the fifth root. B1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = (x_n + 2)^(1/5) with x₁ = 1.2 to find α correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation tan θ = 2θ, where θ is in radians, has a root between 1 and 1.2. Show that θ satisfies θ = arctan(2θ), and show that the root lies between 1 and 1.2.
parts.working: tan θ = 2θ gives θ = arctan(2θ). f(1) = 1.5574 − 2 < 0 and f(1.2) = 2.5722 − 2.4 > 0. M1 rearrange, M1 values, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula θ_{n+1} = arctan(2θ_n) with θ₁ = 1.2 to find θ correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation 2 ln(x + 1) = x has a root between 2 and 3. Show that this root satisfies x = 2 ln(x + 1), and show by calculation that the root lies between 2 and 3.
parts.working: f(2) = 2 ln 3 − 2 = 0.1972; f(3) = 2 ln 4 − 3 = −0.2274. Sign change. M1 rearrange, M1 values, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = 2 ln(x_n + 1) with x₁ = 2.5 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.
parts.working: x₂ = 2.5055, x₃ = 2.5087, x₄ = 2.5105, x₅ = 2.5115, x₆ = 2.5121 → x = 2.513 (the derivative 2/(x + 1) is about 0.6, so the iteration converges). M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation cos x = x³, where x is in radians, has a root α. Show that α lies between 0.8 and 0.9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = ∛(cos x_n) with x₁ = 0.8 to find α correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x eˣ = 3 has a root α. Show that α lies between 1 and 1.1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Newton–Raphson method with x₁ = 1 to find α correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The product of three consecutive values x, x + 1 and x + 2 is 100. Show that x³ + 3x² + 2x − 100 = 0, and show that the equation has a root between 3 and 4.
parts.working: Expanding gives x³ + 3x² + 2x = 100. f(3) = 27 + 27 + 6 − 100 = −40; f(4) = 64 + 48 + 8 − 100 = 20. M1 expand, M1 values, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Newton–Raphson method with x₁ = 4 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box has a square base of side x cm and height (x + 4) cm, and its volume is 60 cm³. Show that x³ + 4x² − 60 = 0, and show that the equation has a root between 2 and 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation can be written as x = √(60/(x + 4)). Use this with x₁ = 3 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

practice.stem: A circle has centre O and radius r cm. Points A and B lie on the circle, and angle AOB = x radians, where 0 < x < π. The area of triangle AOB is two thirds of the area of the sector OAB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that x satisfies the equation x = 1.5 sin x.
parts.answer: ½r² sin x = (2/3)(½r²x) gives x = 1.5 sin x
parts.working: Triangle ½r² sin x, sector ½r²x (B1). ½r² sin x = ⅔ × ½r²x, so sin x = ⅔x, x = 1.5 sin x (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation that the root lies between 1.4 and 1.6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = 1.5 sin xₙ, with x₁ = 1.5, to find x correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a market, the quantity demanded is D = 400e^(−0.1p) and the quantity supplied is S = 3p, where p is the price in rupees. At equilibrium D = S. Show that the price p satisfies 400e^(−0.1p) = 3p, and show that there is a solution between p = 19 and p = 20.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that p = 10 ln(400/(3p)) can be used as an iterative formula that converges, and use it with p₁ = 19 to find p correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Derivative of 10 ln(400/(3p)) is −10/p, which has magnitude about 0.5 near p = 19, so the iteration converges. p₂ = 19.484, p₃ = 19.233, p₄ = 19.362, p₅ = 19.295, p₆ = 19.330, p₇ = 19.312 → p = 19.3. M1 justify, M1 iterate, M1 converge, A1, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation 2ˣ + x = 10 has a root α. Show that α lies between 2 and 3, and show that the equation can be written as x = log₂(10 − x).
parts.answer: f(2) = −4 < 0 and f(3) = 1 > 0; 2ˣ = 10 − x gives x = log₂(10 − x)
parts.working: f(x) = 2ˣ + x − 10. f(2) = 4 + 2 − 10 = −4; f(3) = 8 + 3 − 10 = 1. Rearranging: 2ˣ = 10 − x so x = log₂(10 − x). M1 values, M1 rearrange, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = log₂(10 − x_n) with x₁ = 2.5 to find α correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rectangle has its base on the x-axis, with vertices (−x, 0) and (x, 0), and its top corners on the curve y = 4 − x², where 0 < x < 2. Show that the area of the rectangle is A = 8x − 2x³, and show that the rectangle has area 3 when 2x³ − 8x + 3 = 0.
parts.working: Width 2x and height 4 − x² gives A = 2x(4 − x²) = 8x − 2x³. Setting A = 3 gives 2x³ − 8x + 3 = 0. M1 width and height, M1 area, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation 2x³ − 8x + 3 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the Newton–Raphson method with x₁ = 0.4 to find this root correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curves y = x² and y = 6 − 2 ln x meet at a point where x > 0. Show that the x-coordinate satisfies f(x) = x² − 6 + 2 ln x = 0, and show that this root lies between 2 and 2.5.
parts.working: Equating: x² = 6 − 2 ln x. f(2) = 4 − 6 + 2 ln 2 = −0.614; f(2.5) = 6.25 − 6 + 2 ln 2.5 = 2.083. M1 equation, M1 values, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation can be written as x = √(6 − 2 ln x), and use this iteration with x₁ = 2.1 to find the root correct to 3 decimal places. Give each iteration to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation 3ˣ = x + 5 has a root α. Show that α lies between 1 and 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation can be written as x = ln(x + 5)/ln 3. Use this iteration with x₁ = 1.5 to find α correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of road accidents reported in a city each month has the distribution Po(20). Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that more than 25 accidents are reported in a given month.
parts.working:
B1 N(20, 20)
B1 continuity correction 25.5
M1 z = 5.5/√20 = 1.230
A1 0.109

parts.label: b
parts.text: Justify the use of the approximation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers enter a large supermarket in Islamabad at random at an average rate of 45 per hour. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that between 40 and 50 customers inclusive enter in a given hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of visitors to a museum in Lahore in one hour is modelled by X ~ Po(36). (a) State the distribution of the approximating normal random variable Y, with its mean and variance. (b) Use a suitable normal approximation, with a continuity correction, to find P(X ≤ 30). (c) Give a reason why the normal approximation is suitable here.
parts.answer: (a) Y ~ N(36, 36); (b) 0.180 (3 s.f.); (c) λ = 36 is large, so the Poisson distribution is approximately normal.
parts.working: (a) B1 mean 36 and variance 36, Y ~ N(36, 36). (b) M1 standardise with continuity correction: P(Y < 30.5) = P(Z < (30.5 − 36)/6); M1 z = −0.9167; A1 0.180 (3 s.f.). (c) B1 λ is large (greater than about 10 to 15)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vehicles pass a toll plaza on a motorway at random at an average rate of 52 per hour. The number of vehicles in one hour, X, has the distribution Po(52). Use a suitable approximation to find P(45 ≤ X ≤ 60). Use a continuity correction.
parts.working: M1 mean 52, variance 52, so Y ~ N(52, 52) approximately; M1 P(44.5 < Y < 60.5); M1 standardise: z = (60.5 − 52)/√52 and (44.5 − 52)/√52; A1 0.732 (3 s.f.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A website receives complaints at random at an average rate of 3.5 per day. Find the probability that it receives at most 18 complaints in a 6-day period, using a suitable approximating distribution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The exact Poisson probability is 0.302. Explain why the approximation is reasonable but not exact.
parts.answer: λ = 21 > 15 so a normal approximation is valid, but a discrete, slightly skewed distribution is replaced by a continuous symmetric one

parts.label: a
parts.text: A radioactive source emits particles at random at an average rate of 1.8 per second. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that at least 120 particles are emitted in one minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution Po(30). Using a normal approximation, find the smallest integer k such that P(X > k) < 0.05.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Flaws in a woven carpet occur at random at an average rate of 0.6 per m². Find the probability that a carpet of area 40 m² has fewer than 20 flaws, using a suitable approximation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of complaints received by a call centre in one day has distribution Po(50). Use a normal approximation with a continuity correction to find the probability that fewer than 40 complaints are received on a given day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Emails sent to a school office in one day are random, with a mean of 72 per day, so the number of emails is Po(72). Use a suitable approximation, with a continuity correction, to find the probability that at least 80 emails are sent on a given day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of orders received per day by an online bookshop has the distribution Po(λ), where λ is large. Using a normal approximation with a continuity correction, P(more than 50 orders) = 0.1. Show that λ + 1.282√λ − 50.5 = 0.
parts.working:
B1 50.5
M1 (50.5 − λ)/√λ = 1.282
A1 given equation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find λ.
parts.working:
M1 quadratic in √λ
A1 √λ = 6.494
A1 λ = 42.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: X ~ Po(16). Use a normal approximation to find P(X ≥ 20).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of P(X ≥ 20) using the Poisson distribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage error of the approximation and suggest why it is fairly small.
parts.answer: About 1.6%; λ = 16 is above 15, so the Poisson distribution is nearly symmetric

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calls to a taxi company in Karachi arrive at random at an average rate of 4.5 per hour. Using a suitable approximation, find the probability that more than 40 calls arrive during an 8-hour shift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that more than 40 calls arrive in at least one of 5 independent shifts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has distribution Po(12). (a) Use a normal approximation with a continuity correction to find P(X ≥ 15). (b) Find the exact value of P(X ≥ 15) using the Poisson distribution. (c) Calculate the percentage error in your approximation, relative to the exact value, and comment on its size.
parts.answer: (a) 0.235; (b) 0.228; (c) the approximation is about 3.2% higher than the exact value; the error is small but not negligible because λ = 12 is only moderately large.
parts.working: (a) M1 Y ~ N(12, 12); M1 P(Y > 14.5); M1 z = (14.5 − 12)/√12 = 0.722; A1 0.235 (3 s.f.). (b) M1 1 − P(X ≤ 14); A1 0.228 (3 s.f.). (c) B1 percentage error = (approx − exact)/exact × 100; B1 comment that the error is noticeable because λ = 12 is only moderately large

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four independent random variables X₁, X₂, X₃, X₄ each have distribution Po(10). The total number of events T = X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄ is recorded. (a) State the exact distribution of T. (b) Use a normal approximation with a continuity correction to find P(T > 50).
parts.working: (a) B1 T ~ Po(40), since sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson with the sum of the means. (b) M1 T ≈ N(40, 40); M1 P(T > 50) ≈ P(Y > 50.5); M1 z = (50.5 − 40)/√40 = 1.66; A1 0.0484

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calls to a helpline in Lahore arrive at random at an average rate of 3.2 per 10-minute period. Find the probability that exactly 2 calls arrive in a 10-minute period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least 3 calls arrive in a 10-minute period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that no calls arrive in a 5-minute period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A typist makes errors at random at an average rate of 1.5 per page. Find the probability that a randomly chosen page has no errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that there are at most 2 errors in a 3-page letter.

practice.stem:
The numbers of customers arriving at a pharmacy in Hyderabad were counted in each of 100 one-minute periods.
Number of customers: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Frequency: 14 | 28 | 30 | 16 | 8 | 3 | 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the variance of the number of customers per minute.
parts.working:
B1 Σfx = 189
M1 Σfx² = 531, variance 5.31 − 1.89²
A1 1.89 and 1.74

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these results suggest that a Poisson distribution may be a suitable model.
parts.answer: The mean and the variance are approximately equal

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using a Poisson distribution with mean 1.89, find the expected number of these 100 minutes in which no customers arrived.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potholes on a stretch of road near Multan occur at random, at an average rate of 0.5 per kilometre. Let X be the number of potholes in a 3 km stretch. (a) State the distribution of X, giving its mean. (b) Find P(X = 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Accidents at a busy junction in Karachi happen at random, at an average rate of 0.4 per week. (a) Let Y be the number of accidents in 3 weeks. State the distribution of Y. (b) Find the probability that there are no accidents at the junction in a 3-week period. (c) State one assumption you have made.
parts.answer: (a) Y ~ Po(1.2); (b) 0.3012; (c) accidents occur at random and independently, at a constant average rate.
parts.working: (a) B1 Po(1.2). (b) M1 P(Y = 0) = e^(−1.2); A1 0.3012. (c) B1 accidents are independent and random with a constant mean rate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Faults occur in a roll of cotton cloth from a mill in Faisalabad at an average rate of 0.8 per metre. State two conditions needed for the number of faults in a given length to be modelled by a Poisson distribution.
parts.answer: Faults occur randomly and independently of each other; at a constant average rate (per metre); faults occur singly

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a 5-metre length contains more than 2 faults.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution Po(λ), and P(X = 2) = P(X = 3). Find λ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(X ≥ 2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the variance of X.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cars pass a checkpoint on a rural road at random at an average rate of 4 per minute. Find the probability that exactly 5 cars pass in a given minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that in each of three separate minutes, fewer than 3 cars pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of goals scored by a hockey team in a match has a Poisson distribution with mean λ. It is found that P(X = 0) = 0.2. (a) Find λ, giving your answer correct to 2 decimal places. (b) Find P(X ≥ 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of phone calls, X, received by a help desk in one hour has distribution Po(4.4). (a) State the value of X that is most likely to occur. (b) Find the probability that this value occurs.
parts.working: (a) B1 mode of a Poisson distribution is the integer part of λ, here 4; M1 check P(4) > P(3) and P(4) > P(5). (b) M1 P(X = 4) = e^(−4.4) × 4.4⁴ / 4!; A1 0.1917

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has distribution Po(λ). It is given that P(X = 4) = 2P(X = 3). (a) Show that λ = 8. (b) Find P(X ≤ 5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Small earth tremors are recorded in a region of northern Pakistan at random at an average rate of 2.4 per year. Find the probability that exactly one tremor is recorded in a given 3-month period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the smallest whole number of months, n, for which the probability of recording at least one tremor in n months is greater than 0.95.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of messages received by a shopkeeper's business phone in a 15-minute period has the distribution Po(2.6). Given that at least one message is received in a 15-minute period, find the probability that exactly 2 are received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that at least one message is received, find the probability that at least 2 are received.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of system alerts per day on a server has distribution Po(0.9), independently on different days. (a) Find the probability that on a given day there are at least 2 alerts. (b) Find the expected number of days, out of 30 days, on which there are at least 2 alerts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has distribution Po(λ), where λ > 0. It is given that P(X = 2) = 0.12. (a) Show that λ satisfies λ² e^(−λ) = 0.24. (b) Find both possible values of λ, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: (a) M1 P(X = 2) = e^(−λ)λ²/2; A1 multiply by 2 to get λ²e^(−λ) = 0.24. (b) M1 sketch or tabulate f(λ) = λ²e^(−λ) − 0.24 and find sign changes; M1 numerical root finding gives one root between 0.5 and 1 and one between 4 and 5; A1 λ = 0.693 (3 s.f.) or λ = 4.38 (3 s.f.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: On average 1.2% of LED bulbs made by a factory are faulty. A box contains 250 bulbs. Explain why a Poisson distribution is a suitable approximation for the number of faulty bulbs in the box.
parts.answer: n = 250 is large (> 50) and np = 3 < 5 (p small)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a suitable Poisson approximation to find the probability that the box contains at most 2 faulty bulbs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A newspaper has, on average, one misprint in every 400 words. An article contains 1000 words. State the exact distribution of the number of misprints, X, in the article, and a suitable approximating distribution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the article has at least 2 misprints.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Seeds from a packet are checked at random. On average 1.5% of seeds in such packets fail to germinate. A packet contains 120 seeds. Let X be the number of seeds that fail to germinate, so X ~ B(120, 0.015). (a) Explain why a Poisson distribution is a suitable approximation to this binomial distribution. (b) Use a suitable Poisson approximation to find P(X ≤ 3).
parts.answer: (a) n is large (120) and p is small (0.015), so the binomial can be approximated by a Poisson with λ = np = 1.8; (b) 0.8913

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory makes circuit boards in batches. The probability that a board has a faulty chip is 0.004, independently of other boards. A batch contains 400 boards and Y is the number of faulty boards. (a) State the exact distribution of Y and state a suitable Poisson approximation to it. (b) Use the Poisson approximation to find P(Y = 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rare blood type is found in 0.4% of the population. A blood bank in Karachi tests 800 donors. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that more than 4 donors have this blood type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly 3 donors have this blood type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution B(200, 0.015). Find P(X = 2) using the binomial distribution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(X = 2) using a Poisson approximation, and find the percentage error in using the approximation, relative to the exact value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On average, 1 in 500 smartphones assembled in a factory has a faulty camera. A batch of 1500 phones is checked. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that exactly 4 phones have faulty cameras.
parts.working:
B1 Po(3) with justification n large, np = 3 < 5
M1 e⁻³ × 3⁴/4!
A1 0.168

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at most 1 phone in the batch has a faulty camera.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has distribution B(600, 0.004). (a) Find P(X = 1) using the binomial distribution, giving your answer to 4 significant figures. (b) Find P(X = 1) using a suitable Poisson approximation. (c) Calculate the percentage error in using the Poisson approximation, relative to the exact binomial value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pharmacy dispenses 3000 prescriptions in a month. The probability that any one prescription is labelled wrongly is 1 in 2000, independently. Let W be the number of wrongly labelled prescriptions. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that at least 2 prescriptions are wrongly labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charity raffle sells 800 tickets. Each ticket independently has a probability of 0.0025 of being a winning ticket. (a) State the exact distribution of the number of winning tickets, N. (b) Use a suitable Poisson approximation to find the probability that there is at least one winning ticket.
parts.working: (a) B1 N ~ B(800, 0.0025). (b) M1 approximately Po(2), since np = 2; M1 P(N ≥ 1) = 1 − e^(−2); A1 0.8647

parts.label: a
parts.text: A courier company finds that 0.2% of its parcels are damaged in transit. Using a Poisson approximation, find the least number of parcels n that must be sent for the probability that at least one is damaged to exceed 0.9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a reason why the Poisson approximation is appropriate here.
parts.answer: n is large and p is small, with np ≈ 2.3 < 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each egg packed at a farm in Sheikhupura has probability 0.005 of being broken, independently. A carton contains 360 eggs. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that a carton contains more than 2 broken eggs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shop receives 10 such cartons. Find the probability that at most 1 of them contains more than 2 broken eggs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A seed merchant estimates that 0.5% of seed packets contain a damaged seed, independently between packets. A buyer receives n packets. (a) Show that the number of damaged packets, X, can be approximated by Po(0.005n) and hence that P(X ≥ 1) ≈ 1 − e^(−0.005n). (b) Find the least value of n for which P(X ≥ 1) > 0.6, using this Poisson approximation. (c) Find the least value of n for which the exact binomial probability P(X ≥ 1) > 0.6, and comment on the result.
parts.answer: (a) np = 0.005n, so X ≈ Po(0.005n) and P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − e^(−0.005n); (b) n = 184; (c) exact binomial gives n = 183, so the approximation gives one extra packet; the difference is small because p is small.
parts.working: (a) M1 X ~ B(n, 0.005), λ = np = 0.005n; A1 P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − e^(−0.005n). (b) M1 1 − e^(−0.005n) > 0.6; M1 n > ln 2.5 / 0.005 = 183.3; A1 n = 184. (c) B1 exact: 1 − 0.995ⁿ > 0.6 gives n = 183; B1 comment: e^(−0.005) > 0.995, so the Poisson gives P(X = 0) slightly larger than the binomial value and slightly underestimates P(X ≥ 1); this is why it needs one extra packet, and the error is small because p is small

parts.label: a
parts.text: A delivery company makes 2000 trips in a year. On each trip the probability that the van breaks down is 0.0008, independently. Let B be the number of breakdowns. (a) Explain why a Poisson approximation to B is suitable and state its parameter. (b) Use the approximation to find P(B ≥ 3).
parts.answer: (a) n = 2000 is large and p = 0.0008 is small, so B ≈ Po(1.6); (b) 0.2166

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 50 items is taken from a large batch in which 2% of items are defective. Let D be the number of defective items in the sample. (a) State the distribution of D and find P(D ≥ 3) exactly, giving your answer to 4 decimal places. (b) Find P(D ≥ 3) using a suitable Poisson approximation. (c) Find the percentage error in the approximation, and comment on whether it is suitable for this sample size.
parts.answer: (a) D ~ B(50, 0.02); P(D ≥ 3) = 0.0784; (b) 0.0803; (c) 2.4%, a small error, so the approximation is reasonable here.
parts.working: (a) B1 D ~ B(50, 0.02); M1 1 − [P(D=0) + P(D=1) + P(D=2)]; A1 0.0784. (b) M1 λ = 1; M1 1 − e^(−1)(1 + 1 + ½); A1 0.0803. (c) B1 percentage error = (approx − exact)/exact × 100; B1 comment on the small error with n = 50 and p = 0.02

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher receives personal emails at random at an average rate of 2.5 per hour and work emails independently at random at an average rate of 4.1 per hour. Find the probability that she receives exactly 5 emails in total in a given hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that she receives no work emails and exactly 2 personal emails in a given hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a bakery, cakes sell at random at an average rate of 1.1 per hour and pastries sell at random at an average rate of 0.9 per hour, independently of each other. Let N be the total number of cakes and pastries sold in one hour. (a) State the distribution of N. (b) Find the probability that exactly 2 items are sold in one hour.
parts.working: (a) B1 the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson, with mean 1.1 + 0.9 = 2, so N ~ Po(2). (b) M1 P(N = 2) = e^(−2) × 2²/2!; A1 0.2707

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two entrance gates to a sports stadium are monitored. People enter through gate A at random at an average rate of 0.6 per 15 minutes and through gate B at random at an average rate of 0.4 per 15 minutes, independently. (a) Find the distribution of the total number of people entering through the two gates in a 30-minute period. (b) Find the probability that no one enters through either gate in a 30-minute period. (c) State one assumption you have made.
parts.answer: (a) Po(2); (b) 0.1353; (c) people arrive at random, independently, at constant average rates.
parts.working: (a) B1 mean in 30 min: gate A 1.2 and gate B 0.8, total mean 2, so Po(2). (b) M1 P(X = 0) = e^(−2); A1 0.1353. (c) B1 arrivals at random, independent and at a constant average rate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Machine A in a textile factory breaks down at random at an average rate of 0.3 times per week, and machine B independently at an average rate of 0.5 times per week. Find the probability that there are fewer than 3 breakdowns in total over a 4-week period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that in a 4-week period machine A breaks down exactly once and machine B does not break down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In football matches in a local league, the numbers of goals scored by the home team and by the away team are independent and have distributions Po(1.6) and Po(1.1) respectively. Find the probability that at least 3 goals are scored in a match.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a match ends with a score of 1–1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop in Gujranwala sells electric kettles and irons. Daily sales of kettles have distribution Po(2.2) and daily sales of irons have distribution Po(1.3), independently. Find the probability that more than 8 of these items in total are sold over a 2-day period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption needed for your answer to part (a) to be valid.
parts.answer: Sales of kettles and irons are independent (and sales occur randomly at a constant average rate)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of emails, X, received by a manager in one hour has distribution Po(3). The number of text messages, Y, received by the same manager in one hour has distribution Po(2). X and Y are independent. (a) Find the distribution of X + Y. (b) Find P(X + Y ≤ 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two bus routes stop at the same bus stop. Buses on route 1 arrive at random at an average rate of 1.25 per 10 minutes, and buses on route 2 arrive at random at an average rate of 0.75 per 10 minutes, independently. Find the probability that at least 3 buses arrive in a given 10-minute period.
parts.working: M1 total number of buses ~ Po(1.25 + 0.75) = Po(2); M1 P(total ≥ 3) = 1 − e^(−2)(1 + 2 + 2); A1 0.3233

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let X ~ Po(2) and Y ~ Po(3) be independent. (a) Explain why, given that X + Y = 4, the conditional distribution of X is binomial, and state its parameters. (b) Hence find P(X = 2 | X + Y = 4).
parts.answer: (a) given X + Y = 4, X ~ B(4, 0.4) since X + Y ~ Po(5) and the probability of each event being from X is 2/5; (b) 0.3456
parts.working: (a) M1 X + Y ~ Po(5); M1 conditional distribution of X given total n is B(n, λ/(λ + μ)); A1 B(4, 0.4). (b) M1 C(4,2) × 0.4² × 0.6²; A1 0.3456

parts.label: a
parts.text: Machine A in a bottling plant stops at random at an average rate of 0.6 times per 5 minutes. Machine B, independent of A, stops at random at an average rate of 0.9 times per 10 minutes. (a) Find the distribution of the total number of stops of the two machines in a 20-minute period. (b) Find the probability that there are exactly 6 stops in total in a 20-minute period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three independent random variables each have distribution Po(1.2). Find the probability that their sum is at least 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers arrive at the two counters of a bank branch independently and at random: at counter A at an average rate of 1.2 per 5 minutes and at counter B at 0.8 per 5 minutes. Find the probability that exactly 4 customers arrive in total in a 5-minute period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that exactly 4 customers arrive in a 5-minute period, find the probability that all 4 arrive at counter A.
parts.working:
M1 P(A = 4)P(B = 0)/P(T = 4)
A1 correct expression
A1 0.1296 (= 0.6⁴)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Buses on route A arrive at a stop at random at an average rate of 4 per hour, and buses on route B arrive independently at random at an average rate of 2 per hour. Find the probability that exactly 3 buses arrive in a 30-minute period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly 3 buses arrive in a 30-minute period and at least one of them is from each route.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two independent random variables satisfy X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(2λ). (a) Show that X + Y ~ Po(3λ). (b) Given that P(X + Y = 0) = 0.05, find λ, giving your answer to 4 significant figures. (c) Using this value of λ, find P(X + Y ≥ 2), correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.answer: (a) X + Y has mean 3λ and is Poisson, so Po(3λ); (b) λ = ln 20 / 3 = 0.9986; (c) 0.8002
parts.working: (a) B1 sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with mean λ + 2λ = 3λ. (b) M1 e^(−3λ) = 0.05; M1 3λ = ln 20; A1 λ = 0.9986. (c) M1 P(X + Y ≥ 2) = 1 − e^(−3λ)(1 + 3λ); M1 3λ = ln 20 so P = 1 − 0.05(1 + ln 20); A1 0.8002

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four independent random variables each have distribution Po(0.5). Let S be their sum. (a) State the distribution of S. (b) Find P(S ≥ 2), giving your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The point P(4, −3) lies on the curve y = f(x). State the coordinates of the image of P on the curve y = f(x + 2).
parts.working: B1: translation by 2 units in the negative x-direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordinates of the image of P on the curve y = 3f(x).
parts.working: B1: stretch parallel to the y-axis, y-coordinate multiplied by 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the coordinates of the image of P on the curve y = f(−x) − 1.
parts.working: B1 x-coordinate −4 (reflection in the y-axis); B1 y-coordinate −4 (translation 1 unit down).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe fully the single transformation that maps the curve y = sin x onto the curve y = sin(x/3).
parts.answer: A stretch parallel to the x-axis with scale factor 3 (y-axis invariant).
parts.working: B1 stretch parallel to the x-axis; B1 scale factor 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe fully the single transformation that maps the curve y = sin x onto the curve y = −sin x.

A1 when x = 4.5, f(x) = 0; f(x) grows without bound as x decreases, so range is [0, ∞)

practice.stem: The function k is defined by k(x) = 6/(2x − 1) for x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ ½.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the range of the function k(x) = 6/(2x − 1) for x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ ½.
parts.working:
M1 k(x) is never equal to 0, since the numerator is 6
A1 every other real value is attained, so range is all real y ≠ 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f is defined by f(x) = 3/(x + 2) for x ≥ 1. Find the range of f.
parts.working: B1 f(1) = 1 and f decreasing; B1 f(x) > 0 (tends to 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The function g is defined by g(x) = x² − 1 for x ∈ ℝ. Find an expression for gf(x) and the range of gf.
parts.working: B1 gf(x); M1 use the range of f as the domain of g; A1 −1 < gf(x) ≤ 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f is defined by f(x) = 4 sin x − 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 7π/6. Find the range of f.
parts.working: B1 maximum of sin x is 1 at x = π/2, giving 3; M1 least value of sin x on the domain is sin(7π/6) = −½; A1 −3 ≤ f(x) ≤ 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the largest value of a such that f, with domain 0 ≤ x ≤ a, has an inverse.
parts.working: B1 f is increasing up to x = π/2 only.

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 4 + 2 cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the range of f.
parts.working:
M1 cos x has greatest value 1 (at x = 0) and least value −½ (at x = 2π/3) in this interval
M1 f = 4 + 2 cos x is greatest when cos x = 1, giving 6
A1 least value 4 + 2(−½) = 3, so 3 ≤ f(x) ≤ 6

practice.stem: The function h is defined by h(x) = (x − 2)² + 3 for x ≤ 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the range of h.
parts.working:
M1 for x ≤ 1, (x − 2)² ≥ 1, since x − 2 ≤ −1
A1 least value 1 + 3 = 4 at x = 1, and h(x) increases without bound as x decreases

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = |2x − 6| − 4 for −1 ≤ x ≤ 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the range of f.
parts.working:
M1 f(−1) = |−8| − 4 = 4
M1 f(3) = |0| − 4 = −4 (the least value, where 2x − 6 = 0)
A1 f(5) = |4| − 4 = 0, so the range is −4 ≤ f(x) ≤ 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 6x + c for 1 ≤ x ≤ 7, where c is a constant. The range of f is −4 ≤ f(x) ≤ 12. Find the value of c and verify that the greatest value is 12.
parts.working: M1 minimum at x = 3: c − 9 = −4; A1 c = 5; B1 f(7) = 12 and f(1) = 0 < 12.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why f does not have an inverse, and state the largest domain of the form 3 ≤ x ≤ b, with b ≤ 7, on which it would have one.
parts.answer: f(1) = f(5) = 0, so f is not one-one; on 3 ≤ x ≤ 7 it is one-one (b = 7).
parts.working: B1 not one-one with example; B1 b = 7.

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 2x − 3 for x ≥ k, where k is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the least value of k for which f is one-to-one, and state the range of f.
parts.working:
M1 f(x) = (x − 1)² − 4 has its turning point at x = 1
A1 for one-to-one the domain must be x ≥ 1, so k = 1
A1 minimum value f(1) = −4, so range is f(x) ≥ −4

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = (x − 2)/(x + 1) for x > −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the range of f.
parts.working:
M1 rewrite f(x) = 1 − 3/(x + 1)
M1 for x > −1, 3/(x + 1) > 0, so f(x) < 1
A1 as x → −1 from above, f(x) → −∞; as x → ∞, f(x) → 1, so the range is f(x) < 1

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² + 6x + c for x ≥ −3, where c is a constant. The range of f is f(x) ≥ 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of c for which f has range f(x) ≥ 1.
parts.working:
M1 f(x) = (x + 3)² − 9 + c, so the minimum is at x = −3 (the least x in the domain)
M1 f(−3) = 9 − 18 + c = c − 9
M1 set c − 9 = 1
A1 c = 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 0.4 kg is projected with speed 8 m s⁻¹ up a line of greatest slope of a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Use an energy method to find the distance the particle travels up the plane before coming to instantaneous rest.
parts.working: M1 KE lost = PE gained: ½ × 0.4 × 8² = 0.4 × 10 × d sin 30°. A1 12.8 = 2d. A1 d = 6.4 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the particle when it has travelled 4 m up the plane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A child of mass 30 kg slides from rest down a playground slide in a park in Islamabad. The slide is 5 m long and its top is 2.5 m vertically above its bottom. The child reaches the bottom with speed 5 m s⁻¹. Find the work done against resistance.
parts.working: B1 PE lost = 30 × 10 × 2.5 = 750 J. B1 KE gained = ½ × 30 × 25 = 375 J. B1 WD against resistance = 375 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the resistance is constant, find its magnitude.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block of mass 5 kg is pulled from rest across a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 40 N. The frictional force is 25 N. Find the work done by the 40 N force and the work done against friction when the block has moved 6 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the work-energy principle to find the speed of the block at this point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A cyclist and her bicycle have a total mass of 75 kg. She reaches the bottom of a hill, inclined at an angle α to the horizontal where sin α = 0.06, with speed 8 m s⁻¹ and then free-wheels (does not pedal) up the hill. The resistance to motion is a constant 15 N. Find how far up the hill she travels before coming to rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A ball of mass 0.2 kg is thrown vertically downwards with speed 6 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 25 m above the sea at Gwadar. Ignoring air resistance, use an energy method to find the speed with which the ball hits the sea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In fact the ball does 40 J of work against air resistance. Find the speed with which it hits the sea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A stone of mass 0.8 kg is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with speed 15 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. Use the work–energy principle to find the greatest height of the stone above the ground.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the stone when it is 5 m above the ground. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A van of mass 1200 kg travels along a straight level road. Its speed increases from 8 m s⁻¹ to 14 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 200 m. The resistance to motion is a constant 300 N. Find the work done by the driving force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the average driving force over the 200 m.
parts.working: Average force = work done / distance = 139 200 / 200 = 696 N (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1200 kg travels 400 m down a straight hill inclined at an angle α, where sin α = 0.05, with its engine switched off. The resistance to motion is a constant 300 N. The speed of the car at the top is 10 m s⁻¹. Find the loss in potential energy and the work done against resistance.
parts.answer: PE loss 240 000 J; WD against resistance 120 000 J

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the car at the bottom of the hill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 2 kg is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is 0.3. Find the work done against friction as the particle slides 12 m down the plane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use an energy method to find the speed of the particle after it has slid 12 m.
parts.working: M1 ½ × 2v² = 2 × 10 × 12 sin 25° − WD. A1 correct values. A1 v = 6.01.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A crate of mass 25 kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor in a warehouse by a rope inclined at 20° above the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 80 N and the coefficient of friction is 0.25. Find the normal reaction and the frictional force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The crate passes a point A with speed 1 m s⁻¹. Use the work-energy principle to find its speed after it has moved a further 15 m.
parts.working: M1 WD by tension = 80 cos 20° × 15; WD against friction = F × 15. M1 ½ × 25(v² − 1) = difference. A1 v = 4.94.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A crane on a building site in Lahore raises a load of mass 800 kg vertically from rest through a height of 20 m. At the top the load is moving at 2 m s⁻¹. Ignoring resistances, find the work done by the tension in the cable.
parts.working: B1 PE gain 160 000 J. B1 KE gain 1600 J. B1 total 161 600 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lifting took 40 s. Find the average power of the crane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A skier of mass 70 kg skis down a straight slope of length 200 m at a resort in Malam Jabba. The bottom of the slope is 40 m vertically below the top. The skier's speed increases from 3 m s⁻¹ at the top to 20 m s⁻¹ at the bottom. Find the work done against resistances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the average resistance to motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A ball of mass 0.3 kg is projected horizontally with speed 10 m s⁻¹ from a point 20 m above horizontal ground. Air resistance is negligible. Find the speed with which the ball strikes the ground, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the gain in kinetic energy of the ball during its fall.
parts.working: Initial KE = ½ × 0.3 × 10² = 15 J; KE on striking the ground = ½ × 0.3 × 500 = 75 J. Gain = 75 − 15 = 60 J (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 0.5 kg slides along a rough horizontal floor. It is projected with speed 6 m s⁻¹ and comes to rest after travelling 3.6 m. Find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the floor.
parts.working: Work–energy: friction work = KE lost: F × 3.6 = ½ × 0.5 × 6² = 9 (M1, A1). F = 2.5 N (A1). R = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N, so μ = 2.5/5 = 0.5 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A small block of mass 0.5 kg slides down a smooth curved ramp. It passes the point A with speed 2 m s⁻¹ and reaches the lowest point B, which is 3 m vertically below A. Find the speed of the block at B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: From B the block moves along a rough horizontal surface, where the coefficient of friction is 0.25, and comes to rest at C. Find the distance BC and the work done against friction between B and C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The block is now replaced at A and projected with speed u m s⁻¹ so that it stops at a point 20 m beyond B. Find u.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A block of mass 3 kg is projected with speed 12 m s⁻¹ up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 30°. The coefficient of friction is 0.2. Using the work-energy principle, find the distance the block travels up the plane before coming to rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the block then slides back down, and find its speed when it returns to the point of projection.
parts.answer: tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.2 so it slides back; speed 8.36 m s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 component of weight 15 N > maximum friction 6 cos 30° = 5.20 N. M1 ½ × 3v² = (15 − 5.196)d. A1 correct substitution. A1 v = 8.36.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1500 kg moves up a straight hill inclined at an angle α to the horizontal, where sin α = 0.1. The engine exerts a constant driving force of 2500 N and the resistance to motion is a constant 1500 N. The car passes point A at 25 m s⁻¹ and later passes point B at 15 m s⁻¹. Use the work-energy principle to find the distance AB.
parts.working: M1 work-energy equation with four terms. A1 ½ × 1500(625 − 225) = 1500 × 10 × 0.1d + 1500d − 2500d. A1 300 000 = 500d. A1 d = 600 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done by the driving force between A and B and the increase in potential energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². Particle A of mass 3 kg lies on a rough horizontal table, where the coefficient of friction is 0.2. It is attached to a light inextensible string which passes over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to particle B of mass 2 kg, which hangs freely. The system is released from rest. Use an energy method to find the speed of the particles when B has fallen 1.5 m (A has not reached the pulley).
parts.working: B1 PE lost by B = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J. B1 WD against friction = 0.2 × 30 × 1.5 = 9 J. M1 ½ × (3 + 2)v² = 30 − 9. A1 v² = 8.4. A1 v = 2.90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At this instant the string breaks. Find how much further A travels along the table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 0.5 kg moves up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 20° to the horizontal. It passes point A with speed 9 m s⁻¹ and point B, 5 m further up the plane, with speed 4 m s⁻¹. Find the work done against friction between A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 2 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough plane of length 5 m, inclined at 30° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom of the plane with speed 6 m s⁻¹. Find the work done against friction.
parts.working: Height lost = 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m, so PE lost = 2 × 10 × 2.5 = 50 J (M1). KE gained = ½ × 2 × 36 = 36 J (M1). Work against friction = 50 − 36 = 14 J (A1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Friction force F = 14/5 = 2.8 N (M1). Normal reaction R = 2 × 10 × cos 30° = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 N (M1). μ = 2.8/17.32 = 0.162 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car travels along a straight level motorway at a constant speed of 25 m s⁻¹. The engine is working at 30 kW. Find the resistance to motion.
parts.working: M1 driving force = 30 000 ÷ 25. A1 constant speed so resistance = 1200 N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The resistance is unchanged. Find the power needed to travel at a constant 20 m s⁻¹ on the same road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 1000 kg moves along a straight level road with its engine working at 20 kW. The resistance to motion is 500 N. Find the acceleration of the car at the instant when its speed is 10 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest possible steady speed of the car on this road with the same power and resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist and her bicycle have total mass 80 kg. On a level road her maximum power is 240 W and the resistance to motion is a constant 20 N. Find her greatest steady speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find her acceleration when she is working at 240 W and travelling at 5 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 driving force 48 N. M1 48 − 20 = 80a. A1 0.35.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A train of mass 200 tonnes travels on a straight level track. Its engine has a maximum power of 800 kW and its greatest steady speed is 40 m s⁻¹. Find the resistance to motion, assumed constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the train when it is travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ at full power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A locomotive works at a constant power of 3 MW and exerts a constant driving force of 60 kN. Find the speed of the locomotive, in m s⁻¹.
parts.working: Power = driving force × speed, so v = P/F = 3 000 000/60 000 = 50 m s⁻¹ (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A crane lifts a load of mass 500 kg vertically upwards at a constant speed of 0.6 m s⁻¹. Find the power of the crane's lifting force, in kW.
parts.working: Lifting force = mg = 5000 N (M1). Power = 5000 × 0.6 = 3000 W = 3 kW (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done by the lifting force during 20 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1400 kg travels at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹ up a straight hill inclined at angle α, where sin α = 0.08. The resistance to motion is 700 N. Find the power of the car's engine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the top of the hill the road becomes level. The power and resistance are unchanged. Find the initial acceleration of the car on the level road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 1500 kg moves on a level road. The resistance to motion is kv newtons, where v m s⁻¹ is the speed and k is a constant. With the engine working at 45 kW, the greatest steady speed is 30 m s⁻¹. Find k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the car when it is travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ with the engine working at 45 kW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A lorry of mass 8000 kg has a maximum power of 120 kW. The resistance to motion is 3000 N. Find the greatest steady speed of the lorry up a hill inclined at angle α to the horizontal, where sin α = 1/40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the lorry at an instant when it is moving up the hill at 15 m s⁻¹ with the engine at full power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1250 kg moves down a straight hill inclined at angle α, where sin α = 0.04. Its engine works at 15 kW and the resistance to motion is 900 N. Find the acceleration of the car when its speed is 20 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest steady speed of the car down the hill with the same power and resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A minibus of mass 1100 kg travels at a constant speed of 18 m s⁻¹ up a straight road which rises 1 m for every 25 m travelled along the road. The resistance to motion is 450 N. Find the power of the engine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done by the engine while the minibus travels 500 m along the road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1000 kg moves along a straight level road at 15 m s⁻¹ with its engine working at 30 kW. The resistance to motion is 600 N. Find the acceleration of the car.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pump in Thar raises water from a well at a rate of 25 kg per second through a vertical height of 12 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find the useful power output of the pump, in kW.
parts.working: Useful power = mgh per second = 25 × 10 × 12 = 3000 W = 3 kW (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pump has an efficiency of 60%. Find the power input to the pump, in kW.
parts.working: Efficiency = useful power / input power, so input = 3/0.6 = 5 kW (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist and her bicycle move along a straight level road. Her power output is a constant 150 W. The resistance to motion is 4v newtons, where v m s⁻¹ is her speed. Show that, at her maximum steady speed, v² = 37.5.
parts.answer: Steady speed: driving force = resistance = 4v, so power = 4v × v = 4v² = 150 gives v² = 37.5
parts.working: At steady speed the driving force equals the resistance, 4v (M1). Power 150 = 4v × v, so v² = 37.5 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum steady speed, in m s⁻¹, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 1200 kg tows a trailer of mass 400 kg along a straight level road using a light rigid tow-bar. The resistances to motion are 400 N on the car and 200 N on the trailer. The car's engine works at 24 kW. Find the acceleration when the speed is 15 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the tension in the tow-bar at this instant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the greatest steady speed of the car and trailer on this road with the same power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car of mass 1000 kg has a constant power P W and experiences a constant resistance R N. Its greatest steady speed up a hill inclined at angle α, where sin α = 0.05, is 20 m s⁻¹, and its greatest steady speed down the same hill is 30 m s⁻¹. Find P and R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest steady speed of the car on a level road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 900 kg moves on a level road with its engine working at a constant 30 kW. The resistance to motion is (400 + 2v²) N when the speed is v m s⁻¹. Find the acceleration when v = 25 and state whether the car is speeding up or slowing down.
parts.working: B1 driving force 1200 N. M1 1200 − (400 + 1250) = 900a. A1 a = −0.5, slowing down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the greatest steady speed V satisfies V³ + 200V − 15 000 = 0 and find V correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 30 000/V = 400 + 2V². A1 V³ + 200V − 15 000 = 0. B1 V = 22.0 (by calculator / iteration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates along a straight level road. Its engine works at a constant 25 kW for 20 s, during which its speed increases from 10 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹. Find the work done by the engine and the work done against resistance during these 20 s.
parts.answer: 500 000 J by the engine; 237 500 J against resistance
parts.working: B1 WD by engine = 25 000 × 20 = 500 000 J. B1 KE gain = ½ × 1000 × (625 − 100) = 262 500 J. M1 WD against resistance = difference. A1 237 500 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The car travels 400 m in this time. Find the average resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the driving force is not constant during the motion.
parts.answer: Power is constant, so F = P/v decreases as v increases
parts.working: B1 F = P/v and v changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A van of mass 1000 kg climbs a straight hill inclined at an angle α to the horizontal, where sin α = 0.1. The van's engine works at a constant power of 20 kW and the van moves at a steady speed of 10 m s⁻¹. Find the resistance to motion.
parts.working: Driving force = 20 000/10 = 2000 N (M1). Steady speed: driving force = mg sin α + R = 1000 + R (M1). So R = 2000 − 1000 = 1000 N (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The van now travels along a straight level road with the same engine power and the same resistance. Find its steady speed.
parts.working: Driving force = R = 1000 N (M1). Speed = power / driving force = 20 000/1000 = 20 m s⁻¹ (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A lift car of mass 800 kg is raised from rest vertically upwards with constant acceleration. Its speed reaches 3 m s⁻¹ after 4 s. Find the driving force of the motor during the lift.
parts.working: Acceleration = 3/4 = 0.75 m s⁻² (M1). Driving force F = m(g + a) = 800 × 10.75 = 8600 N (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the power of the motor at the instant when t = 4 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the average power of the motor over the first 4 s.
parts.working: Distance = ½ × 0.75 × 4² = 6 m, so work = 8600 × 6 = 51 600 J (M1). Average power = 51 600/4 = 12 900 W (A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box is dragged at constant speed across a horizontal floor by a force of 50 N inclined at 30° above the horizontal. Find the work done by the force when the box moves 8 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The box takes 4 s to move the 8 m. Find the average power of the force and the magnitude of the frictional force.
parts.working: B1 346 ÷ 4 = 86.6 W. B1 constant speed so friction = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trolley is pulled 12 m along a horizontal floor by a rope. The tension in the rope is 50 N and the rope makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find the work done by the tension, in joules, correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block is pushed 8 m along a horizontal floor by a force of magnitude 40 N acting at 60° below the horizontal. Find the work done by the force.
parts.working: The force makes 60° with the horizontal displacement, so W = 40 × 8 × cos 60° = 160 J (M1, A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A constant force of magnitude 5 N acts on a particle. The particle is displaced by 4 m, and the angle between the force and the displacement has cosine 0.6. Find the work done by the force.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child pulls a sledge 20 m along level snow using a rope inclined at 45° to the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 25 N. Find the work done by the tension, correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A horse pulls a cart at a constant speed of 2.5 m s⁻¹. The pulling force has magnitude 600 N and acts at 20° above the horizontal, in the direction of motion. Find the power of the pulling force, in kW, correct to 2 decimal places.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves with speed 4 m s⁻¹. A constant force of magnitude 15 N acts on it at 60° to its direction of motion. Find the power of the force.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A pump on a farm near Multan raises water from a well. Each minute it lifts 300 kg of water through a vertical height of 15 m and delivers it at a speed of 4 m s⁻¹. Find the work done by the pump each minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the power of the pump and the work it does in one hour.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A crate is pulled 15 m along a rough horizontal floor by a rope. The tension in the rope is 90 N and acts at 25° above the horizontal. A resistance of 60 N opposes the motion. Find the work done by the tension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done against the resistance, and the net work done on the crate.
parts.answer: Work against resistance 900 J; net work 323.5 J
parts.working: Work done by the resistance = −60 × 15 = −900 J, so 900 J is done against it (M1, A1). Net work = 1223.5 − 900 = 323.5 J (A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box is pulled along a horizontal floor at a constant speed of 1.5 m s⁻¹ by a rope. The tension is 80 N and the rope is inclined at 35° to the horizontal. Find the power of the tension, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Power = Fv cos θ = 80 × 1.5 × cos 35° (M1, M1) = 98.3 W (A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves 4 m along a straight line AB. A constant force of magnitude 10 N acts on the particle at 120° to AB. Find the work done by the force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the work done in part (a) is positive or negative, and explain why.
parts.answer: Negative: the force has a component opposite to the direction of motion, since cos 120° < 0.
parts.working: cos 120° is negative, so the force does negative work on the particle (B1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A constant force of magnitude F acts on a particle. The work done by the force when the particle moves through displacement d, where the angle between F and d is θ, is Fd cos θ. For a certain displacement the work done is half of the value Fd. Find θ.
parts.working: Fd cos θ = ½Fd, so cos θ = ½ (M1). θ = 60° (M1, A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A man pushes a lawnmower 40 m across a lawn. He pushes with a force of 90 N directed 30° below the horizontal. Find the work done by the force, in kJ, correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tractor pulls a trailer along a straight road at a constant speed of 12 m s⁻¹. The tension in the tow rope is 2000 N and the rope is inclined at 15° to the horizontal. Find the power of the tension, in kW, correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A constant force of magnitude 50 N acts on a box at an angle θ above the horizontal. The box moves 10 m horizontally and the work done by the force is 400 J. Find θ, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the vertical component of the force.
parts.working: Vertical component = 50 sin θ = 50 × 0.6 = 30 N (M1, A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves in a straight line with constant velocity 3 m s⁻¹. A constant force of magnitude F newtons acts on the particle at 60° to the direction of motion, and the power of the force is 18 W. Find F.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done by the force in the first 10 s.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A block of mass 6 kg is on a rough horizontal floor, where the coefficient of friction is 0.3. It is pulled by a force of magnitude P newtons acting at 30° above the horizontal, and it moves at a constant speed of 2 m s⁻¹. Find P, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the power of the force P.

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: A constant force of magnitude 13 N acts on a particle, which moves 6 m in a straight line from P to Q. The work done by the force is −39 J. Find the angle between the force and the displacement PQ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The particle takes 3 s to move from P to Q. Find the average rate at which the force does work during this time.
parts.working: Average rate of working = work done ÷ time = −39 ÷ 3 = −13 W (M1, A1).

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A block of mass 5 kg is at rest on a smooth plane inclined at 20° to the horizontal. It is pulled up the plane by a force of 40 N acting parallel to the plane, and it moves 3 m up the plane. Find the work done by the 40 N force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the work done against gravity and hence the speed of the block after it has moved 3 m. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Work against gravity 51.3 J; speed 5.24 m s⁻¹

practice.subtopic: Work done & power by a force

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 2 kg is moving with speed 5 m s⁻¹ in a direction 30° below the horizontal. Find the rate at which the weight of the particle does work at this instant.
parts.answer: 50 W (the weight does positive work at 50 W)
parts.working: The downward component of the velocity is 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m s⁻¹ (M1). Power of the weight = mg × 2.5 = 20 × 2.5 = 50 W (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the rate in part (a) is positive or negative and interpret it.
parts.answer: Positive: the particle is moving downwards, so the weight does work on it
parts.working: The velocity has a downward component, so gravity adds energy to the particle (B1).
