practice.stem: The six letters of the word LAHORE are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements that begin with L and end with E.
parts.working: L and E fixed (M1); remaining 4 letters 4! = 24 (A1).

practice.stem: Seven students, including Ali and Sara, stand in a line for a class photograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which Ali and Sara stand next to each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which Ali and Sara are not next to each other.

practice.stem: Four-digit numbers are formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. No digit may be used more than once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different four-digit numbers can be formed?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these are even?

practice.stem: Eight different cards, numbered 1 to 8, are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which cards 1 and 2 are next to each other.
parts.working: M1 treat cards 1 and 2 as one block, giving 7 units: 7! arrangements; M1 × 2 for the order of 1 and 2 inside the block; A1 2 × 7! = 10080.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which cards 1 and 2 are next to each other and card 3 is at one end of the row.
parts.working: M1 card 3 is at one of the 2 ends; M1 the block and the other 5 cards form 6 units in 6! ways, and the block has 2 internal orders; A1 2 × 6! × 2 = 2880.

practice.stem: The six letters of the word PLANET are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two vowels are next to each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two vowels are not next to each other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements which begin and end with a consonant.

practice.stem: Four boys and three girls, all different, stand in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the three girls stand together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which no two girls stand next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange boys 4! = 24 (B1). 5 gaps, choose and order 3 for the girls: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 (M1). 24 × 60 = 1440 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which boys and girls alternate.

practice.stem: A shelf holds 10 different books: 5 mathematics books, 3 physics books and 2 chemistry books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of ways of arranging the books so that the books of each subject are kept together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of ways of arranging the books so that no two physics books are next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange the other 7 books: 7! = 5040 (B1). 8 gaps, place the 3 physics books: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 (M1). 5040 × 336 = 1 693 440 (A1).

practice.stem: Five-digit numbers are formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, with no digit repeated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many of these numbers are greater than 50 000?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of the numbers greater than 50 000 are odd?
parts.working: Case first digit 5 or 7 (odd): last digit from the other 3 odd digits: 2 × 3 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360 (M1 A1). Case first digit 6: last digit any of 4 odd digits: 1 × 4 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 240 (M1). Total 600 (A1).

practice.stem: A family of 3 adults and 4 children sit in a row of 7 chairs for a photograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the 3 adults sit together. The children may be in any order.
parts.working: M1 treat the 3 adults as one block: 5 units, 5! ways; M1 × 3! ways to order the adults; A1 120 × 6 = 720.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the 3 adults sit together and the 4 children sit together.
parts.working: M1 two blocks can be ordered in 2! ways; M1 3! for the adults and 4! for the children; A1 2 × 6 × 24 = 288.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the first chair is occupied by a child.
parts.working: M1 4 choices of child for the first chair, then 6! for the other six people; A1 4 × 720 = 2880.

practice.stem: Four-digit numbers are formed from the digits 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9. No digit may be repeated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many of these numbers are divisible by 5?
parts.working: M1 the last digit must be 5, the only available digit that is 0 or 5: 1 way; M1 the other three digits are chosen in order from the remaining 5 digits: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60; A1 60.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these numbers are divisible by 5 and greater than 5000?
parts.working: The last digit is 5 and the first digit must be 6, 8 or 9 (3 choices); M1 the middle two digits are chosen in order from the remaining 4 digits: 4 × 3 = 12; A1 3 × 12 = 36.

practice.stem: Eight people, including Parveen, Qasim and Rehan, stand in a queue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which Parveen and Qasim are at the two ends of the queue.
parts.working: 2 ways for the ends (M1), 6! for the rest: 1440 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which exactly two of Parveen, Qasim and Rehan are next to each other (the third is not next to either of them).
parts.working: Arrange the other 5 people: 5! = 120 (B1). Choose the pair and its order: 3 × 2 = 6 (M1). Place the pair-unit and the third person in different gaps among the 6 gaps: 6 × 5 = 30 (M1). 120 × 6 × 30 = 21 600 (A1).

practice.stem: Six men and four women, all different, sit in a row of ten seats at a wedding in Faisalabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which a man sits in each end seat and no two women sit next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange the men: 6! = 720 (B1). Women must go in the 5 gaps between men (not the ends) (M1): 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120 (M1). 720 × 120 = 86 400 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which all four women sit together.
parts.working: Treat the four women as one unit: 7 units in 7! ways (M1); women within the unit 4! ways: 5040 × 24 = 120 960 (A1).

practice.stem: Numbers between 3000 and 6000 are formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, with no digit repeated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many of these numbers are divisible by 5?
parts.working: Last digit must be 5 (B1). First digit 3 or 4 (5 is used) (M1): 2 × 5 × 4 = 40 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these numbers are odd?
parts.working: First digit 3: last from 1, 5, 7: 3 × 5 × 4 = 60 (M1). First 4: last from 1, 3, 5, 7: 4 × 20 = 80 (A1). First 5: last from 1, 3, 7: 60 (A1). Total 200 (A1).

practice.stem: Seven students, P, Q, R, S, T, U and V, stand in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which P does not stand at either end of the line.
parts.working: M1 P must be in one of the 5 middle positions; M1 × 6! for the other six people; A1 5 × 720 = 3600.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which P does not stand at either end of the line and Q and R are not next to each other.
parts.working: M1 for each of the 5 middle positions of P, the 6 remaining positions contain exactly 4 adjacent pairs; M1 Q and R next to each other in 4 × 2 ways, and S, T, U, V in 4! ways: 192 per position, so 5 × 192 = 960 arrangements to exclude; A1 3600 − 960 = 2640.

practice.stem: Ten people, including Aisha and Bilal, sit in a row of ten seats numbered 1 to 10 from left to right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of seating arrangements in which Aisha sits in an odd-numbered seat and Bilal sits in an even-numbered seat.
parts.working: Aisha has 5 odd seats and Bilal has 5 even seats; the other 8 people sit in 8! = 40320 ways. 5 × 5 × 40320 = 1 008 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a random seating arrangement has Aisha in an odd-numbered seat and Bilal in an even-numbered seat. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

practice.stem: A committee of 5 people is to be chosen from 7 men and 6 women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In how many ways can the committee be chosen?

parts.label: b
parts.text: In how many ways can it be chosen if it contains exactly 2 women?

practice.stem: A cricket squad has 15 players, including the captain and the vice-captain. A team of 11 is chosen from the squad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different teams include the captain?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many different teams include the captain but not the vice-captain?

practice.stem: A class has 9 students: 4 girls and 5 boys. A group of 3 students is chosen at random from the class.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different groups that can be chosen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of groups containing exactly one girl.
parts.working: Choose 1 girl from 4 and 2 boys from 5: C(4,1) × C(5,2) = 4 × 10 = 40.

practice.stem: A committee of 4 is to be chosen from 10 teachers. Three of the teachers teach science.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of committees that contain at least one science teacher.
parts.working: M1 total C(10,4) = 210; M1 committees with no science teacher: C(7,4) = 35; A1 210 − 35 = 175.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of committees that contain exactly 2 science teachers.

practice.stem: A team of 4 is to be selected from 5 men and 4 women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of possible teams.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of teams that contain at least 2 women.
parts.working: 2 women: ⁴C₂ × ⁵C₂ = 60; 3 women: ⁴C₃ × 5 = 20; 4 women: 1 (M1 A1). Total 81 (A1).

practice.stem: Six students are to be chosen from a class of 12 to represent their school at a science fair in Peshawar. Two of the students, Hina and Bilal, refuse to be in the group together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of possible groups.
parts.working: Total ¹²C₆ = 924 (B1). Groups with both: ¹⁰C₄ = 210 (M1). 924 − 210 = 714 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of groups that contain Hina but not Bilal.

practice.stem: A restaurant in Lahore offers 6 different starters, 8 different main courses and 4 different desserts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer chooses one starter, one main course and one dessert. How many different meals are possible?

parts.label: b
parts.text: A family chooses 4 different dishes from the whole menu. Find the number of selections that include at least one main course.
parts.working: Total ¹⁸C₄ = 3060 (B1). No main course: ¹⁰C₄ = 210 (M1). 3060 − 210 = 2850 (A1).

practice.stem: Twelve students are to be divided into three groups of four, to work on three different projects: Solar, Water and Recycling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of ways of dividing the students into the three project groups.
parts.working: The groups are distinct because each goes to a different project: 12!/(4! × 4! × 4!) = 34650.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The three groups of four are formed as unnamed groups, with no project attached. Find the number of ways of doing this.
parts.working: 34650 ÷ 3! = 34650 ÷ 6 = 5775, since the three groups can be put in 3! orders.

practice.stem: A pizza shop offers 8 different toppings. Each pizza has exactly 3 different toppings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different pizzas are possible?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these pizzas contain pepperoni but not mushrooms?
parts.working: Pepperoni is included and mushrooms are excluded; choose the other 2 toppings from the remaining 6: C(6,2) = 15.

practice.stem: A panel of 6 people is to be chosen from 7 men and 5 women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of panels that contain more men than women.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of panels that contain at least one woman.
parts.working: M1 C(12,6) − C(7,6) (all-men panels removed); A1 924 − 7 = 917.

practice.stem: A craft box contains 9 different beads: 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green. Five beads are chosen to make a bracelet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of selections that contain at least one bead of each colour.
parts.working: Total ⁹C₅ = 126 (B1). No red: ⁵C₅ = 1; no blue: ⁶C₅ = 6; no green: ⁷C₅ = 21 (M1 A1). Two colours missing is impossible with 5 beads. 126 − 28 = 98 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of selections with exactly 3 red beads.
parts.working: Choose 3 of the 4 red beads and 2 of the 5 non-red beads: ⁴C₃ × ⁵C₂ (M1) = 4 × 10 = 40 (A1).

practice.stem: Nine volunteers at a flood-relief camp are to be divided into groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of ways of dividing them into a group of 4, a group of 3 and a group of 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of ways of dividing them into three groups of 3, where the groups are not labelled.
parts.working: ⁹C₃ × ⁶C₃ × ³C₃ = 1680 (M1). Groups unlabelled: divide by 3! (M1). 1680/6 = 280 (A1).

practice.stem: A project committee of 6 is chosen from 8 Pakistani engineers and 5 Chinese engineers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of committees with more Pakistani than Chinese engineers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two of the Pakistani engineers refuse to serve together. Find the number of committees with more Pakistani than Chinese engineers that do not include both of them.
parts.working: Committees containing both: 4P 2C: ⁶C₂ × 10 = 150; 5P 1C: ⁶C₃ × 5 = 100; 6P: ⁶C₄ = 15, total 265 (M1 A1). 1008 − 265 = 743 (A1).

practice.stem: A squad of 7 players is to be chosen from 12 players, including Imran and Kamran.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of squads in which Imran and Kamran are not both selected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of squads that include Imran but not Kamran.
parts.working: Imran is in and Kamran is out; choose the other 6 from the remaining 10: C(10,6) = 210.

practice.stem: Three different whole numbers are chosen at random from the numbers 1 to 15 inclusive. No number is chosen twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of ways of choosing three numbers whose sum is even.
parts.working: There are 8 odd and 7 even numbers. An even sum needs 3 even numbers or 2 odd and 1 even: C(7,3) + C(8,2) × C(7,1) = 35 + 28 × 7 = 35 + 196 = 231.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of ways of choosing three numbers whose sum is odd.

practice.stem: A bag contains 5 red sweets and 4 blue sweets. Three sweets are taken at random without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that all three sweets are red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one sweet is red.

practice.stem: A box holds 8 chocolates: 3 dark and 5 milk. Three chocolates are taken at random without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly two of the chocolates are dark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least two of the chocolates are milk.
parts.working: Exactly 2 milk and 1 dark: C(5,2) × C(3,1) = 30; all 3 milk: C(5,3) = 10. Total 40 out of C(8,3) = 56, so 40/56 = 5/7.

practice.stem: A club has 6 women and 4 men. A group of 4 people is chosen at random from the 10 members.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the group contains exactly 2 women.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the group contains at least 3 women.

practice.stem: A group of 6 people is chosen at random from 5 boys and 5 girls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the group has exactly 3 boys and 3 girls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the group has more girls than boys.
parts.working: By symmetry (5 boys and 5 girls), P(more girls) = P(more boys) = (1 − 10/21)/2 = (11/21)/2 = 11/42.

practice.stem: A committee of 4 is chosen at random from 6 men and 5 women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the committee contains more women than men.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a particular man, Usman, is on the committee.

practice.stem: A box of 12 LED bulbs contains 3 faulty bulbs. An electrician takes 4 bulbs at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that none of the 4 bulbs is faulty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one is faulty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly 2 are faulty.

practice.stem: A teacher chooses 4 questions at random, without replacement, from a list of 10 questions. Four of the 10 questions are on differentiation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that at least 3 of the 4 chosen questions are on differentiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that none of the chosen questions is on differentiation.

practice.stem: Ten tickets, numbered 1 to 10, are put into a box. Three tickets are drawn at random without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the sum of the three numbers is even.
parts.working: There are 5 odd and 5 even tickets. An even sum needs 3 even tickets or 1 even and 2 odd: [C(5,3) + C(5,1) × C(5,2)]/C(10,3) = (10 + 50)/120 = 1/2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that all three numbers are odd, or all three numbers are even.
parts.working: P(all odd) = C(5,3)/120 = 1/12 and P(all even) = 1/12. These events cannot both happen, so the total is 1/12 + 1/12 = 1/6.

practice.stem: Ayesha and Bilal are two of 10 candidates. A panel of 4 is chosen at random from the 10 candidates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that both Ayesha and Bilal are on the panel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one of Ayesha and Bilal is on the panel.

practice.stem: A raffle has 50 tickets. Three tickets are drawn at random without replacement, and each drawn ticket wins a prize. Aisha holds 5 of the 50 tickets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that Aisha wins at least one prize. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that Aisha wins exactly 2 prizes. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: Four married couples attend a dinner. Four of the eight people are chosen at random to give short speeches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that no married couple is chosen.
parts.working: Total ⁸C₄ = 70 (B1). No couple: one person from each couple, 2⁴ = 16 (M1). 16/70 = 8/35 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one married couple is chosen.
parts.working: Choose the couple: 4; choose 2 of the other 3 couples, one person from each: ³C₂ × 2² = 12 (M1). 4 × 12 = 48 (A1). 48/70 = 24/35 (A1).

practice.stem: A debate team of 5 is chosen at random from 7 girls and 6 boys.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the team contains at least 2 girls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the team contains at least 2 girls, find the probability that it contains exactly 3 girls.

practice.stem: A box contains 12 tools, 5 of which are faulty. A technician takes 4 tools at random without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one of the 4 tools is faulty. Give your answer as a fraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that at least one tool is faulty, find the probability that exactly one tool is faulty.

practice.stem: Three different integers are chosen at random from 1, 2, 3, ..., 12, without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the three integers are consecutive integers, such as 4, 5 and 6.
parts.working: There are 10 sets of three consecutive integers from 1 to 12, out of C(12,3) = 220 sets: 10/220 = 1/22.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the three integers add up to exactly 12.

practice.stem: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Four balls are taken at random from the bag without replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that all three colours appear among the four balls.

practice.stem: The letters of the word PAKISTAN are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements that begin with K.

practice.stem: The letters of the word LETTER are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements of the six letters.
parts.working: 6!/(2! × 2!) = 720/4 = 180, since the two Es and the two Ts are identical in pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two Es are not next to each other.
parts.working: Treat the two Es as one block: the block, L, T, T and R form 5 units with 2 identical Ts, giving 5!/2! = 60 arrangements with the Es together. 180 − 60 = 120.

practice.stem: The letters of the word SCHOOL are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two Os are next to each other.
parts.working: Treat OO as one block: 5 distinct units, 5! = 120.

practice.stem: Four-digit numbers are formed using the digits 1, 1, 2 and 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different four-digit numbers can be formed?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these numbers are odd?
parts.working: Last digit 1: the other digits 1, 2, 3 can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways. Last digit 3: the other digits 1, 1, 2 can be arranged in 3!/2! = 3 ways. Total 9.

practice.stem: The letters of the word BANANAS are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements in which the three A's are together.
parts.working: AAA as one unit: 5 units with N twice: 5!/2! (M1) = 60 (A1).

practice.stem: The letters of the word TOMORROW are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements which begin and end with O.
parts.working: Middle letters T, O, M, R, R, W: 6!/2! (M1) = 360 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements in which the two R's are not next to each other.

practice.stem: The letters of the word MISSISSIPPI are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the total number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which all four Ss are together.
parts.working: Treat SSSS as one block: 8 units (the block, M, four Is and two Ps). 8!/(4! × 2!) = 40320/48 = 840.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the word begins with M and ends with I.
parts.working: Fix M at the start and I at the end. The middle 9 letters are three Is, four Ss and two Ps: 9!/(3! × 4! × 2!) = 362880/288 = 1260.

practice.stem: The letters of the word SUCCESS are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the three Ss are not all next to each other.
parts.working: Three Ss together: the block with U, C, C and E gives 5 units with 2 identical Cs, so 5!/2! = 60. 420 − 60 = 360.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements that begin and end with S.
parts.working: Fix S at both ends. The middle 5 letters are S, U, C, C and E: 5!/2! = 60.

practice.stem: Nine beads are threaded in a line: 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green. Beads of the same colour are identical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which no two red beads are next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange the 5 non-red beads (3 blue, 2 green): 5!/(3! × 2!) = 10 ways. This gives 6 gaps; choose 4 of them for the red beads: C(6,4) = 15. Total 10 × 15 = 150.

practice.stem: A six-letter code is made using each of the letters A, A, B, B, C and C exactly once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different codes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of codes in which the two As are not next to each other.
parts.working: Treat AA as one block: 5 units with 2 identical Bs and 2 identical Cs, so 5!/(2! × 2!) = 30 codes have the As together. 90 − 30 = 60.

practice.stem: The letters of the word KARACHI are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two As are not next to each other.
parts.working: Treat AA as one block: 6 distinct units, 6! = 720 arrangements have the As together. 2520 − 720 = 1800.

practice.stem: The nine letters of the word ISLAMABAD are arranged in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements in which no two A's are next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange I, S, L, M, B, D: 6! = 720 (B1). Choose 3 of the 7 gaps for the A's: ⁷C₃ = 35 (M1). 720 × 35 = 25 200 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements that begin and end with A.
parts.working: Middle 7 letters I, S, L, M, B, D, A all different: 7! (M1) = 5040 (A1).

practice.stem: The letters of the word ARRANGE are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which no two identical letters are next to each other.
parts.working: Inclusion–exclusion on the two pairs (A and R). A's together: 6!/2! = 360; R's together: 360; both together: 5! = 120. Neither: 1260 − 360 − 360 + 120 = 660.

practice.stem: The letters of the word NOTATION are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which no two identical letters are next to each other.
parts.working: Inclusion–exclusion over the pairs N, O and T. Total 5040. One pair together (3 choices): 7!/(2! × 2!) = 1260 each, 3780 in all. Two pairs together (3 choices): 6!/2! = 360 each, 1080. All three together: 5! = 120. Result 5040 − 3780 + 1080 − 120 = 2220.

practice.stem: The letters of the word LEVEL are arranged in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements in which the two Ls are next to each other.
parts.working: Treat LL as one block: units LL, E, E and V, giving 4!/2! = 12.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of arrangements that begin and end with the same letter.
parts.working: Both ends L: the middle E, E, V give 3!/2! = 3. Both ends E: the middle L, L, V give 3. Total 6.

practice.stem: The letters of the word TABLE are arranged at random in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with the letter T or ends with the letter E.
parts.working: P(begins with T) = 1/5 and P(ends with E) = 1/5. P(T first and E last) = 3!/5! = 1/20. P(T first or E last) = 1/5 + 1/5 − 1/20 = 7/20.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that T and E are at the two ends of the arrangement.
parts.working: T and E at the ends in 2 ways; the other 3 letters in 3! = 6 ways: 12 arrangements out of 5! = 120, so 12/120 = 1/10.

practice.stem: The letters of the word ORANGE are arranged at random in a row. All six letters are different.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with a vowel.
parts.working: The vowels are O, A and E: 3 of the 6 letters, so 3/6 = 1/2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with a consonant and ends with a vowel.
parts.working: First letter: 3 consonants (R, N, G); last letter: 3 vowels; the middle 4 letters in 4! = 24 ways. Favourable: 3 × 3 × 24 = 216 out of 6! = 720, so 216/720 = 3/10.

practice.stem: Five people, A, B, C, D and E, stand in a random order in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that A and B stand next to each other.
parts.working: Treat AB (or BA) as one block: 2 × 4! = 48 arrangements out of 5! = 120, so 48/120 = 2/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that A and B stand at the two ends of the line.
parts.working: A and B at the ends in 2 ways; the other 3 people in 3! = 6 ways: 12 out of 120, so 1/10.

practice.stem: The six letters of the word QUETTA are arranged in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the two T's are next to each other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins and ends with a vowel.
parts.working: Choose and order 2 of the 3 vowels U, E, A for the ends: 3 × 2 = 6 (M1). Middle 4 letters with T twice: 4!/2! = 12 (M1). 72/360 = 1/5 (A1).

practice.stem: Five boys and three girls stand in a line in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the three girls are all next to each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that there is a boy at each end of the line.

practice.stem: The letters of the word PAPER are arranged in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the two Ps are next to each other.
parts.working: Total arrangements 5!/2! = 60. Treat PP as one block: 4 distinct units, 4! = 24. 24/60 = 2/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the two Ps are not next to each other.

practice.stem: The letters of the word BANANA are arranged at random in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the two Ns are next to each other.
parts.working: Total 6!/(3! × 2!) = 60. Treat NN as one block: 5 units (the block, B and three As), so 5!/3! = 20 arrangements. 20/60 = 1/3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with B.
parts.working: The remaining letters A, A, A, N, N can be arranged in 5!/(3! × 2!) = 10 ways. 10/60 = 1/6.

practice.stem: Six students, including Maryam and Omar, stand in a random order in a line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that Maryam is at the left end of the line and Omar is standing immediately to her right.
parts.working: P(Maryam at the left end) = 1/6. Then Omar must be in position 2, which has probability 1/5. 1/6 × 1/5 = 1/30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly two students stand between Maryam and Omar.
parts.working: Their positions differ by 3: the pairs of positions (1,4), (2,5) and (3,6) give 3 choices, and Maryam and Omar can be in either order (× 2). The other 4 students can be ordered in 4! = 24 ways. Favourable 3 × 2 × 24 = 144 out of 6! = 720, so 144/720 = 1/5.

practice.stem: A row of 7 people consists of 4 boys and 3 girls, in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that no two girls are next to each other.
parts.working: Arrange the 4 boys: 4! = 24 ways, which leaves 5 gaps. Choose 3 gaps for the girls: C(5,3) = 10. Arrange the girls: 3! = 6. Favourable 24 × 10 × 6 = 1440; total 7! = 5040; 1440/5040 = 2/7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that all three girls are next to each other.
parts.working: The girls form one block with the 4 boys: 5 units in 5! ways, and the girls order themselves in 3! ways. 5! × 3! = 720; 720/5040 = 1/7.

practice.stem: The letters of the word RADAR are arranged at random in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement reads the same forwards and backwards.
parts.working: Total 5!/(2! × 2!) = 30. A palindrome needs D in the middle and the two Rs and two As in mirror positions: RADAR and ARDRA, so 2 arrangements. 2/30 = 1/15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins and ends with R.
parts.working: Fix R at both ends (the two Rs are identical, so 1 way). The middle letters A, A, D can be arranged in 3!/2! = 3 ways. 3/30 = 1/10.

practice.stem: The eight letters of the word PESHAWAR are arranged in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with a vowel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that there are exactly two letters between the two A's.

practice.stem: The letters of the word STATISTICS are arranged at random in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that all three Ts are next to each other.
parts.working: Total 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 50400. Treat TTT as one block: 8 units (the block, three Ss, A, two Is, C), so 8!/(3! × 2!) = 3360. 3360/50400 = 1/15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that all three Ss are together and both Is are together.
parts.working: Blocks SSS and II, with T, T, T, A and C: 7 units with three identical Ts, so 7!/3! = 840. 840/50400 = 1/60.

practice.stem: The letters of the word ELEVEN are arranged at random in a row.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different arrangements of the letters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins and ends with E.
parts.working: Fix E at each end (two of the three Es). The middle four letters E, L, V, N are all different: 4! = 24. 24/120 = 1/5.

practice.stem: Three married couples sit in a random order in a row of six chairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that each couple sits next to each other, with both people of each couple in adjacent chairs.
parts.working: Treat each couple as one block: 3! = 6 orders of the blocks, and each couple can be ordered in 2 ways: 2³ = 8. 6 × 8 = 48 out of 6! = 720, so 48/720 = 1/15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that no couple sits next to each other.

practice.stem: A four-digit number is made by arranging four different digits chosen from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Every such number is equally likely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the number is even and greater than 3000. Give your answer as a fraction.
parts.working: Total 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120. Even: last digit 2 or 4. Last 2: first digit 3, 4 or 5 (3 choices), middle two from the remaining 3 digits in 3 × 2 = 6 ways: 18. Last 4: first digit 3 or 5 (2 choices), middle 6 ways: 12. Favourable 30, so 30/120 = 1/4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe fully the locus of points in an Argand diagram representing complex numbers z that satisfy |z − 3 + 2i| = 4.
parts.answer: A circle with centre (3, −2), i.e. the point 3 − 2i, and radius 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest value of |z| for points on this locus. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 distance from origin to centre = √(3² + 2²) = √13; A1 √13 + 4 = 7.61.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = x + iy satisfies |z − 1| = |z + 3i|. Describe the locus of z geometrically.
parts.answer: The perpendicular bisector of the line joining the points 1 and −3i (i.e. (1, 0) and (0, −3)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the Cartesian equation of the locus in the form ax + by + c = 0.
parts.working: M1 (x − 1)² + y² = x² + (y + 3)²; M1 expand and simplify: −2x + 1 = 6y + 9; A1 x + 3y + 4 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The locus of z is given by arg(z + 2) = π/3. Find a Cartesian equation for the locus, stating any restriction on x.
parts.working: M1 tan(π/3) = y/(x + 2); A1 with x > −2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether the point representing 1 + 3√3 i lies on the locus.
parts.working: M1 z + 2 = 3 + 3√3 i; A1 argument is π/3, so yes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies both |z| = 5 and |z − 6| = 5. Explain why Re z = 3.
parts.answer: z is equidistant from 0 and 6, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector x = 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two possible values of z.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies |z + 4 − 3i| = 5. Show that the origin lies on the locus of z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest value of |z| for points on this locus.
parts.working: Centre −4 + 3i with |−4 + 3i| = 5, and radius 5. The greatest |z| is at the point opposite the origin, z = −8 + 6i, giving |z| = 5 + 5 = 10 (M1, M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies |z − 2i| = 3. Describe the locus of z in words, giving the centre and the radius.
parts.working: |z − 2i| is the distance from z to 2i, so the locus is a circle centre 0 + 2i and radius 3 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest and least values of Im z for points on this locus.
parts.working: Im z ranges from 2 − 3 = −1 to 2 + 3 = 5 on the circle (M1, A1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies |z − 4 − 3i| = 2. Find the least value of |z|.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest value of arg z for points on this locus. Give your answer in radians correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B1 arg(4 + 3i) = tan⁻¹(3/4) = 0.6435; M1 angle between the line to the centre and the tangent = sin⁻¹(2/5) = 0.4115; A1 0.6435 + 0.4115 = 1.055 ≈ 1.06.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The region R in an Argand diagram consists of points z satisfying both |z − 2 − 3i| ≤ 3 and |z| ≥ |z − 4|. Describe R in words.
parts.answer: The part of the disc with centre 2 + 3i and radius 3 that lies on or to the right of the line Re z = 2 (the perpendicular bisector of 0 and 4).
parts.working: B1 disc centre (2, 3), radius 3; B1 |z| ≥ |z − 4| ⇔ Re z ≥ 2, so R is the right-hand half of the disc.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest value of |z| for points in R. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 farthest point lies on the line through O and the centre (it has Re z = 2 + 6/√13 > 2, so it is in R); A1 √13 + 3 = 6.61.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the least value of Re z for points in R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = x + iy satisfies |z − 4i| = |z − 6|. Find the Cartesian equation of the locus of z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of |z| for points on this locus, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 perpendicular distance from O to 3x − 2y − 5 = 0 is 5/√(9 + 4); A1 1.39.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = x + iy satisfies |z − 3| = 2|z + 3|. Show that the locus of z is a circle, and find its centre and radius.
parts.working: Square both sides: (x − 3)² + y² = 4[(x + 3)² + y²] (M1). Expand: x² − 6x + 9 + y² = 4x² + 24x + 36 + 4y² (M1). Simplify: x² + 10x + y² + 9 = 0 (M1). Complete the square: (x + 5)² + y² = 16, a circle with centre (−5, 0) and radius 4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest and least values of |z| for points on this locus.
parts.working: Distance from the origin to the centre is 5, so |z| ranges from 5 − 4 = 1 to 5 + 4 = 9 (M1, A1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = x + iy satisfies arg(z + 2 − i) = 3π/4. Find the Cartesian equation of the locus of z, and state any restriction on x.
parts.working: z + 2 − i = (x + 2) + (y − 1)i. An argument of 3π/4 means the real part is negative and the imaginary part is positive with equal magnitude (M1, M1). So y − 1 = −(x + 2), giving y = −x − 1 (A1). The real part x + 2 must be negative, so x < −2 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether the point with z = −4 + 3i lies on this locus.
parts.working: Check y = −x − 1 with x = −4, y = 3: −(−4) − 1 = 3, and x < −2, so it lies on the locus (M1, A1). Direct check: arg(−2 + 2i) = 3π/4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The locus L₁ is given by arg(z − 1 − i) = ¼π and the locus L₂ by |z − 5 − i| = 3. Describe each locus.
parts.answer: L₁: half-line from the point 1 + i (excluded) at angle π/4 to the positive real direction. L₂: circle centre 5 + i, radius 3.
parts.working: B1 half-line from (1, 1) at 45°; B1 circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in exact form, the complex numbers represented by the points where L₁ meets L₂.
parts.working: M1 points on L₁: (1 + t) + (1 + t)i, t > 0; M1 (t − 4)² + t² = 9 ⇒ 2t² − 8t + 7 = 0; A1 t = 2 ± √2/2 (both positive, so both points lie on the half-line); A1 both complex numbers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies |z + 2 − i| = 1. Show that the locus of z touches the real axis, and state the point of contact.
parts.answer: Centre −2 + i is 1 unit from the real axis, equal to the radius; contact at z = −2.
parts.working: B1 centre (−2, 1), radius 1; B1 distance to real axis = 1, contact at (−2, 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least and greatest values of arg z for points on the locus, where −π < arg z ≤ π. Give the least value in radians correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Least ≈ 2.21 rad (exactly π − 2 tan⁻¹(½)); greatest = π
parts.working: B1 greatest is π, at the point of contact −2; M1 arg(−2 + i) = π − tan⁻¹(½) = 2.678; M1 subtract sin⁻¹(1/√5) = 0.4636 for the other tangent; A1 2.214 ≈ 2.21.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The region R consists of points z satisfying |z − 3i| ≤ 2 and Re z ≥ 1. Find the least value of arg z for points in R. Give your answer in radians correct to 3 significant figures, and show that the point where it occurs is in R.
parts.answer: ≈ 0.841 rad (π/2 − sin⁻¹(2/3)); at the tangent point Re z = 2√5/3 ≈ 1.49 ≥ 1
parts.working: M1 tangent from O to circle centre 3i, radius 2; M1 angle = π/2 − sin⁻¹(2/3); A1 0.841; B1 tangent length √(9 − 4) = √5, so Re z = √5 cos(π/2 − sin⁻¹(2/3)) = √5 × 2/3 = 2√5/3 ≈ 1.49 ≥ 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest value of |z| for points in R. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 on the circle x² + (y − 3)² = 4 we have |z|² = 6y − 5, so maximise y subject to x ≥ 1; M1 x = 1 gives y = 3 + √3; A1 |z| = √(13 + 6√3) = 4.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = x + iy satisfies |z − 4| = 2|z − 1|. Show that the locus of z is the circle with centre the origin and radius 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in exact form, the two points on this circle where Re z = 1.
parts.working: Put x = 1: 1 + y² = 4, so y² = 3 and y = ±√3 (M1, M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex numbers z and w are given by z = 3 − 4i and w = 1 + 2i. Find zw in the form x + iy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find z/w in the form x + iy, showing all necessary working.
parts.working: M1 multiply numerator and denominator by 1 − 2i; M1 denominator 5; A1 (−5 − 10i)/5 = −1 − 2i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z² − 6z + 13 = 0, giving your answers in the form x + iy.
parts.working: M1 use the formula or complete the square; M1 √(36 − 52) = √(−16) = 4i; A1 3 ± 2i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sum and the product of the two roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express (3 + 2i)/(4 − i) in the form x + iy, where x and y are exact fractions.
parts.working: M1 multiply by (4 + i)/(4 + i); M1 denominator 17, numerator 12 + 3i + 8i − 2 = 10 + 11i; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the modulus of (3 + 2i)/(4 − i), giving your answer in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex numbers z = 2 + 5i and w = 3 − i are given. Find zw in the form x + iy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find z/w in the form x + iy.
parts.working: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 3 + i: (2 + 5i)(3 + i)/(9 + 1) = (1 + 17i)/10 = 0.1 + 1.7i (M1, M1, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z² + 4z + 20 = 0, giving your answers in the form x + iy.
parts.working: Complete the square: (z + 2)² + 16 = 0, so (z + 2)² = −16 (M1). z + 2 = ±4i (M1), z = −2 ± 4i (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that each root has modulus √20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the argument of the root with positive imaginary part, in radians correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Argument = π − arctan 2 = 2.034…, so 2.03 (M1 for π − arctan 2, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the complex number z satisfying 2z + 3iz* = 7 + 8i, where z* is the complex conjugate of z. Give your answer in the form x + iy.
parts.working: M1 substitute z = x + iy, z* = x − iy; M1 2x + 2iy + 3ix + 3y; M1 equate real and imaginary parts: 2x + 3y = 7, 3x + 2y = 8; A1 x = 2; A1 y = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number u is given by u = (7 + i)/(1 − i). Express u in the form x + iy, showing all your working.
parts.working: M1 multiply by (1 + i)/(1 + i); A1 (6 + 8i)/2 = 3 + 4i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find u² in the form x + iy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that u² + pu + q = 0, where p and q are real, find p and q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number w = a + 3i, where a is real, satisfies |w − 2| = 5. Find the two possible values of a.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the value of a with a > 2, find w² and arg(w²), giving the argument in radians correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z satisfies z − z* = 6i, where z* is the complex conjugate of z. Find the imaginary part of z.
parts.working: Let z = x + iy, so z − z* = 2iy = 6i, giving y = 3 (M1, A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The complex number z also satisfies |z| = 5, and Re z > 0. Find z in the form x + iy.
parts.working: x² + 3² = 25 gives x² = 16, so x = ±4; Re z > 0 gives x = 4 (M1 for |z|² = x² + y², M1 for x² = 16, A1 for z = 4 + 3i)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that k is real and (k + 3i)/(2 + i) is a real number, find k and the value of the quotient.
parts.working: Multiply by the conjugate: (k + 3i)(2 − i)/5 = [(2k + 3) + (6 − k)i]/5 (M1, A1). Imaginary part zero: 6 − k = 0, so k = 6 (M1, A1). Value = (2 × 6 + 3)/5 = 3 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the real numbers a and b such that (a + bi)(2 + i) = 1 + 7i.
parts.working: (a + bi)(2 + i) = (2a − b) + (a + 2b)i (M1), so 2a − b = 1 and a + 2b = 7 (A1). Then b = 2a − 1 and a + 4a − 2 = 7 gives a = 9/5 (M1), b = 13/5 (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find |a + bi| in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Solve the simultaneous equations
(1 + i)z + w = 1 + 2i
2z + iw = 3 + 6i,
giving z and w in the form x + iy.
parts.working: M1 eliminate w: multiply first by i: (i − 1)z + iw = i − 2; M1 subtract from second: (3 − i)z = 5 + 5i; M1 z = (5 + 5i)/(3 − i) = (5 + 5i)(3 + i)/10; A1 z = 1 + 2i; M1 w = 1 + 2i − (1 + i)(1 + 2i); A1 w = 2 − i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the complex numbers z which satisfy the equation zz* + 2iz = 12 + 6i, where z* is the complex conjugate of z.
parts.working: M1 put z = x + iy: x² + y² + 2ix − 2y = 12 + 6i; M1 equate parts: 2x = 6, x² + y² − 2y = 12; A1 x = 3; M1 y² − 2y − 3 = 0; A1 y = 3 or −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number 3 + 2i is a root of z² + pz + q = 0, where p and q are real. Find p and q, and state the other root.
parts.working: (3 + 2i)² + p(3 + 2i) + q = 0 gives 5 + 12i + 3p + 2pi + q = 0 (M1). Real parts: 5 + 3p + q = 0 (M1). Imaginary parts: 12 + 2p = 0, so p = −6 (M1), and q = 13 (A1). Sum of roots = −p = 6, so the other root is 6 − (3 + 2i) = 3 − 2i (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation (z + i)/(z − 2) = i, giving z in the form x + iy.
parts.working: z + i = iz − 2i, so z(1 − i) = −3i (M1 cross-multiplying, M1 collecting terms). z = −3i(1 + i)/2 = (3 − 3i)/2 (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find |z| in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z is given by z = −1 + √3 i. Find the modulus and argument of z, giving the argument as an exact multiple of π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write z in the form re^{iθ} and hence find z³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = 3 − 3i. Find the modulus of z and the argument of z in radians, giving the argument in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find z⁴ in the form x + iy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the complex number 4 + 4i in the form re^{iθ}, with θ in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find (4 + 4i)⁵ in the form x + iy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the modulus and the argument, in radians correct to 3 significant figures, of the complex number −5 + 12i.
parts.working: |−5 + 12i| = √(25 + 144) = 13 (M1, A1). The point is in the second quadrant, so arg = π − arctan(12/5) = 1.97 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the argument of (−5 + 12i)² in radians correct to 3 significant figures, in the range −π < θ ≤ π.
parts.working: Argument of the square is 2 × 1.9656 = 3.931, and subtracting 2π gives −2.352 = −2.35 (M1, A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex numbers z and w are given by z = 2e^{iπ/6} and w = 3e^{−iπ/4}. Find zw and z/w, each in the form re^{iθ} with r > 0 and −π < θ ≤ π.
parts.working: M1 multiply moduli, add arguments; A1 zw; A1 z/w (divide moduli, subtract arguments).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express zw in the form x + iy, giving x and y correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z is given by z = 4e^{iπ/3}. Find z³, giving your answer in the form x + iy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the smallest positive integer n for which zⁿ is real and positive, and state the value of zⁿ in this case.
parts.working: M1 nπ/3 must be a multiple of 2π; A1 n = 6, z⁶ = 4⁶ = 4096.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = 3 + 4i. Write z in the form re^{iθ}, giving θ correct to 3 significant figures in radians.
parts.working: r = 5 and θ = arctan(4/3) = 0.927 (M1, A1, A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find z⁴ in the form x + iy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number u = 2 − 2i. Write u in the form re^{iθ}, where −π < θ ≤ π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find u⁹ in the form x + iy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = e^{iθ}. Show that |1 + z|² = 2 + 2 cos θ.
parts.working: |1 + z|² = (1 + z)(1 + z*) = 1 + z + z* + zz* (M1). With z z* = 1 and z + z* = 2 cos θ (M1), the result follows (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find |1 + z| in exact form when θ = π/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the smallest positive integer n for which (1 + i)ⁿ is real and positive, and state the value of (1 + i)ⁿ for this n.
parts.working: 1 + i = √2 e^{iπ/4}, so (1 + i)ⁿ = 2^{n/2} e^{inπ/4}. This is real and positive when nπ/4 is a multiple of 2π, so n is a multiple of 8 (M1, M1, A1). For n = 8, (1 + i)⁸ = 2⁴ = 16 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex numbers u and v are given by u = 1 + i and v = √3 − i. Find the modulus and argument of each of u and v.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the modulus and argument of u/v.

parts.label: c
parts.text: By writing u/v in the form x + iy, show that tan(5π/12) = 2 + √3.
parts.working: M1 multiply by (√3 + i)/(√3 + i); A1 correct x + iy; A1 rationalise (√3 + 1)²/2 = (4 + 2√3)/2 = 2 + √3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that z = e^{iθ}, where 0 < θ < π, show that 1 + z = 2cos(½θ)e^{iθ/2}.
parts.working: M1 factor out e^{iθ/2}; M1 e^{iα} + e^{−iα} = 2cos α; A1 shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence state the modulus and argument of 1 + z when θ = 2π/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find all six complex numbers z with |z| = 2 and z⁶ = −64. Give in exact form the roots with Re z > 0.
parts.working: z = 2e^{iθ} gives z⁶ = 64e^{6iθ} = −64, so 6θ = π + 2kπ and θ = π/6 + kπ/3 (M1, M1). The six roots are 2e^{iπ/6}, 2e^{iπ/2}, 2e^{5iπ/6}, 2e^{7iπ/6}, 2e^{3iπ/2}, 2e^{11iπ/6} (M1). Those with Re z > 0 are 2e^{iπ/6} = √3 + i and 2e^{−iπ/6} = √3 − i (A1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex number z = (1 + √3 i)/(1 − i). Express z in the form re^{iθ}, with θ in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that Re z = (1 − √3)/2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the least positive integer n for which |(1 + 2i)ⁿ| > 1000, and give |(1 + 2i)ⁿ| for this n correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: |(1 + 2i)ⁿ| = (√5)ⁿ = 5^(n/2) (M1). For n = 8 this is 5⁴ = 625, which is too small (M1). For n = 9, 5^4.5 = 1397.5… > 1000 (M1), so n = 9 (A1) and the modulus is 1.40 × 10³ (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of 8i, giving your answers in the form x + iy, where x and y are real.
parts.working: M1 (x + iy)² = 8i: x² − y² = 0, 2xy = 8; M1 x = y (since xy > 0), x² = 4; A1 2 + 2i; A1 −2 − 2i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of 3 + 4i in the form x + iy.
parts.working: (x + iy)² = 3 + 4i gives x² − y² = 3 and 2xy = 4 (M1). |3 + 4i| = 5 so x² + y² = 5 (M1). Then x² = 4 and y² = 1 (M1). With 2xy > 0, x and y have the same sign: x + iy = ±(2 + i) (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of −9 + 40i in the form x + iy.
parts.working: x² − y² = −9, 2xy = 40. Modulus 41 so x² + y² = 41 (M1). x² = 16 and y² = 25 (M1). xy > 0 so same sign: ±(4 + 5i) (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of −7 − 24i in the form x + iy.
parts.working: x² − y² = −7 and 2xy = −24, with x² + y² = 25 (M1). x² = 9 and y² = 16 (M1). xy < 0, so x and y have opposite signs: ±(3 − 4i) (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of 2i in the form x + iy.
parts.working: x² − y² = 0 and 2xy = 2, so x² = y² and xy = 1 (M1). Hence x = y = ±1 (M1), giving ±(1 + i) (A1). Check (1 + i)² = 2i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing (x + iy)² = 5 − 12i, show that x⁴ − 5x² − 36 = 0.
parts.answer: x² − y² = 5 and xy = −6, so x² − 36/x² = 5, giving x⁴ − 5x² − 36 = 0
parts.working: M1 equate real and imaginary parts; M1 eliminate y; A1 given quartic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the square roots of 5 − 12i.
parts.working: M1 x² = 9 (x² = −4 rejected); A1 both roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the square roots of 24 + 10i in the form a + ib, where a and b are real, showing all your working.
parts.working: M1 x² − y² = 24, xy = 5; M1 x⁴ − 24x² − 25 = 0; A1 x² = 25; A1 x = ±5, y = ±1; A1 both roots stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the modulus of each square root and verify that its square equals |24 + 10i|.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the square roots of 1 + 4√3 i in the form x + iy, where x and y are exact.
parts.working: Modulus of 1 + 4√3 i is √(1 + 48) = 7 (M1). x² + y² = 7 and x² − y² = 1 give x² = 4 and y² = 3 (M1). 2xy = 4√3 > 0, so x and y have the same sign: ±(2 + √3 i) (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the square roots of 15 − 8i in the form x + iy.
parts.working: Modulus 17: x² + y² = 17 and x² − y² = 15 give x² = 16, y² = 1 (M1, M1). 2xy = −8, so x and y have opposite signs: x = 4, y = −1 or x = −4, y = 1 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z² − (3 + i)z + (4 + 3i) = 0, giving the roots in the form x + iy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two square roots of 1 − i, giving each in the form re^{iθ}.
parts.working: 1 − i = √2 e^{−iπ/4} (M1). Square roots have modulus (√2)^(1/2) = 2^(1/4) (M1). Arguments are −π/8 and −π/8 + π = 7π/8 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the square roots of −3 + 4i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the quadratic equation z² − 3z + (3 − i) = 0, giving your answers in the form x + iy.
parts.working: M1 discriminant 9 − 4(3 − i) = −3 + 4i; M1 z = (3 ± (1 + 2i))/2; A1 2 + i and 1 − i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z² = z*, where z* is the complex conjugate of z. Give your roots in the form x + iy.
parts.working: Taking moduli: |z|² = |z|, so |z| = 0 or |z| = 1 (M1, M1). If z = 0 that is a root. If |z| = 1 then z* = 1/z, so z² = 1/z and z³ = 1 (M1). The cube roots of 1 are 1 and −1/2 ± (√3/2)i (M1, A1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let w = 1 + √3 i. Express w in the form re^{iθ}, and hence find the principal square root of w in the form x + iy with exact x and y.
parts.working: w = 2e^{iπ/3} (M1). Square roots have modulus √2 and argument π/6 (M1, M1). √2(cos π/6 + i sin π/6) = √2(√3/2 + i/2) = (√6 + √2 i)/2 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z⁴ = 7 − 24i, giving the four roots in the form x + iy with exact values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The polynomial p(z) is defined by p(z) = z³ − 5z² + 17z − 13. Show that z = 1 is a root of p(z) = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the other two roots of p(z) = 0 in the form x + iy.
parts.working: M1 divide by (z − 1): z² − 4z + 13; A1 quadratic factor; M1 solve: (4 ± √(−36))/2; A1 2 ± 3i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 + i is a root of the equation z³ − 3z² + 4z − 2 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find all the roots of the equation.
parts.working: Since the coefficients are real, 1 − i is also a root (M1). Dividing: z³ − 3z² + 4z − 2 = (z − 1)(z² − 2z + 2) (M1). Roots 1, 1 + i and 1 − i (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that z = −2 is a root of z³ + 8 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the other two roots of z³ + 8 = 0, in the form x + iy with exact values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation z² + pz + q = 0, where p and q are real, has root 2 − 3i. Find p and q.
parts.working: Since p and q are real, 2 + 3i is also a root (M1). Sum of roots = 4 = −p, so p = −4 (M1, A1). Product = (2 − 3i)(2 + 3i) = 13 = q (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cubic equation z³ − 3z² + 9z − 27 = 0 has real coefficients and has root 3i. Write down another root.
parts.working: Complex roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the third root.
parts.working: Sum of roots = 3 (from the z² coefficient), so the third root is 3 − (3i) − (−3i) = 3 (M1, A1). Check: z³ − 3z² + 9z − 27 = (z − 3)(z² + 9).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z⁴ + 4 = 0, giving each root in the form re^{iθ} with −π < θ ≤ π.
parts.working: z⁴ = −4 = 4e^{iπ}, so |z| = √2 (M1). The arguments satisfy 4θ = π + 2kπ, giving θ = π/4, 3π/4, −3π/4, −π/4 (M1, M1, A1, A1). Check: (1 + i)⁴ = −4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z³ = 1, giving the roots in the form x + iy with exact values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let ω = −1/2 + (√3/2)i. Show that 1 + ω + ω² = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation z³ + pz² + 9z + q = 0, where p and q are real, has root 2 + i. The third root is real. Find p, q and the real root.
parts.working: Other root 2 − i. Let the real root be r. Product of the pair is 5, so 5r = −q (M1). Sum of products of pairs: 5 + 4r = 9 gives r = 1 (M1, A1). Sum of roots = 4 + 1 = 5 = −p, so p = −5 (M1). q = −5 (A1). Check: (z − 1)(z² − 4z + 5) = z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cubic polynomial z³ + az + b, where a and b are real, has root 1 + i. (i) State the other complex root. (ii) Find a and b. (iii) Find the real root.
parts.working: (i) 1 − i by conjugate roots (B1). (ii) No z² term, so the sum of the roots is 0 and the real root is −2 (M1, A1). Sum of pairwise products: 2 + (−2 − 2i) + (−2 + 2i) = −2, so a = −2 (M1, A1). Product of roots = 2 × (−2) = −4 = −b, so b = 4 (M1, A1). (iii) z = −2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Verify that z = 1 + 2i is a root of the equation z⁴ − 2z³ + 6z² − 2z + 5 = 0.
parts.working: B1 z² and z³ (or z⁴) correct; M1 substitute; A1 sum equals 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the other three roots of the equation.
parts.working: B1 1 − 2i (conjugate, real coefficients); M1 quadratic factor z² − 2z + 5; M1 divide: z² + 1; A1 ±i.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation z³ + az² + bz + 10 = 0, where a and b are real, has a root 1 + 3i. Write down a second root and find the quadratic factor of z³ + az² + bz + 10 with these two roots.
parts.working: B1 conjugate; M1 sum 2, product 10; A1 z² − 2z + 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of a and b and the third root.
parts.working: M1 (z² − 2z + 10)(z + c) has constant 10c = 10; A1 c = 1, third root −1; M1 expand z³ − z² + 8z + 10; A1 a = −1, b = 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 + i is a root of z⁴ − 4z³ + 8z² − 8z + 4 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find all the roots, stating any repeated roots.
parts.working: z⁴ − 4z³ + 8z² − 8z + 4 = (z² − 2z + 2)² (M1, M1). z² − 2z + 2 = 0 gives 1 ± i (M1). Each root is a repeated root of the quartic (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation z⁴ − 2z³ + 6z² − 8z + 8 = 0 has real coefficients and root 2i. Write down a second root and explain why.
parts.answer: −2i; complex roots of real polynomials occur in conjugate pairs
parts.working: The complex conjugate −2i is also a root (B1, B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that 1 + i is a root and find all four roots.
parts.working: (z² + 4)(z² − 2z + 2) = z⁴ − 2z³ + 6z² − 8z + 8 (M1, M1). Roots of z² + 4 are ±2i, roots of z² − 2z + 2 are 1 ± i, so 1 + i is a root (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation z² + (2 + i)z + k = 0, where k is a complex constant, has root z = i. Find k and the other root.
parts.working: i² + (2 + i)i + k = 0 gives −1 + 2i − 1 + k = 0, so k = 2 − 2i (M1, M1, A1). Sum of roots = −(2 + i), so the other root is −(2 + i) − i = −2 − 2i (M1, A1). Check: product i(−2 − 2i) = 2 − 2i = k.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z⁴ − 2z² + 4 = 0, giving each root in the form x + iy with exact values.
parts.working: Let w = z²: w² − 2w + 4 = 0 gives w = 1 ± √3 i (M1). Since ((√6 + √2 i)/2)² = 1 + √3 i, the roots with z² = 1 + √3 i are ±(√6 + √2 i)/2 (M1, A1). Conjugate values give z² = 1 − √3 i and roots ±(√6 − √2 i)/2 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write z⁴ − 2z² + 4 as a product of two quadratic factors with real coefficients, each containing √6.
parts.working: (z² + 2)² − 6z² = z⁴ + 4z² + 4 − 6z² = z⁴ − 2z² + 4 (M1). So the factors are z² + 2 − √6 z and z² + 2 + √6 z (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The lines l and m have vector equations
l: r = (i + 2j − k) + s(2i − j + 3k)
m: r = (5i − j + 4k) + t(i − j + k).
Show that l and m intersect and find the position vector of the point of intersection.
parts.working:
M1 equate two components, e.g. 1 + 2s = 5 + t and 2 − s = −1 − t
A1 s = 1, t = −2
A1 check third component: −1 + 3 = 2 = 4 − 2
A1 3i + j + 2k

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two lines have equations
l₁: r = (2, 0, 1) + s(1, 2, −1)
l₂: r = (1, 3, 0) + t(2, 1, 1).
Show that the lines are skew.
parts.answer: Not parallel; the equations 2 + s = 1 + 2t, 2s = 3 + t give s = 7/3, t = 5/3, but then z: 1 − 7/3 = −4/3 ≠ 5/3, so no intersection; hence skew
parts.working:
B1 directions not parallel
M1 solve two component equations
A1 s = 7/3, t = 5/3
A1 third equation fails, so skew

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acute angle between the directions of the two lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The points A and B have position vectors 3i − j + 2k and 5i + 3j − 4k. Find a vector equation of the line AB.
parts.working:
B1 direction AB = 2i + 4j − 6k
B1 correct equation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether the point C(8, 9, −13) lies on the line AB.
parts.answer: Yes: λ = 2.5 using direction 2i + 4j − 6k (or μ = 5 using i + 2j − 3k) satisfies all three components
parts.working:
M1 solve one component, test the others
A1 C lies on AB

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether the point D(7, 6, −5) lies on the line AB.
parts.answer: No: x gives λ = 2 but then z = 2 − 12 = −10 ≠ −5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The points P(2, −1, 4), Q(5, 2, 1) and R(8, 5, −2) are given. (a) Show that P, Q and R are collinear. (b) The point (11, 8, k) lies on the line through P, Q and R. Find the value of k.
parts.working: Q − P = 3i + 3j − 3k and R − P = 6i + 6j − 6k = 2(Q − P) (M1 A1); the point P + 3(Q − P) = (11, 8, −5), so k = −5 (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The points A(2, −3, 5) and B(4, 1, −1) are given. (a) Find a vector equation of the line AB. (b) Show that the point C(6, 5, −7) lies on AB.
parts.answer: (a) r = 2i − 3j + 5k + λ(2i + 4j − 6k)  (b) C lies on AB, at λ = 2
parts.working: Direction AB = B − A = 2i + 4j − 6k (M1 A1); r = a + λd with a = OA (A1); C − A = 4i + 8j − 12k = 2d, so C is at λ = 2 and lies on AB (M1 A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three lines are given by
l₁: r = (1, −2, 3) + λ(2, −4, 6)
l₂: r = (0, 1, 1) + μ(−1, 2, −3)
l₃: r = (1, −8, 11) + ν(1, 1, −1).
Show that l₁ and l₂ are parallel and distinct.
parts.answer: (2, −4, 6) = −2(−1, 2, −3), so parallel; (0, 1, 1) − (1, −2, 3) = (−1, 3, −2) is not a multiple of the direction, so distinct
parts.working:
B1 parallel directions
B1 a point of l₂ is not on l₁

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that l₁ and l₃ intersect, and find the point of intersection.
parts.working:
M1 equate components
A1 λ = 1, ν = 2, all three equations satisfied
A1 (3, −6, 9)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether l₂ and l₃ intersect.
parts.answer: They do not intersect: from x and y, μ = −10/3, ν = 7/3, but then z gives 11 on l₂ and 26/3 on l₃; the lines are not parallel, so they are skew
parts.working:
M1 solve two equations
A1 μ = −10/3, ν = 7/3
A1 third equation fails, skew

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line l passes through the point (−1, a, 1) and has direction 2i + j + 2k. The line m has equation r = (i + 6j + 2k) + t(2i − j + 3k). Given that l and m intersect, find the value of the constant a and the point of intersection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acute angle between l and m.
parts.working:
M1 scalar product 4 − 1 + 6 = 9
M1 cos θ = 9/(3√14)
A1 36.7°

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two delivery drones in Islamabad fly in straight lines. Relative to a fixed origin, with distances in metres, their paths are
Drone A: r = (0, 0, 10) + s(4, 3, 1)
Drone B: r = (20, −7, 8) + t(−2, 4, 1).
Show that the paths do not cross.

parts.text: A student says, 'There is a 95% probability that the population mean lies in this confidence interval.' Explain why this statement is incorrect.
parts.answer: The population mean is a fixed value, so it either lies in the interval or it does not; the 95% describes the proportion of intervals, constructed this way from repeated samples, that would contain the mean
parts.working: The mean μ is fixed, not random (B1); the 95% is a long-run proportion of intervals containing μ (B2)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 50 values of a variable X gives a 95% confidence interval for the population mean of (24.6, 27.8), calculated using an unbiased estimate s² of the population variance. Find the sample mean and the value of s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find Σx and Σx² for the sample, giving Σx² to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mobile network claims that 40% of its customers use its streaming service. In a random sample of 450 customers, 150 use the service. Calculate an approximate 90% confidence interval for the proportion of customers who use the service.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the network's claim.
parts.answer: 0.4 lies outside the interval, so the evidence suggests the claim is too high
parts.working: B1 0.4 not in the interval, claim doubtful.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate an approximate 99% confidence interval from the same data and state whether it leads to the same conclusion about the claim.
parts.answer: (0.276, 0.391); yes, 0.4 still lies outside the interval, so the claim still appears too high
parts.working: M1 1/3 ± 2.576√((1/3)(2/3)/450). A1 (0.276, 0.391) and 0.4 not in the interval, same conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a random sample of 400 households in Peshawar, 96 had solar panels. An approximate α% confidence interval for the proportion of households with solar panels was found to be (0.2, 0.28). Find α, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the width of a 95% confidence interval based on the same sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each of 30 students independently takes a random sample from the same population and calculates a 90% confidence interval for the population mean μ. Find the expected number of intervals that do not contain μ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at most one of the 30 intervals does not contain μ.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The masses, in grams, of a random sample of 8 mangoes from an orchard near Multan are:
212, 198, 225, 240, 205, 219, 230, 211
Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of the masses, giving the variance correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 12 values of X gives Σx = 372 and Σx² = 11 870. Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by an unbiased estimate of a population parameter.
parts.answer: An estimate whose expected value (mean over all possible samples) equals the parameter

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a random sample of 250 cars passing a toll plaza near Islamabad, 85 were hybrid or electric. Find an unbiased estimate of the proportion of all cars passing the plaza that are hybrid or electric.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the standard deviation of the sample proportion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 10 values of a variable X has Σx = 165 and Σx² = 2785. (a) Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean. (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The masses, in kilograms, of a random sample of six bags of flour from a shop in Multan are: 1.02, 0.98, 1.01, 0.99, 1.03, 0.97. Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and the population variance of the masses.
parts.working: Mean = 6.00/6 = 1.00 (B1); deviations from 1.00 have squares summing to 0.0028 (M1); unbiased variance = 0.0028/5 = 0.00056 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 8 values of a variable x has mean 12.5 and unbiased estimate of population variance 5.25. Let z = 4 − 3x. Find unbiased estimates of (a) the population mean of z, (b) the population variance of z.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lengths, x cm, of 40 randomly chosen fish caught at a fishing harbour are summarised by Σ(x − 50) = −36 and Σ(x − 50)² = 964. Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of the lengths.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second random sample of 60 fish has mean length 48.6 cm. Find the best estimate of the population mean using both samples together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: From a random sample of 25 observations, unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance were found to be 12.4 and 3.5 respectively. Find Σx and Σx² for the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One further observation of value 15 is added to the sample. Find the new unbiased estimate of the population variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 20 values of y gives Σy = 88 and Σy² = 720. The variable x is related to y by y = 2x − 7. (a) Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean of x. (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance of x, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: ȳ = 88/20 = 4.4, so x̄ = (4.4 + 7)/2 = 5.7 (M1 A1); unbiased variance of y is (720 − 20 × 4.4²)/19 = 332.8/19 (M1); variance of x = variance of y/4 = 4.38 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 15 values of a variable X has Σx = 225. An unbiased estimate of the population variance is 12. Find Σx².

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 8 values gives an unbiased estimate of the population variance of 3.2. Find the value of Σ(x − x̄)², and the estimate that would be obtained by dividing Σ(x − x̄)² by 8 instead of 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dividing by n − 1 is used for the unbiased estimate, and what happens when n is used.
parts.answer: Dividing by n − 1 gives an unbiased estimate because one degree of freedom is lost by using x̄; dividing by n gives an estimate that underestimates the population variance on average
parts.working: n − 1 corrects for using the sample mean, giving an unbiased estimate (B1); dividing by n underestimates on average (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two random samples are taken from the same population of daily electricity use, x kWh, for homes in Hyderabad.
Sample A: n = 20, Σx = 304, Σx² = 4700
Sample B: n = 30, Σx = 438, Σx² = 6540
Combine the samples to find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unbiased estimate of the population variance from sample A alone, and explain why the combined estimate is preferable.
parts.answer: 4.17; the combined estimate uses a larger sample so is more reliable

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student found the variance of a random sample of 25 values by dividing Σ(x − x̄)² by 25, obtaining 18.4. Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dividing by n tends to underestimate the population variance.
parts.answer: Deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is the value that minimises Σ(x − a)²; so Σ(x − x̄)² is on average smaller than Σ(x − μ)², and dividing by n − 1 corrects this
parts.working: B1 deviations from x̄ rather than μ. B1 Σ(x − x̄)² ≤ Σ(x − μ)², so dividing by n gives values that are too small on average.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of 14 values is summarised in the frequency table: the value 2 occurs 3 times, 4 occurs 5 times, 6 occurs 4 times and 8 occurs 2 times. (a) Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean. (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance, giving exact values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random sample of 10 values has mean 6 and unbiased estimate of population variance 4. An independent random sample of 5 values from the same population has mean 9 and unbiased estimate of population variance 1. The two samples are combined into one sample of 15 values. (a) Find the mean of the combined sample. (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance from the combined sample.
parts.working: Combined mean = (10 × 6 + 5 × 9)/15 = 7 (M1 A1); Σx² for first sample = 9 × 4 + 10 × 36 = 396 and for second sample = 4 × 1 + 5 × 81 = 409 (M1 M1); combined Σ(x − 7)² = 805 − 15 × 49 = 70 (A1); unbiased variance = 70/14 = 5 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The amount a customer spends in a café has mean Rs 400 and standard deviation Rs 120; the distribution is not normal. A random sample of 50 customers is taken. State the approximate distribution of the sample mean amount spent, giving its parameters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the sample mean is more than Rs 420.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lifetimes, in hours, of a certain type of battery have mean 30 and standard deviation 4. A random sample of 36 batteries is taken. Use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate the probability that the sample mean lifetime lies between 29 and 31 hours. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: X̄ is approximately N(30, 4²/36), so the standard deviation is 2/3 (M1); z = ±(31 − 30)/(2/3) = ±1.5 (M1); P(−1.5 < Z < 1.5) = 0.866 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of tonnes of rice in each of 50 independent sacks has mean 3.2 and variance 1.44. (a) State the mean and the variance of the total mass T of the 50 sacks. (b) Use a suitable approximation to find P(T < 150), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The population mean of a variable is 50 and its standard deviation is 6. A random sample of 9 values is taken. Use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate the probability that the sample mean exceeds 52.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of phone calls received per day by a helpline follows a Poisson distribution with mean 3.6. The numbers of calls on 40 randomly chosen days are recorded. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that the mean number of calls per day for these 40 days is less than 3.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Central Limit Theorem is needed in part (a).
parts.answer: The population (number of calls) is not normally distributed

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair six-sided die is thrown. Show that the score X has mean 3.5 and variance 35/12.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The die is thrown 60 times. Find the approximate probability that the mean score is greater than 3.8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The masses of parcels handled by a courier have standard deviation 5 kg and unknown mean μ. A random sample of n parcels is taken, where n is large. Find the smallest n such that the probability that the sample mean exceeds μ by more than 1 kg is less than 0.05.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the answer to part (a) does not depend on the distribution of the masses being normal.
parts.answer: n is large, so the sample mean is approximately normal by the Central Limit Theorem

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of emails received by a company per hour follows a Poisson distribution with mean 1.6. Find an approximate probability that the total number of emails received in a period of 50 hours is at most 70. Use a normal approximation with a continuity correction, and give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A population has standard deviation 6. A random sample of n values is taken from this population and its mean is X̄. Given that P(|X̄ − μ| < 1.5) ≥ 0.9, use the Central Limit Theorem and the value z = 1.645 to find the smallest value of n.
parts.working: Standard deviation of X̄ is 6/√n, so P(|X̄ − μ| < 1.5) = P(|Z| < 1.5√n/6) (M1); require 1.5√n/6 ≥ 1.645 (M1); √n ≥ 6.58, so n ≥ 43.3 (A1); smallest integer n = 44 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair four-sided die has faces numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. The die is thrown 48 times and the total score is T. (a) Find the mean and the variance of the score on one throw, and hence the mean and variance of T. (b) Use a normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate P(T ≤ 110), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: (a) per throw mean 2.5, variance 1.25; for T, mean 120 and variance 60  (b) 0.110

parts.label: a
parts.text: The time, in minutes, taken to complete one task is uniformly distributed between 2 and 6. Thirty independent tasks are carried out and T is their total time. (a) Find the mean and the variance of the time for one task. (b) Use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate P(T > 125), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The time taken to process a visa application has mean 5 minutes and standard deviation 1.5 minutes. An officer processes 100 randomly chosen applications in one shift. Find the approximate probability that the total processing time is more than 520 minutes.
parts.working: M1 total T: mean 500, variance 100 × 1.5² = 225. M1 approximately normal by CLT. M1 z = 20/15 = 1.333. A1 0.0912.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time t such that the officer has a 95% chance of finishing 100 applications within t minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 3x²/8 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Show that E(X) = 1.5 and Var(X) = 0.15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A random sample of 40 observations of X is taken. Find the approximate probability that the sample mean is less than 1.45.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each item produced by a factory is faulty independently with probability 0.2. A batch contains 100 items and N is the number of faulty items in the batch. (a) State the mean and variance of N. (b) Use a suitable normal approximation with a continuity correction to estimate P(N ≥ 25), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A continuous random variable X is uniformly distributed on the interval [0, 1]. A random sample of 48 independent values of X is taken, with sample mean X̄. (a) State the mean and variance of X. (b) Use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate P(X̄ ≤ 0.45), giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: (a) E(X) = 1/2 and Var(X) = 1/12 (B1 B1); (b) X̄ is approximately N(1/2, (1/12)/48) with standard deviation 1/24 (M1); z = (0.45 − 0.5) × 24 = −1.2 (M1); P(Z ≤ −1.2) = 0.115 (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Rawalpindi has 600 students. The principal wants a random sample of 30 students to answer a questionnaire about the canteen. Describe how random numbers could be used to choose the sample.
