parts.text: Given that all the balls taken are red, find the probability that the spinner showed 1. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a factory, 8% of items are defective. Each item is checked by a first inspector, who rejects a defective item with probability 0.9. Any defective item that she misses is checked by a second inspector, who rejects it with probability 0.7. Non-defective items are never rejected. Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is rejected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that an item is accepted, find the probability that it is defective. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On her journey to school in Multan, Ayesha passes three traffic lights. At each light, the probability that it is red is 0.4, independently of the others. Find the probability that exactly two of the lights are red. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Tree: 3 branches with two red and one green: 3 × 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.6 (M1, M1) = 0.288 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that at least one of the lights is red, find the probability that exactly two are red. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: P(at least one red) = 1 − 0.6³ = 0.784 (M1). P(exactly two | at least one) = 0.288/0.784 = 0.3673… (M1, A1) ≈ 0.367.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled. If the score is 1, 2 or 3, a coin with P(head) = 0.25 is tossed. If the score is 4, 5 or 6, a coin with P(head) = 0.7 is tossed. Find the probability of getting a head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that a head is obtained, find the probability that the die showed 1, 2 or 3. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ahmed and Bilal take turns to throw a fair six-sided die, starting with Ahmed. The first person to throw a 6 wins. If neither has thrown a 6 after each has had three throws, the game is a draw. Find the probability that Ahmed wins. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the game is a draw. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rule is changed so that the game continues until someone throws a 6. Show that the probability that Ahmed wins is 6/11.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bag A contains 4 red and 6 green balls. Bag B contains 5 red and 3 green balls. A fair coin is tossed: if it shows heads, two balls are taken at random from bag A without replacement; if tails, two balls are taken from bag B without replacement. Find the probability that the two balls are the same colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the two balls are the same colour, find the probability that they came from bag A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zainab plays two games of squash. The probability that she wins the first game is p. If she wins the first game, the probability that she wins the second is p + 0.3; if she loses the first game, the probability that she wins the second is ½p. The probability that she wins both games is 0.18. Find p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that she wins exactly one of the two games.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that she wins exactly one game, find the probability that it was the first game.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 2 red balls and 3 white balls. Ahmed and Bushra take turns to draw a ball at random without replacement, starting with Ahmed. The first person to draw a red ball wins and the game stops. Find the probability that Ahmed wins.
parts.working: Ahmed wins if the first red is drawn on draw 1 or draw 3 (draw 5 is impossible with 3 whites). P(R first) = 2/5 (M1). P(W, W, R) = (3/5)(2/4)(2/3) = 1/5 (M1, M1). Total 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that Bushra wins.
parts.working: Bushra wins if the first red is drawn on draw 2 or 4. P(W, R) = (3/5)(2/4) = 3/10 and P(W, W, W, R) = (3/5)(2/4)(1/3) = 1/10 (M1). Total 2/5 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dana throws a dart repeatedly at a target. Each throw hits the target with probability p, independently. She stops as soon as she hits the target, or after 3 throws if she has not hit it. Given that the probability she needs exactly 2 throws is 0.16, and that p > 0.5, find p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that she throws exactly 3 darts.
parts.working: She throws 3 darts only if the first two miss: (1 − p)² = 0.2² = 0.04 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.35 and P(B) = 0.45. Given that A and B are mutually exclusive, find P(A ∪ B) and the probability that neither A nor B occurs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given instead that A and B are independent, find P(A ∪ B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Find P(A ∪ B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that A and B are independent.
parts.working: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) (M1). 0.1 = 0.1, so they are independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events X and Y are independent, with P(X′) = 0.35 and P(Y) = 0.5. Find P(X ∪ Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. Find P(A ∪ B).
parts.working: Mutually exclusive, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.75 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A | B′).
parts.working: A ∩ B′ = A (since A and B do not overlap), so P(A ∩ B′) = 0.3 (M1). P(B′) = 0.55 (M1). P(A | B′) = 0.3/0.55 = 6/11 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: At a school in Lahore, a student is chosen at random. The probability that the student takes Urdu is 0.6, the probability that the student takes Computer Science is 0.35, and the probability that the student takes both is 0.15. Find the probability that the student takes neither subject.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a calculation, whether taking Urdu and taking Computer Science are independent.
parts.working: Compare P(Urdu) × P(CS) = 0.21 with P(both) = 0.15 (M1). They differ, so the events are not independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. Find P(A ∩ B) and the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether A and B are independent.
parts.answer: Independent, since P(A) × P(B) = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find P(A | B′).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three friends, Asad, Bushra and Chen, each try independently to solve a puzzle. The probabilities that they solve it are ½, ⅓ and ¼ respectively. Find the probability that the puzzle is solved by at least one of them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one of them solves the puzzle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.4, P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Find P(B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A | A ∪ B).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find P(A′ ∪ B′).
parts.working: A′ ∪ B′ is the complement of A ∩ B, so P = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9 (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three friends, Sana, Hamza and Omar, each take a driving theory test independently. The probabilities that they pass are 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 respectively. Find the probability that exactly two of them pass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one of them passes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Event A is 'the score is prime' and event B is 'the score is even'. Show that A and B are not independent.
parts.answer: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/2, P(A ∩ B) = P(2) = 1/6; since 1/6 ≠ 1/4, they are not independent
parts.working: Prime scores are 2, 3, 5 so P(A) = 1/2 (M1). Even scores 2, 4, 6 so P(B) = 1/2 and P(A ∩ B) = P(2) = 1/6 (M1). 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 ≠ 1/6, so the events are not independent (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A | B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.65. Show that A and B are independent.
parts.working: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.15 (M1). P(A) × P(B) = 0.15 (M1), equal to P(A ∩ B), so they are independent (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find P(A′ | B).
parts.working: Independence gives P(A′ | B) = P(A′) = 0.5 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fair six-sided die is thrown twice. Event A is 'the total is 7', event B is 'the first throw is a 4' and event C is 'the product of the two scores is even'. Show that A and B are independent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(C) and P(A ∩ C), and determine whether A and C are independent.
parts.working: P(C) = 1 − (1/2)(1/2) = 3/4 B1; a total of 7 needs one odd and one even score, so its product is always even: P(A ∩ C) = 1/6 M1 A1; (1/6)(3/4) = 1/8 ≠ 1/6, not independent A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find P(A ∪ C).
parts.working: Since A ⊂ C, P(A ∪ C) = P(C) = 3/4 B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A, B and C are independent, with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(C) = 0.3. Find P(A ∪ B ∪ C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one of the three events occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A ∪ B) = 0.9, P(A′ ∩ B) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ B′) = 0.4. Find P(A ∩ B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find P(A) and P(B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B are independent, with P(A ∪ B) = 0.72 and P(A) = 2P(B). Find P(A) and P(B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A′ ∩ B′).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. Find the probability that both counters are red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the counters are of different colours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 6 red counters and 4 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. Find the probability that the second counter is red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the second counter is red, find the probability that the first counter was red.
parts.working: P(first red and second red) = 1/3 (M1). P(first red | second red) = (1/3)/(3/5) = 5/9 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box contains 7 pens, of which 3 are defective. Two pens are picked at random without replacement. Find the probability that at least one of them is defective.
parts.working: P(no defective) = (4/7)(3/6) = 2/7 (M1). P(at least one) = 1 − 2/7 = 5/7 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A debating society in Islamabad has 5 boys and 7 girls. Two members are chosen at random to speak at an event, one after the other, without replacement. Find the probability that both chosen members are girls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cards numbered 1 to 6 are placed face down. Two cards are taken at random without replacement. Find the probability that both cards are odd.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the two cards add up to 7.
parts.working: The pairs {1, 6}, {2, 5} and {3, 4} give a sum of 7; there are C(6, 2) = 15 pairs, so 3/15 = 1/5 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box contains 12 chocolates: 5 caramel, 4 nut and 3 plain. Fatima takes three chocolates at random without replacement. Find the probability that the three chocolates are all of different types.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one of the three chocolates is caramel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly two of the three chocolates are nut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shelf holds 6 Urdu books and 4 English books. A student picks books at random, one at a time without replacement, until she picks an English book. Find the probability that the first English book is the third book picked.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that she picks at most two books.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that she needs to pick more than four books.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Three balls are taken at random without replacement. Find the probability that the three balls are all different colours.
parts.working: Choose the order of one of each colour: 3! orderings, probability (4 × 3 × 2)/(9 × 8 × 7) = 24/504 each (M1, M1). Total 6 × 24/504 = 2/7 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A box contains 10 light bulbs, of which 2 are defective. Bulbs are tested one at a time, without replacement, until a defective bulb is found. Find the probability that exactly 3 bulbs are tested.
parts.working: The first two bulbs are good and the third is defective: (8/10)(7/9)(2/8) = 112/720 = 7/45 (M1, M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at most 2 bulbs are tested.
parts.working: P(first defective) = 2/10 and P(first good, second defective) = (8/10)(2/9) = 16/90 (M1). Total 18/90 + 16/90 = 17/45 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sadia's drawer contains 5 black socks and 3 white socks. She takes socks at random, one at a time, without replacement. Find the probability that the first two socks she takes are a matching pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that she needs exactly 3 socks to obtain a matching pair.
parts.working: The first two socks must be different colours: 2 × (5/8)(3/7) = 30/56 = 15/28. After that the third sock always matches one of them (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ali picks 3 different numbers at random from 1 to 8, without replacement. Find the probability that all three numbers are even.
parts.working: Number of ways to choose 3 even numbers from {2, 4, 6, 8} = C(4, 3) = 4. Total ways to choose 3 numbers from 8 = C(8, 3) = 56 (M1, M1). Probability = 4/56 = 1/14 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains n red sweets and 4 green sweets. Two sweets are taken at random without replacement. The probability that both are red is ⅓. Show that n² − 5n − 6 = 0 and hence find n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the two sweets are of different colours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A third sweet is now taken from the bag. Given that the first two sweets were of different colours, find the probability that the third sweet is red.
parts.working: After one red and one green are removed: 5 red out of 8 B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 4 white counters and n black counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. The probability that they are of different colours is 4/7. Show that n² − 7n + 12 = 0.
parts.working: P(different colours) = 2 × (4/(n+4)) × (n/(n+3)) (M1). Set equal to 4/7: 56n = 4(n + 4)(n + 3) (M1). So 14n = n² + 7n + 12, i.e. n² − 7n + 12 = 0 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that there are fewer black counters than white counters, find n.
parts.working: n² − 7n + 12 = (n − 3)(n − 4) = 0 gives n = 3 or 4 (M1). Fewer black than white means n < 4, so n = 3 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bag B contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Balls are drawn one at a time, without replacement, until a red ball is drawn. Find the probability that exactly 3 balls are drawn.
parts.working: The first two balls are blue and the third is red: (6/10)(5/9)(4/8) = 120/720 (M1, M1) = 1/6 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that more than 2 balls are drawn.
parts.working: P(1st red) = 4/10 and P(1st blue, 2nd red) = (6/10)(4/9) (M1). P(more than 2 draws) = 1 − 4/10 − 24/90 = 1/3 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha picks 3 different numbers at random from the numbers 1 to 6, without replacement. Find the probability that the sum of the three numbers is 10.
parts.working: The sets with sum 10 are {1, 3, 6}, {1, 4, 5} and {2, 3, 5} (M1, M1). The total number of ways to choose 3 numbers is C(6, 3) = 20 (M1). Probability = 3/20 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A café records the drink chosen by 150 customers. Of the 75 customers under 30, 30 chose tea and 45 chose coffee. Of the 75 customers aged 30 or over, 50 chose tea and 25 chose coffee. A customer is chosen at random. Find the probability that the customer chose tea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the customer chose tea, given that the customer is under 30.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the events 'chose tea' and 'under 30' are independent.
parts.answer: Not independent, since P(tea | under 30) = 2/5 ≠ 8/15 = P(tea)
parts.working: Compare 2/5 with 8/15 M1; not equal so not independent A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Quetta has 90 teachers. 54 teach Science and 36 teach Arts. 30 of the teachers are women, and 18 of the women teach Science. A teacher is chosen at random. Find the probability that the teacher is a woman.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the teacher teaches Science, given that the teacher is a woman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A showroom has 200 cars. 120 use petrol and 80 use diesel. 50 cars are automatic and 30 of these are diesel. A car is chosen at random. Find P(automatic | petrol).
parts.working: Automatic petrol cars = 50 − 30 = 20, so P(automatic | petrol) = 20/120 = 1/6 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a calculation, whether 'petrol' and 'automatic' are independent events.
parts.answer: Not independent: P(petrol and automatic) = 0.1 but P(petrol) × P(automatic) = 0.15
parts.working: P(petrol and automatic) = 20/200 = 0.1 (M1). P(petrol) × P(automatic) = 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.15. These differ, so the events are not independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.45, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.56. Show that A and B are independent.
parts.working: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.09 (M1). P(A) × P(B) = 0.09 (M1), so A and B are independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a survey of 150 residents of Karachi, 70 said they enjoy cricket, 60 said they enjoy football and 25 said they enjoy both. A resident is chosen at random. Find the probability that the resident enjoys neither sport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a resident enjoys cricket, given that the resident enjoys football.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a college in Peshawar there are 200 first-year students: 120 girls and 80 boys. Of the girls, 72 study science and the rest study arts. Of the boys, 48 study science and the rest study arts. Copy and complete a two-way table for this information.
parts.answer: Girls: science 72, arts 48; boys: science 48, arts 32; totals: science 120, arts 80

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student is chosen at random. Show that the events 'the student is a girl' and 'the student studies science' are independent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the student is a boy, given that the student studies arts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A class of 40 students took a test. 25 students passed and 15 failed. There are 22 boys and 18 girls, and 12 of the girls passed. Complete the two-way table showing the number of boys who passed and the number of boys who failed, and the number of girls who failed.
parts.answer: Boys passed 13, boys failed 9, girls failed 6
parts.working: Boys passed = 25 − 12 = 13 (M1). Boys failed = 22 − 13 = 9 and girls failed = 18 − 12 = 6 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(passed | boy) and P(passed | girl).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether passing the test is independent of gender.
parts.working: Independence needs equal conditional probabilities for boys and girls (M1). 13/22 ≈ 0.59 and 2/3 ≈ 0.67 are different, so they are not independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, P(A | B) = 0.4 and P(B | A) = 0.5. Find P(A) and P(B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that A and B are independent.
parts.working: The product P(A) × P(B) = 0.2 equals P(A ∩ B) (M1), so the events are independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.4, P(B | A) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.6. Find P(B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A | B) and state whether A and B are independent.
parts.working: P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5 (M1). P(A) × P(B) = 0.16 ≠ 0.2 = P(A ∩ B), so not independent (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a survey of 80 households in Faisalabad, 48 own a bicycle, 36 own a motorbike and 12 own neither. Find the number of households that own both a bicycle and a motorbike.
parts.working: Own at least one = 80 − 12 = 68, so both = 48 + 36 − 68 = 16 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a household owns a bicycle, given that it owns a motorbike.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The members of a gym in Karachi are classified as follows. Male, morning: 24; male, evening: x; female, morning: 36; female, evening: 54. The events 'a randomly chosen member is male' and 'a randomly chosen member attends in the morning' are independent. Find x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a randomly chosen member who attends in the evening is female.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Two members are chosen at random without replacement. Find the probability that both attend in the morning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A group of 120 people contains 72 men and 48 women. 60 people drink tea and the rest drink coffee. Gender and drink are independent. Complete the two-way table, giving the number of women who drink tea.
parts.answer: Women drink tea 24; men drink tea 36; men coffee 36; women coffee 24
parts.working: P(tea) = 60/120 = 1/2, so expected women who drink tea = 48 × 1/2 = 24 (M1). The other entries follow: men tea 36, men coffee 36, women coffee 24 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the probability that a person who drinks tea is a woman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.5. Find P(B).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(A′ ∩ B′).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 2/5, P(B) = 1/2 and P(A ∪ B) = 7/10. Show that P(A ∩ B) = 1/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Events A and B satisfy P(B) = 0.3, P(A | B) = 0.4 and P(A | B′) = 0.1. Find P(A).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(B | A), giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the values of the constant k for which the equation 2x² + kx + 18 = 0 has two equal roots.
parts.working: Equal roots: b² − 4ac = 0 (M1). k² − 4(2)(18) = 0 so k² = 144 (A1). k = ±12 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation 3x² − 5x + 4 = 0 has no real roots.
parts.working: b² − 4ac = 25 − 48 = −23 (M1). Negative, so no real roots (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant p for which the equation x² + 6x + p = 0 has two distinct real roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 2x + c is a tangent to the curve y = x² − 4x + 7. Find the value of c and the coordinates of the point where the line touches the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation 4x² + (m − 1)x + 1 = 0 has equal roots. Find the possible values of the constant m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant c for which the line y = 3x + c does not meet the curve y = x² + x − 3.
parts.working: Equate: x² + x − 3 = 3x + c, so x² − 2x − (3 + c) = 0 (M1). No real solutions needs discriminant < 0: 4 + 4(3 + c) < 0 (M1), so 16 + 4c < 0 and c < −4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that c = −4 gives a line that touches the curve, and state the coordinates of the point of contact.
parts.working: With c = −4, x² − 2x + 1 = 0, so (x − 1)² = 0 and the discriminant is zero: the line is a tangent (M1). The repeated root is x = 1 (M1) and y = 3(1) − 4 = −1, so the point of contact is (1, −1) (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation kx² + (k + 3)x + 1 = 0 is a quadratic equation in x, where k is a non-zero constant. Show that its discriminant is k² + 2k + 9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By completing the square, show that the equation has two distinct real roots for every non-zero value of k.
parts.working: (k + 1)² + 8 (M1). A square is never negative, so the discriminant is at least 8 > 0: two distinct real roots for every k ≠ 0 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant m for which the line y = mx − 1 does not meet the curve y = x² + 3x + 3.
parts.working: x² + 3x + 3 = mx − 1 gives x² + (3 − m)x + 4 = 0 (M1). No intersection: (3 − m)² − 16 < 0 (M1). Critical values 3 − m = ±4, m = −1, 7 (A1). −1 < m < 7 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x² − 2kx + 3k + 4 lies completely above the x-axis. Find the set of possible values of the constant k.
parts.working: No real roots of x² − 2kx + 3k + 4 = 0: 4k² − 4(3k + 4) < 0 (M1). k² − 3k − 4 < 0 (A1). (k − 4)(k + 1) < 0, critical values −1, 4 (M1). −1 < k < 4 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant k for which 2x² − 4kx + (k + 6) > 0 for all real values of x.
parts.working: The graph is a positive quadratic, so it is above the x-axis for all x when the discriminant is negative (M1). (−4k)² − 4(2)(k + 6) < 0 gives 16k² − 8k − 48 < 0 (M1), so 2k² − k − 6 < 0 (A1). (2k + 3)(k − 2) < 0 (M1), so −3/2 < k < 2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = mx + 2 is a tangent to the curve y = 3x² − 2x + 6. Find the two possible values of m, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the tangent with m = −2 + 4√3, find the exact coordinates of the point of contact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = mx + 5 is a tangent to the curve y = 2x² − 3x + 7. Find the two possible values of m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each value of m, find the coordinates of the point of contact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation kx² + 6x + (k − 8) = 0, where k ≠ 0, has two distinct real roots. Find the set of possible values of k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of k for which the equation has equal roots and that root is positive. State the root.
parts.working: Equal roots when k = −1 or 9 (B1). k = −1: −x² + 6x − 9 = 0, x = 3 (positive) (M1). k = 9: 9x² + 6x + 1 = 0, x = −1/3 (negative), so k = −1, root 3 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line x + 2y = c is a tangent to the curve y = 4/x. Find the possible values of c, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point of contact for the positive value of c.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 2x + k meets the curve y = x² − 4x + 9 at two points P and Q. The x-coordinates of P and Q differ by 4. Find the value of k.
parts.working: x² − 4x + 9 = 2x + k gives x² − 6x + (9 − k) = 0 (M1). Roots α, β: α + β = 6 and αβ = 9 − k. (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ = 36 − 4(9 − k) = 4k (M1). (α − β)² = 16, so 4k = 16 and k = 4 (A1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of P and Q.
parts.working: With k = 4 the equation is x² − 6x + 5 = 0, so x = 1 or 5 (M1). y = 2x + 4 gives y = 6 or 14 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x² − 1 has tangents through the point (0, −5). Each tangent has equation y = mx − 5 for some constant m. Show that m² = 16 for each tangent and state the two equations of the tangents.
parts.working: Equate x² − 1 = mx − 5, giving x² − mx + 4 = 0 (M1). Tangency: m² − 16 = 0 (M1), so m = ±4 (A1). Tangents: y = 4x − 5 and y = −4x − 5 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point of contact of each tangent.
parts.working: Repeated root x = m/2, so x = 2 for m = 4 and x = −2 for m = −4 (M1). y = x² − 1 = 3 in both cases (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 2x² − 12x + 23 in the form a(x + b)² + c, where a, b and c are constants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence state the minimum value of 2x² − 12x + 23 and the value of x at which it occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 7 + 8x − x² in the form a − (x − b)².

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordinates of the maximum point of the curve y = 7 + 8x − x².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express x² + 5x + 1 in the form (x + p)² + q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the equation x² + 5x + 1 = 0, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 3x² + 12x + 7 in the form a(x + b)² + c, where a, b and c are constants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the equation 3x² + 12x + 7 = 0, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 9 − 6x − x² in the form p − (x + q)², where p and q are constants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence state the coordinates of the maximum point of the curve y = 9 − 6x − x².
parts.working: (x + 3)² ≥ 0 is subtracted, so the maximum occurs at x = −3 where y = 18 (B1).

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 3x² + 18x + 20 for x ≥ k, where k is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express f(x) in the form a(x + b)² + c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the smallest value of k for which f is a one-one function.
parts.working: B1: the vertex is at x = −3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For this value of k, state the range of f.

practice.stem: The function g is defined for all real x by g(x) = 4x² − 12x + 13.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express g(x) in the form (ax + b)² + c, where a > 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence explain why g(x) > 0 for all x, and find the range of the function h(x) = 1/g(x).
parts.working: (2x − 3)² ≥ 0 so g(x) ≥ 4 (B1). Largest value of h is 1/4 at x = 3/2 (M1). h(x) > 0 and tends to 0 as |x| grows: 0 < h(x) ≤ 1/4 (A1).

practice.stem: A farmer near Sahiwal has 60 m of fencing. She uses it for three sides of a rectangular goat pen; the fourth side is an existing brick wall. The two sides perpendicular to the wall each have length x m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area A m² of the pen is given by A = 60x − 2x².
parts.working: Side parallel to wall = 60 − 2x, so A = x(60 − 2x) (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express A in the form p − q(x − r)² and hence find the greatest possible area and the value of x that gives it.
parts.answer: A = 450 − 2(x − 15)²; greatest area 450 m² when x = 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is thrown upwards from a balcony in Karachi. Its height above the ground, h metres, after t seconds is given by h = 1 + 12t − 3t². Express h in the form a − b(t − c)², where a, b and c are constants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the greatest height reached by the ball and the time taken to reach it.
parts.working: The term −3(t − 2)² is at most 0, so the greatest height is 13 m when t = 2 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 2x² + 5x − 3 in the form 2(x + p)² − q, where p and q are constants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the inequality 2x² + 5x − 3 < 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two positive numbers x and y have x + y = 20. Show that x² + y² = 2(x − 10)² + 200.
parts.working: Substitute y = 20 − x: x² + 400 − 40x + x² = 2x² − 40x + 400 (M1). Complete the square: 2(x² − 20x + 100) + 200 = 2(x − 10)² + 200 (M1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the least possible value of x² + y², and the values of x and y at which it occurs.
parts.working: 2(x − 10)² is least when x = 10, giving 200 (M1). Then y = 10 (A1).

practice.stem: The function f is defined for all real x by f(x) = −2x² + 8x + c, where c is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express f(x) in the form a(x + b)² + d, giving d in terms of c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The line y = 3 is a tangent to the curve y = f(x). Find the value of c.
parts.working: The maximum value 8 + c equals 3 (M1), c = −5 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For this value of c, find the set of values of x for which f(x) > −15.

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 1 for x ≤ 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express f(x) in the form a(x + b)² + c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of f.
parts.working: f is decreasing for x ≤ 1, f(1) = −5 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find an expression for f⁻¹(x) and state its domain.
parts.working: y = 2(x − 2)² − 7 so (x − 2)² = (y + 7)/2 (M1). x ≤ 1 so take the negative root: x = 2 − √((y + 7)/2) (A1). Domain x ≥ −5 (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The expression x² + 2ax + 3a, where a is a constant, can be written as (x + a)² + k. Find k in terms of a.
parts.working: x² + 2ax = (x + a)² − a², so x² + 2ax + 3a = (x + a)² + 3a − a² (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of a for which the expression has a minimum value that is positive.
parts.working: The minimum value is 3a − a², which is positive when a(3 − a) > 0 (M1). So 0 < a < 3 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f(x) = −2x² + kx + 3, where k is a constant, has a maximum value of 11. Express f(x) in the form −2(x − p)² + q, giving p and q in terms of k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find both values of k and, for each value, the x-coordinate of the maximum point.
parts.working: Maximum value 3 + k²/8 = 11 gives k² = 64 (M1), so k = ±8 (A1). The maximum is at x = k/4, so x = 2 or −2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2x − 7√x + 3 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2^(2x) − 9 × 2^x + 8 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x² − 5|x| + 6 = 0, where |x| is the modulus of x.
parts.working: Since x² = |x|², let u = |x|: u² − 5u + 6 = 0 (M1). (u − 2)(u − 3) = 0, so u = 2 or u = 3 (M1). |x| = 2 gives x = ±2 and |x| = 3 gives x = ±3 (A1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2(x + 1)² − 7(x + 1) + 3 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x^(2/3) − 5x^(1/3) + 4 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact real solutions of the equation 3x² + 4 = 20/x².
parts.working: Multiply by x²: 3x⁴ + 4x² − 20 = 0 (M1). (3x² + 10)(x² − 2) = 0 (M1 A1). x² = −10/3 has no real solution; x = ±√2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x − 1/x = 2, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 9^x − 4 × 3^(x+1) + 27 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 6/x² + 1 = 5/x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation (x² − 3x)² − 2(x² − 3x) − 8 = 0.
parts.working: Let u = x² − 3x: u² − 2u − 8 = 0 (M1), u = 4 or −2 (A1). x² − 3x − 4 = 0 gives x = 4 or −1 (A1). x² − 3x + 2 = 0 gives x = 1 or 2 (M1 A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant k for which the equation x − 4√x + k = 0 has two distinct real roots.
parts.working: Let u = √x (u ≥ 0): u² − 4u + k = 0 needs two distinct non-negative roots u (M1). Discriminant 16 − 4k > 0 gives k < 4 (A1). Sum of roots 4 > 0 and product k ≥ 0 (k = 0 gives u = 0 or 4, i.e. x = 0 or 16) (M1). 0 ≤ k < 4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation when k = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation (x + 1)⁴ − 10(x + 1)² + 9 = 0.
parts.working: Let v = (x + 1)²: v² − 10v + 9 = 0, so (v − 1)(v − 9) = 0 (M1). v = 1 gives (x + 1)² = 1, so x = 0 or x = −2 (M1, A1). v = 9 gives (x + 1)² = 9, so x = 2 or x = −4 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation x⁴ − kx² + 16 = 0, where k is a constant, has four distinct real roots. Find the set of possible values of k.
parts.working: Let y = x²: y² − ky + 16 = 0. Four distinct real roots for x needs two distinct positive roots for y (M1). Discriminant k² − 64 > 0 (M1), and the sum of roots k > 0 (M1). So k > 8 (A2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation √(2x + 5) = x − 1, giving your answer in exact form.
parts.working: Square both sides: 2x + 5 = x² − 2x + 1 (M1), so x² − 4x − 4 = 0 (M1). x = 2 ± 2√2 (M1), so the possible values are 2 + 2√2 and 2 − 2√2 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one of the values from part (a) is rejected.
parts.answer: 2 − 2√2 ≈ −0.83 gives x − 1 < 0, but a square root is never negative
parts.working: For 2 − 2√2 the right-hand side x − 1 is negative, which is impossible for a square root (B1). So only x = 2 + 2√2 is valid (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the line y = x + 1 meets the curve y = x² − 3x + 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line passes through the points (1, 5) and (4, 8). Find the coordinates of the points where this line meets the curve y = x² − 6x + 10.
parts.working: Gradient = (8 − 5)/(4 − 1) = 1, so the line is y = x + 4 (M1). x² − 6x + 10 = x + 4 gives x² − 7x + 6 = 0 (M1), so (x − 1)(x − 6) = 0 and x = 1 or x = 6 (M1). Points (1, 5) and (6, 10) (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = −x − 3 and the curve y = x² + x + 1 are given. Show that the line does not meet the curve.
parts.answer: x² + x + 1 = −x − 3 gives x² + 2x + 4 = 0; discriminant 4 − 16 = −12 < 0, so no real solutions
parts.working: Equate: x² + 2x + 4 = 0 (M1). Discriminant b² − 4ac = 4 − 16 = −12 (M1), which is negative, so there are no real intersections (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least vertical distance between the line and the curve for real values of x.
parts.working: Vertical distance d = (x² + x + 1) − (−x − 3) = x² + 2x + 4 = (x + 1)² + 3 (M1). Least when (x + 1)² = 0, giving d = 3 at x = −1 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 2x + 1 meets the curve y = x² − 4x + 6 at the points A and B. Find the coordinates of A and B.
parts.working: x² − 4x + 6 = 2x + 1 gives x² − 6x + 5 = 0 (M1). (x − 1)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 1 or x = 5 (M1). When x = 1, y = 3, and when x = 5, y = 11, so A(1, 3) and B(5, 11) (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB.
parts.working: The midpoint of AB is (3, 7) (M1). AB has gradient (11 − 3)/(5 − 1) = 2, so the perpendicular has gradient −1/2 (M1). y − 7 = −½(x − 3), so y = −½x + 8.5 (A1).

practice.stem: The line 2x + y = 9 meets the curve x² + xy = 8 at the points A and B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact length of AB.

practice.stem: The curve y = 2x² − 5x + 3 and the line y = 3 − x meet at the points P and Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of P and Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of PQ.
parts.working: Midpoint (1, 2) (B1). Gradient PQ = −1 so perpendicular gradient 1 (M1). y − 2 = x − 1, y = x + 1 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 5 − 2x meets the curve y = 2x² − 3x + 1 at the points A and B. Find the exact x-coordinates of A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the coordinates of the midpoint of AB.
parts.working: The midpoint has x-coordinate (sum of roots)/2 = (1/2)/2 = 1/4 (M1). y = 5 − 2(1/4) = 4.5 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 2x + c meets the curve y = x² − x + 3 at two distinct points. Find the set of values of c.
parts.working: x² − x + 3 = 2x + c gives x² − 3x + (3 − c) = 0 (M1). Two distinct points needs discriminant 9 − 4(3 − c) > 0 (M1), so 4c − 3 > 0 (M1). c > 3/4 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A straight road has equation y = 0.5x + 3 and a railway track has equation y = 0.25x² − x + 4, where x and y are coordinates in km from a fixed point near Rawalpindi. Show that the road and the track meet at two points.
parts.answer: 0.25x² − 1.5x + 1 = 0, so x² − 6x + 4 = 0; discriminant 36 − 16 = 20 > 0, so two points
parts.working: Equate: 0.25x² − 1.5x + 1 = 0, which is x² − 6x + 4 = 0 (M1). Discriminant 36 − 16 = 20 > 0, so there are two distinct points (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact x-coordinates of the two points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance between the two points, in km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = mx + 2 does not meet the curve y = 2x² − 5x + 6. Find the set of possible values of the constant m, giving your answers in exact form.

practice.stem: The line y = kx − 2 meets the curve y = x² + 2 at two points. The x-coordinate of one point is four times the x-coordinate of the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the x-coordinates satisfy x² − kx + 4 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two possible values of k.
parts.working: Roots r and 4r: product 4r² = 4 so r = ±1 (M1 A1). Sum 5r = k, k = ±5 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the positive value of k, find the coordinates of the two points.

practice.stem: The curve C has equation xy = 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the line x + 2y = 10 meets C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant c for which the line x + 2y = c meets C at two distinct points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 3x + k meets the curve y = 2x² − 5x + 9 at two points whose x-coordinates are α and β. Given that α² + β² = 13, find the value of k.
parts.working: 2x² − 5x + 9 = 3x + k gives 2x² − 8x + (9 − k) = 0, so α + β = 4 and αβ = (9 − k)/2 (M1). α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 16 − (9 − k) = 7 + k (M1). 7 + k = 13 gives k = 6 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the line meets the curve at two distinct points for this value of k.
parts.working: With k = 6 the discriminant of 2x² − 8x + 3 = 0 is 64 − 24 = 40 (M1), which is positive (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line y = 2x + c meets the curve y = x² + 4 at the points P and Q. The midpoint of PQ lies on the line x + y = 10. Find the value of c.
parts.working: x² + 4 = 2x + c gives x² − 2x + (4 − c) = 0, so the x-coordinate of the midpoint is (2/2) = 1 (M1). The midpoint is on y = 2x + c, so its y-coordinate is 2 + c (M1). Using x + y = 10: 1 + 2 + c = 10, so c = 7 (A1). Check: discriminant 4 − 4(4 − 7) = 16 > 0 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordinates of the midpoint of PQ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² − 3x + 2 and the line L has equation y = mx − 2, where m is a constant. Show that the x-coordinates of the points where L meets C have product 4, and explain what this tells you about their signs.
parts.answer: x² − (3 + m)x + 4 = 0, so the product of the roots is 4 > 0; the two x-coordinates always have the same sign
parts.working: Equate: x² − 3x + 2 = mx − 2, so x² − (3 + m)x + 4 = 0 (M1). The product of the roots is c/a = 4 (M1). Since 4 > 0 both roots have the same sign, so the two points lie on the same side of the y-axis for every m (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of m for which L meets C at two distinct points.

practice.stem: The curve C has equation y = x² − 2x − 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where C crosses the axes and the coordinates of its vertex. Describe the shape of C.
parts.answer: x-axis (−2, 0) and (4, 0); y-axis (0, −8); vertex (1, −9); U-shaped (minimum) parabola
parts.working: (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0 (M1), (−2, 0), (4, 0) (A1). (0, −8) (B1). (x − 1)² − 9 gives vertex (1, −9), U-shape since coefficient of x² positive (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the inequality x² − 2x − 8 < 0.
parts.working: B1: the curve is below the x-axis between the roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² − 6x + 5. Find the coordinates of the points where C crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the vertex of C and describe the shape of C.
parts.working: x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4, so the vertex is (3, −4) (M1). The coefficient of x² is positive, so C is U-shaped with a minimum at the vertex (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = −x² + 4x + 12 is given. Find the coordinates of the points where the curve crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the maximum point of the curve.
parts.working: y = −(x − 2)² + 16, so the maximum point is (2, 16) (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = 2x² + 3x − 5 is given. Find the coordinates of the points where the curve crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the turning point, giving the y-coordinate as an exact fraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that x² − 2x + 5 is positive for all real values of x.
parts.working: x² − 2x + 5 = (x − 1)² + 4 (M1). Since (x − 1)² ≥ 0, the expression is at least 4, so it is positive for all x (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum value of y = x² − 2x + 5 and the coordinates of its minimum point.
parts.working: The minimum occurs when (x − 1)² = 0, i.e. x = 1, giving y = 4 (M1, A1).

practice.stem: The curve C has equation y = (3 − x)(x + 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a sketch of C, giving the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes and of its turning point.
parts.answer: ∩-shaped parabola; meets x-axis at (−1, 0) and (3, 0), y-axis at (0, 3); maximum point (1, 4)
parts.working: Roots −1 and 3 and y-intercept 3 (B1). Coefficient of x² is −1 so ∩-shape (B1). Vertex at x = 1, y = 2 × 2 = 4 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of real solutions of the equation (3 − x)(x + 1) = k when (i) k = 5, (ii) k = 4, (iii) k = 0.
parts.working: Maximum value 4: line y = 5 above the curve, none (B1); y = 4 touches at the vertex, one (B1); y = 0 cuts twice (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x² + px + 9 touches the x-axis. Find the possible values of the constant p.
parts.working: Touching the x-axis means the equation x² + px + 9 = 0 has equal roots (M1): p² − 4(9) = 0 (M1), so p² = 36 and p = ±6 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = 4 − (x − 1)(x + 3). Show that C can be written as y = 8 − (x + 1)².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the maximum point of C and the exact x-coordinates of the points where C crosses the x-axis.
parts.working: Maximum where (x + 1)² = 0, giving (−1, 8) (B1). y = 0 gives (x + 1)² = 8, so x = −1 ± 2√2 (M1, A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² + bx + c and the vertex of C is (3, −5). Find the values of b and c.
parts.working: The x-coordinate of the vertex is −b/2 = 3, so b = −6 (M1, A1). Substituting (3, −5): 9 − 18 + c = −5, so c = 4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact coordinates of the points where C meets the x-axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = 3x² − 10x + 3. Find the coordinates of the points where C crosses the axes and the coordinates of its vertex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² − px + q and crosses the x-axis at x = 1 and x = 7. Find the values of p and q.
parts.working: Sum of roots p = 1 + 7 = 8 and product of roots q = 1 × 7 = 7 (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the coordinates of the vertex of C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = x² + kx + 2k, where k is a constant, crosses the x-axis at two distinct points. Find the set of values of k.
parts.working: Discriminant k² − 4(2k) > 0 (M1), so k² − 8k > 0 (M1). k(k − 8) > 0 gives k < 0 or k > 8 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of k for which the minimum point of the curve lies on the x-axis.
parts.working: The minimum y-coordinate is 2k − k²/4 (M1). Setting it to zero: k(8 − k) = 0, so k = 0 or k = 8 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² − 4x + c and its vertex lies on the line y = 2x − 1. Find the value of c.
parts.working: Vertex x-coordinate is 2 and y-coordinate is 4 − 8 + c = c − 4 (M1). On the line: c − 4 = 2(2) − 1 = 3 (M1), so c = 7 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this value of c, explain how many points C has in common with the x-axis.
parts.working: The discriminant of x² − 4x + 7 is 16 − 28 = −12 < 0 (M1), so C does not meet the x-axis (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation |x² − 4| = k, where k is a constant, has real solutions. Find the number of real solutions when k = 2 and when k = 5.
parts.working: For k = 2: x² − 4 = 2 gives x² = 6, and x² − 4 = −2 gives x² = 2; each positive value gives two values of x, so 4 solutions (M1, A1). For k = 5: x² − 4 = 5 gives x² = 9 (x = ±3); x² − 4 = −5 gives x² = −1 (no solutions), so 2 solutions (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of k for which the equation has exactly four real solutions.
parts.working: Four solutions need x² = 4 + k and x² = 4 − k to be two different positive values, so 0 < k < 4 (M1). For k = 4 the value x² = 0 gives only 3 solutions, and for k = 0 only 2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x² − 2x − 3. The curve C′ is the reflection of C in the x-axis. Find the equation of C′.
parts.working: Reflection in the x-axis replaces y by −y: −y = x² − 2x − 3 (M1). So y = −x² + 2x + 3 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the turning point of C′.
parts.working: C has turning point (1, −4) since x² − 2x − 3 = (x − 1)² − 4 (M1). Reflecting gives (1, 4) (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why C and C′ cross the x-axis at the same points.
parts.answer: The reflection maps points on the x-axis (y = 0) to themselves, so the x-intercepts are unchanged
parts.working: A point with y = 0 maps to (x, −0) = (x, 0), so every x-intercept of C is also one of C′ (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of complete turns the wheel makes.
parts.working: One turn = 2π radians, so turns = 142.86/(2π) = 22.74. M1 divide by 2π, A1 22 (complete turns only).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has arc length 18 cm and radius 12 cm. Find the angle of the sector in radians.
parts.working: θ = arc length / r = 18/12 = 1.5 rad. B1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector.
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ = ½ × 144 × 1.5 = 108 cm². M1 for ½r²θ, A1 108.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 75° in radians, giving your answer as an exact multiple of π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express 252° in radians, giving your answer as an exact multiple of π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle of radius 9 cm has angle 40°. Find the arc length of the sector, giving your answer in terms of π.
parts.working: 40° = 2π/9 rad. Arc = rθ = 9 × 2π/9 = 2π cm. M1 for θ in radians, A1 2π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector, giving your answer in terms of π.
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ = ½ × 81 × 2π/9 = 9π cm². M1 for ½r²θ, A1 9π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The inner edge of a circular running track has radius 40 m, with centre O. An athlete runs along the inner edge through an angle of 2π/3 radians at O. Find the length of the inner edge run, in terms of π.
parts.working: Arc = rθ = 40 × 2π/3 = 80π/3 m. M1 rθ, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region enclosed by the two radii to the start and end points and the inner edge, in terms of π.
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ = ½ × 1600 × 2π/3 = 1600π/3 m². M1 ½r²θ, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pie chart is drawn as a circle of radius 6 cm. One sector represents 35% of the whole circle. Find the angle of this sector in radians, in terms of π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the arc length of this sector, in cm, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of this sector, in cm², correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius 4.5 m and arc length 3.6 m. Find the angle of the sector in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the angle of the sector in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of the sector.
parts.working: Area = ½ × 4.5² × 0.8 = 8.1 m². M1 ½r²θ, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Ferris wheel in a fair in Lahore has radius 14 m. A carriage moves 21 m along the rim of the wheel. Find the angle, in radians, through which the wheel turns about its centre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give this angle in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A round cake of radius 15 cm is cut into 8 equal slices, all from the centre. Find the angle of one slice in radians, in terms of π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the top of one slice, in terms of π.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of the curved outer edge (crust) of one slice, in terms of π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius 6 cm and angle π/6 radians. Find the perimeter of the sector, in terms of π.
parts.working: Arc = 6 × π/6 = π; perimeter = 2r + arc = 12 + π cm. M1 arc, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector, in terms of π.
parts.working: Area = ½ × 36 × π/6 = 3π cm². M1 ½r²θ, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB has centre O, radius 10 cm and angle AOB = θ radians. The perimeter of the sector is 32 cm. Find θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region bounded by the chord AB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a park in Islamabad, a curved path is the region between two arcs with the same centre O. The inner arc has radius 7 m and the outer arc has radius 9 m, and both arcs subtend an angle of 1.5 radians at O. The two straight ends of the path lie along radii. Find the area of the path.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total length of the boundary of the path.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Edging is fixed along the whole boundary at a cost of Rs 850 per metre. Find the total cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Points A and B lie on a circle with centre O and radius 8 cm. The chord AB has length 10 cm. Show that angle AOB = 1.350 radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: sin(½AOB) = 5/8 M1; AOB = 2 sin⁻¹(0.625) = 1.3503 A1 (or cosine rule: cos AOB = (64 + 64 − 100)/128)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the minor segment cut off by AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sector OAB has centre O, radius 5 cm and angle AOB = 0.9 radians. The tangent to the arc at A meets the line OB extended at T. Find the area of the region bounded by AT, TB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: AT = 5 tan 0.9 = 6.301 M1; triangle OAT = ½ × 5 × 6.301 = 15.75, sector = 11.25 M1; region = 4.50 cm² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A badge is made from an equilateral triangle ABC of side 4 cm. Each side is replaced by an arc of a circle centred at the opposite vertex (for example, arc BC has centre A and radius 4 cm). Find, in terms of π, the perimeter of the badge.
parts.working: Each arc = 4 × π/3 M1; total = 3 × 4π/3 = 4π A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the badge is 8(π − √3) cm².
parts.working: Triangle area = ½ × 16 × sin(π/3) = 4√3 B1; each segment = ½ × 16 × π/3 − 4√3 = 8π/3 − 4√3 M1 A1; total = 4√3 + 3(8π/3 − 4√3) = 8π − 8√3 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chord AB of a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm subtends an angle of 2π/3 radians at O. Find the exact area of the minor segment cut off by AB.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 36 × 2π/3 = 12π B1; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(2π/3) = 9√3 B1; segment = 12π − 9√3 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact perimeter of the minor segment.
parts.working: Arc = 6 × 2π/3 = 4π B1; AB = 2 × 6 sin(π/3) = 6√3 M1; perimeter = 4π + 6√3 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: OABC is a rhombus with sides of length 7 cm and angle AOC = 1.1 radians. An arc AC of a circle with centre O and radius 7 cm is drawn inside the rhombus. Find the area of the region inside the rhombus but outside the sector OAC, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius r cm and angle θ radians. The perimeter of the sector is equal to twice the length of its arc. Find θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The area of the sector is 36 cm². Find r and the perimeter of the sector.
parts.working: ½r² × 2 = 36 M1; r = 6 A1; perimeter = 12 + 12 = 24 cm A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circular garden in the middle of a roundabout in Lahore has centre O and radius 15 m. A straight footpath crosses the garden along a chord AB of length 24 m. Find angle AOB in radians, correct to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the smaller of the two parts into which the path divides the garden, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sector OAB has centre O, radius 9 cm and angle AOB = 1.2 radians. The point C lies on OA with OC = 5 cm. Find the area of the region R bounded by the line segments CA and CB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 B1; triangle OCB = ½ × 5 × 9 × sin 1.2 = 20.97 M1; R = 27.6 cm² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of R, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector has perimeter 20 cm and area 25 cm². Let the radius be r cm. Show that r² − 10r + 25 = 0 and hence find r.
parts.answer: r = 5 (only one possible value); arc length 10 cm, so θ = 2 rad
parts.working: Arc = 20 − 2r, area = ½r(20 − 2r) = 25 → r² − 10r + 25 = 0 → (r − 5)² = 0. M1 arc = 20 − 2r, M1 area, A1 show, A1 r = 5. Then θ = arc/r = 10/5 = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angle of the sector in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circular pond in a park has radius 10 m. A sector of the pond, with angle 3/8 of a full turn, is covered with lilies. Find the angle of this sector in radians, in terms of π.
parts.working: Full turn = 2π, so angle = (3/8) × 2π = 3π/4 rad. M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the arc length of this sector, in terms of π.
parts.working: Arc = rθ = 10 × 3π/4 = 7.5π m. M1 rθ, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circle of radius 10 cm has centre O. Two sectors of the circle have angles in the ratio 2 : 3. Find the angle of each sector in degrees.
parts.working: Angles sum to 360°: 2x + 3x = 360 → x = 72, so 144° and 216°. M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of each sector, in terms of π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius r and angle θ. The radius is increased by 20% and the angle is decreased by 20%. Find the percentage change in the arc length.
parts.working: New arc = 1.2r × 0.8θ = 0.96rθ, a decrease of 4%. M1 multiply factors, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the percentage change in the area of the sector.
parts.working: New area = ½(1.2r)²(0.8θ) = 1.152 × original area, an increase of 15.2%. M1, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A wire of length 60 cm is bent to form the complete perimeter of a sector of radius 12 cm. Find the angle of the sector in radians.
parts.working: Perimeter = 2r + rθ = 60 → 24 + 12θ = 60 → θ = 3 rad. M1 perimeter formula, M1 solve, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A flowerbed in a Karachi garden is the region between two arcs with the same centre O. The inner arc has radius 4 m and the outer arc has radius 9 m. The angle at O is 0.7 radians. Find the area of the flowerbed.
parts.working: Area = ½ × 0.7 × (81 − 16) = 22.75 m². M1 difference of sectors, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The flowerbed is bordered by a path along its whole boundary (both arcs and the two straight edges). Find the total length of the boundary.
parts.working: Boundary = 0.7 × 4 + 0.7 × 9 + 2 × (9 − 4) = 2.8 + 6.3 + 10 = 19.1 m. M1 arcs, M1 straight edges, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle of radius 6 cm has area equal to the area of a circle of radius 2 cm. Find the angle of the sector in radians, in terms of π.
parts.working: ½ × 36 × θ = π × 4 → 18θ = 4π → θ = 2π/9 rad. M1 both areas, M1 solve, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the angle in degrees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two sectors have the same arc length. The first sector has radius 6 cm and angle 1.5 radians. The second sector has radius 9 cm. Find the angle of the second sector in radians.
parts.working: Arc = 6 × 1.5 = 9 cm, so θ₂ = 9/9 = 1 rad. M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the ratio of the area of the first sector to the area of the second sector, in its simplest form.
parts.working: Area 1 = ½ × 36 × 1.5 = 27 cm², area 2 = ½ × 81 × 1 = 40.5 cm². Ratio 27 : 40.5 = 2 : 3. M1 both areas, A1 ratio, A1 simplest form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bicycle chainring has radius 9 cm and a rear sprocket has radius 4 cm. The chainring turns through 1.2 radians. Find the length of chain that passes over the chainring, in cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The chain moves round the rear sprocket without slipping. Find the angle, in radians, through which the rear sprocket turns.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the number of turns the rear sprocket makes, correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A garden sprinkler waters a sector of radius 12 m. The sector has area 40 m². Find the angle of the sector in radians, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give this angle in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two circles intersect at A and B. The first has centre P and radius 6 cm; the second has centre Q and radius 8 cm, and PQ = 10 cm. Show that angle PAQ is a right angle, and find angles APB and AQB in radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: 6² + 8² = 10² so PAQ = 90° (converse of Pythagoras) B1; cos APQ = 6/10 M1; APB = 2 cos⁻¹ 0.6 = 1.855 A1; AQB = 2 cos⁻¹ 0.8 = 1.287 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region common to both circles, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Segment in circle P: ½ × 36(1.8546 − sin 1.8546) = 16.10 M1 A1; segment in circle Q: ½ × 64(1.2870 − sin 1.2870) = 10.46 M1; total = 26.6 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer in Sindh uses 24 m of fencing to enclose a sector-shaped pen of radius r m and angle θ radians. The fencing goes along both radii and the arc. Show that the area A m² of the pen is given by A = 12r − r².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum area of the pen and the value of θ for which it occurs.
parts.answer: Maximum area 36 m² when r = 6 and θ = 2
parts.working: dA/dr = 12 − 2r = 0 (or complete the square: 36 − (r − 6)²) M1; r = 6, A = 36 A1; θ = (24 − 12)/6 = 2 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three pipes, each with a circular cross-section of radius 5 cm, are tied together so that each pipe touches the other two. Find the exact area of the cross-section of the gap enclosed between the three pipes.
parts.working: Centres form an equilateral triangle of side 10 B1; triangle area = ½ × 100 × sin(π/3) = 25√3 M1; three sectors of angle π/3: 3 × ½ × 25 × π/3 = 25π/2 M1; gap = 25√3 − 25π/2 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence give this area correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB has centre O, radius 12 cm and angle AOB = π/3. A circle with centre C and radius r cm lies inside the sector and touches OA, OB and the arc AB. Show that OC = 2r and hence find r.
parts.working: C lies on the bisector of angle AOB, so the angle between OC and OA is π/6 B1; r = OC sin(π/6) so OC = 2r M1 A1; OC + r = 12 ⇒ 3r = 12, r = 4 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of π, the area of the part of the sector that lies outside the circle.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 144 × π/3 = 24π; circle = 16π M1; 24π − 16π = 8π A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC = 10 cm and angle BAC = 0.8 radians. An arc BC is drawn with centre A and radius 10 cm. A semicircle is drawn on BC as diameter, on the side of BC away from A. Find the length of BC, correct to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region inside the semicircle but outside the sector ABC, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Semicircle = ½π(3.894)² = 23.82 M1 A1; segment of sector = ½ × 100(0.8 − sin 0.8) = 4.132 M1 A1; region = 23.82 − 4.13 = 19.7 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: ABCD is a square of side 8 cm. Two quarter circles of radius 8 cm are drawn inside the square, one with centre A passing through B and D, and one with centre C passing through B and D. Find, in terms of π, the perimeter of the leaf-shaped region that lies inside both quarter circles.
parts.working: Each arc = 8 × π/2 = 4π M1; perimeter = 8π A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the leaf-shaped region is 32(π − 2) cm².
parts.working: Half the leaf = quarter circle − triangle ABD = 16π − 32 M1 A1; leaf = 2(16π − 32) = 32π − 64 = 32(π − 2) A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage of the square that lies outside the leaf, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a rice mill, a tight belt passes around two pulleys with radii 9 cm and 4 cm. The centres of the pulleys are 13 cm apart. The straight parts of the belt are common external tangents to the two circles. Show that each straight part has length 12 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let α = sin⁻¹(5/13). Explain why the belt is in contact with the larger pulley over an angle of (π + 2α) radians, and find α correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: Radii to the tangent points are perpendicular to the straight parts, which make angle α with the line of centres where sin α = 5/13 M1; so the contact angle on the larger pulley is π + 2α (and on the smaller π − 2α) A1; α = 0.3948 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the total length of the belt, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A street vendor in Karachi makes paper cones for roasted chana. Each cone is made by joining the two straight edges of a sector of paper of radius 15 cm and angle θ radians, without overlap. The circular rim of the cone has radius 6 cm. Find θ, giving your answer as an exact multiple of π.
parts.working: Arc length = circumference of rim: 15θ = 2π × 6 M1; θ = 12π/15 = 4π/5 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of π, the area of paper used for each cone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of chana a full cone can hold, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circle has centre O and radius 5 cm. A point T is 13 cm from O, and the tangents from T touch the circle at A and B. Show that angle AOB = 2.352 radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: OA ⟂ TA, so cos AOT = 5/13 M1; AOB = 2 cos⁻¹(5/13) = 2.3520 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region bounded by TA, TB and the minor arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A window in a Mughal-style building is a rectangle 1.2 m wide and 1.5 m tall, topped by a pointed arch. The arch is formed by two arcs, each of radius 1.2 m. One arc has its centre at the top left corner of the rectangle and the other at the top right corner; the arcs meet at the top point P of the window. Explain why the centres of the arcs and P form an equilateral triangle, and show that the area of the arch region above the rectangle is (0.48π − 0.36√3) m².
parts.working: Each centre is 1.2 m from P and the centres are 1.2 m apart, so all sides are 1.2 m B1; each arc subtends π/3 at its centre B1; arch = 2 × ½ × 1.44 × π/3 − ½ × 1.44 × sin(π/3) M1; = 0.48π − 0.36√3 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total area of the window, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the perimeter of the window, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector has radius r and angle θ radians. Its area is equal to its perimeter. Show that θ = 4/(r − 2).
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ and perimeter = 2r + rθ. Setting equal: ½r²θ = 2r + rθ. Divide by r: ½rθ = 2 + θ, so θ(½r − 1) = 2, so θ = 4/(r − 2). M1 both formulae, M1 equate, M1 divide by r, A1 show.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that θ = 1 radian, find the radius and the common value of the area and perimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chord AB of a circle with centre O and radius 13 cm is at a distance 5 cm from O. The angle AOB is θ radians. Show that θ = 2.352, correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: The perpendicular from O bisects the chord, so cos(θ/2) = 5/13. Then θ/2 = arccos(5/13) = 1.1760 and θ = 2.3520 = 2.352. M1 cos(θ/2) = 5/13, M1 inverse cosine and double, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the minor segment cut off by the chord AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector has radius r cm and area 50 cm². Show that its perimeter P cm satisfies P = 2r + 100/r.
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ = 50 → θ = 100/r². Perimeter = 2r + rθ = 2r + 100/r. M1 θ in terms of r, M1 substitute, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the minimum possible perimeter of the sector and the angle of the sector at this minimum. Give the perimeter in exact form.
parts.answer: minimum perimeter 20√2 cm, when r = √50 and θ = 2 rad
parts.working: dP/dr = 2 − 100/r² = 0 → r² = 50, r = 5√2. P = 2(5√2) + 100/(5√2) = 10√2 + 10√2 = 20√2 cm. θ = 100/50 = 2 rad. M1 differentiate, M1 solve, M1 check min, A1 perimeter, A1 angle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The points P(5, 12) and Q(12, 5) lie on the circle with centre the origin O and radius 13. Show that angle POQ = 0.781 radians, correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: OP · OQ = 60 + 60 = 120. cos POQ = 120/(13 × 13) = 120/169, so POQ = arccos(0.7101) = 0.7812 rad. M1 dot product, M1 cos formula, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the minor sector OPQ, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the perimeter of the minor sector OPQ, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A straight road follows a circular bend of radius 400 m and subtends an angle of 0.3 radians at the centre. Find the length of the road along the bend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A straight road (chord) would join the two ends of the bend. Find the length of this chord, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Chord = 2 × 400 × sin(0.15) = 119.55 m. M1 chord formula, A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the difference between the two lengths, correct to 2 decimal places. Show that the approximation Rθ³/24 gives the same result to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Difference = 120 − 119.55 = 0.45 m. Rθ³/24 = 400 × 0.027/24 = 0.45 m. M1 difference, M1 approximation, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB of a circle with radius 1 unit and angle θ radians has area equal to twice the area of the triangle OAB. Show that θ = 2 sin θ.
parts.working: Sector = ½θ, triangle = ½ sin θ. ½θ = 2 × ½ sin θ, so θ = 2 sin θ. M1 sector area, M1 triangle area, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by a sign change that the equation has a root between 1.5 and 2.2, and find the root correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: f(θ) = θ − 2 sin θ; f(1.5) = −0.495 < 0 and f(2.2) = 0.583 > 0 so there is a root. Iterating (or Newton-Raphson) gives θ = 1.895 rad. M1 sign change, M1 method, A1 1.895, A1 correct to 3 dp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sector A has radius 5 cm and angle 2 radians. Sector B has radius r cm and angle 1.5 radians. The two sectors have the same perimeter. Find r, in exact form.
parts.working: Perimeter A = 10 + 10 = 20. Perimeter B = 2r + 1.5r = 3.5r = 20, so r = 40/7. M1 both perimeters, M1 equate, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of each sector, correct to 3 significant figures, and state which sector has the larger area.
parts.answer: Sector A: 25.0 cm²; sector B: 24.5 cm²; sector A is larger

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coin of radius 1 cm rolls, without slipping, around the outside of a fixed coin of radius 3 cm. The centre of the rolling coin moves round a circle. Find the distance travelled by the centre of the rolling coin in one complete circuit, in terms of π.
parts.working: The centre moves on a circle of radius 3 + 1 = 4 cm, so distance = 2π × 4 = 8π cm. M1, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rolling coin makes one complete circuit of the fixed coin. Find the number of complete turns the rolling coin makes about its own centre during this circuit. Explain your answer briefly.
parts.working: Contact arc on the fixed coin = 2π × 3 = 6π, so the coin turns 6π/(2π × 1) = 3 times relative to its own arm, while the arm carrying its centre round once adds one more turn. Total 3 + 1 = 4. M1 contact arc, M1 turns relative to arm, M1 extra turn from circuit, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circle has centre O and radius 10 cm. A chord AB subtends angle θ radians at O, and the minor segment cut off by AB has area equal to one quarter of the area of the circle. Show that θ − sin θ = π/2.
parts.working: Segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 50(θ − sin θ). Quarter of circle = 25π. So 50(θ − sin θ) = 25π, giving θ − sin θ = π/2. M1 segment formula, M1 quarter circle, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that θ lies between 2.3 and 2.4, and hence find θ correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: g(θ) = θ − sin θ − π/2. g(2.3) = −0.0165 < 0, g(2.4) = 0.1537 > 0 so root in (2.3, 2.4). Iterating gives θ = 2.310. M1 sign change, M1 method, A1 value, A1 3 s.f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle of radius r cm and angle θ radians has area numerically equal to the square of its arc length. Show that θ = 1/2.
parts.working: Area = ½r²θ and arc = rθ. ½r²θ = (rθ)² = r²θ². Divide by r²θ (non-zero): ½ = θ. M1 both expressions, M1 equate, M1 divide, A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The square of side 3 cm has the same area as this sector. Find r, and the arc length of the sector.
parts.working: Area of sector = 9 cm² = ½r²(½) → r² = 36, r = 6. Arc = 6 × ½ = 3 cm. M1, M1, A1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution B(10, 0.2). Find P(X = 3).

practice.stem: X ~ B(5, p), where p is a constant, and P(X = 1) = 0.4096.

parts.text: Truck A of mass 5000 kg moving at 4 m s⁻¹ along a straight horizontal track collides with truck B of mass 3000 kg moving at 1 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. After the collision B moves at 3.5 m s⁻¹. Find the speed of A after the collision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After the collision each truck experiences a resistance equal to 0.02 of its weight. Find the distance between the trucks when both have come to rest, and explain why they do not collide again. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
parts.answer: 15 m; A is always slower than B
parts.working:
M1 deceleration 0.02g = 0.2 m s⁻² for both
M1 A: 2.5²/0.4 = 15.625 m; B: 3.5²/0.4 = 30.625 m
A1 15 m
B1 equal decelerations, A starts slower, so A's speed is always less than B's

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle A of mass 3 kg is projected with speed 10 m s⁻¹ along a rough horizontal surface, coefficient of friction 0.4. After travelling 4.5 m it hits a stationary particle B of mass 2 kg and they coalesce. Find the speed of A just before the collision and the speed of the combined particle. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
parts.working:
M1 deceleration 4 m s⁻², v² = 100 − 36
A1 v = 8
M1 3 × 8 = 5V
A1 V = 4.8

parts.label: b
parts.text: The coefficient of friction between the combined particle and the surface is also 0.4. Find the total distance moved by A from projection until it comes to rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle P of mass 0.5 kg moving at 6 m s⁻¹ on a smooth horizontal floor collides with a stationary particle Q of mass 0.25 kg at the foot of a rough plane inclined at angle α, where sin α = 0.28 and cos α = 0.96. The particles coalesce and move up a line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction between the combined particle and the plane is 0.3. Find the deceleration of the combined particle up the plane. Take g = 10 m s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance it travels up the plane, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
M1 v = 4 m s⁻¹ after collision, s = 4²/(2 × 5.68)
A1 1.41 m

parts.label: c

parts.working:
M1 compare component of weight 0.75g sin α = 2.1 N with maximum friction 2.16 N
A1 2.1 < 2.16, so it remains at rest

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle A, of mass 2 kg, is projected along a rough horizontal surface with speed u m s⁻¹ towards particle B, of mass 1 kg, which is at rest 10 m ahead of A. The coefficient of friction between each particle and the surface is 0.1. A collides with B and they coalesce. The combined particle then travels 3 m along the surface before coming to rest. Find u.
parts.working: M1 deceleration of combined particle = μg = 1 m s⁻²; M1 V² = 2 × 1 × 3 = 6; M1 2v₁ = 3V so v₁² = 1.5² × 6 = 13.5 (v₁ = speed of A just before the collision); M1 deceleration of A before collision = μg = 1 m s⁻², so u² = v₁² + 2 × 1 × 10; A1 u² = 33.5, u = 5.79 m s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle A of mass 0.3 kg moving at 5 m s⁻¹ on a smooth horizontal surface collides with a stationary particle B of mass 0.2 kg. After the collision A moves in its original direction with speed 1.4 m s⁻¹. Find the speed of B after the collision.
parts.working:
M1 momentum before = momentum after
A1 0.3 × 5 = 0.3 × 1.4 + 0.2v
A1 v = 5.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: A railway wagon of mass 12 000 kg moving at 3 m s⁻¹ on a straight horizontal track runs into a stationary wagon of mass 8000 kg. The wagons couple together. Find their common speed immediately after the collision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particles P and Q, of masses 2 kg and 3 kg, move towards each other along a straight line on a smooth horizontal floor with speeds 6 m s⁻¹ and 2 m s⁻¹ respectively. They collide and coalesce. Find the speed and direction of the combined particle after the collision.
parts.answer: 1.2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction of P
parts.working:
M1 2 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 5v (signs for opposite directions)
A1 v = 1.2
A1 direction: that in which P was moving

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ali, of mass 70 kg, and Sara, of mass 50 kg, stand at rest facing each other on smooth ice. They push each other apart and Sara moves off with speed 2.1 m s⁻¹. Find Ali's speed and state the direction of his motion.
parts.working:
M1 total momentum zero: 70v = 50 × 2.1
A1 v = 1.5
B1 opposite direction to Sara

parts.label: a
parts.text: Trolley A, of mass 15 kg, moves at 2 m s⁻¹ along a smooth horizontal floor and hits trolley B, of mass 25 kg, which is at rest. The trolleys couple together on impact. Find their common speed immediately after the collision.
parts.working: M1 momentum before = 15 × 2 = 30; M1 momentum after = (15 + 25)v = 40v; A1 v = 0.75 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: A snooker ball P of mass 0.16 kg moves at 3 m s⁻¹ along a smooth horizontal table and hits an identical ball Q, which is at rest. After the impact P is brought to rest. Find the speed of Q immediately after the impact.
parts.working: M1 0.16 × 3 = 0.16 × v (equal masses, P at rest after); A1 v = 3, so Q moves off at 3 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the collision is elastic, that is, kinetic energy is the same before and after the impact.
parts.answer: KE before = ½ × 0.16 × 3² = 0.72 J; KE after = ½ × 0.16 × 3² = 0.72 J (P at rest, Q at 3 m s⁻¹); the two are equal, so KE is conserved.
parts.working: B1 KE before = 0.72 J; B1 KE after = 0.72 J and the statement that KE is conserved

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bumper car A, of mass 180 kg, moving at 2.5 m s⁻¹, hits bumper car B, of mass 120 kg, which is at rest. The two cars stick together. (a) Find their common speed immediately after the impact. (b) Find the impulse that acts on car B during the impact.
parts.working: (a) M1 180 × 2.5 = (180 + 120)v; A1 v = 1.5 m s⁻¹. (b) M1 impulse = change in momentum of B = 120 × 1.5; A1 180 N s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle P of mass 0.4 kg moving at 7 m s⁻¹ collides directly with particle Q of mass 0.6 kg moving at 2 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. After the collision Q moves at 3 m s⁻¹, its direction of motion having been reversed. Find the speed of P after the collision and state its direction.
parts.working:
M1 0.4 × 7 − 0.6 × 2 = 0.4v + 0.6 × 3
A1 1.6 = 0.4v + 1.8
A1 v = −0.5
A1 P moves at 0.5 m s⁻¹ with its direction reversed

parts.text: Three particles A, B and C, of masses 0.5 kg, 0.25 kg and 0.75 kg, lie at rest in that order in a straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. parts.label: b

parts.answer: A moves at 2 m s⁻¹, faster than the combined particle (1 m s⁻¹), in the same direction, so A catches it.
parts.working: B1 compares 2 > 1 with the same direction
